profiles.name: DeepSeek Harness (dsh) — deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness
profiles.one_liner: MIT-licensed TypeScript agent runtime from DeepSeek (developer preview since 2026-08-13) where the model adapter, tools, sandbox, storage and even the agent loop are swappable Cordis plugins over an append-only session log; ships as a `dsh` CLI/Web UI/desktop app with a Python SDK, and is what DeepSeek uses (in "minimal mode") to report its V4 code-agent benchmarks.

dimensions.identity: Maintained by DeepSeek (GitHub org deepseek-ai); the repo was created 2026-08-13 and launched that day as "Harness v0.1" developer preview alongside DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, under the MIT license (THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md for vendored code). It is TypeScript on Node ^22.19 (pnpm workspace, ESM, ~70+ package groups under packages/) built on DeepSeek's own Cordis plugin kernel (@deepseek-ai/cordis, arXiv 2608.25512). Distribution: npm CLI `npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web` (Web UI on 127.0.0.1:3080), `dsh --profile headless|sdk|sdk-minimal|acp`, an Electron desktop app, and a Python SDK `deepseek-harness-sdk` whose `DeepSeekHarness(...).run()` drives a bundled `dsh --profile sdk-minimal` over JSON-RPC stdio. Popularity: the GitHub API on 2026-09-24 reported 236,384 stars, 28,422 forks and 20k commits; secondary sources say 33k stars within hours (New Stack) and 95,386 in 48 hours (Winder, ArceApps). Release cadence is fast (v0.1.5-rc.1 on Sep 10 through v0.1.7-rc.2 on Sep 24, no CHANGELOG.md, notes only on the Releases page); the README warns "THERE WILL BE COMPATIBILITY-BREAKING CHANGES", New Stack says external PRs are not accepted and Composio notes issues are disabled (Discussions/Discord only).
dimensions.loop: `packages/core/agent-loop` (`ctx.agentLoop`) is a ReAct-style single loop: a turn holds zero or more steps, each one model request plus its tool calls, in the documented sequence turn/start → agent/pre-step → step/start → agent/request → llm/stream → assistant/message → tool/call → tools/execute → tool/result → step/end → turn/end, all appended to the session log. A turn ends when the model returns no tool calls, on cooperative `agent.cancel()` (already-streamed text is kept), on model/tool dispatch failure, or when the serial `agent/turn-stopping` extension point ends it; the Claude-Code-compatible `Stop` hook can "force another step with a reason". The package README says there are no inherent step limits and "budgeting requires external policy enforcement"; `maxParallelToolCalls` defaults to 10, with exclusive tools acting as ordering barriers, and retries reuse the rendered assembly without re-running agent/pre-step. Because the loop is itself a plugin it can be replaced outright. Shipped alternatives: Code Mode / PTC, where the model writes one TypeScript program that calls tools as async functions via `run_code` (fresh Node process per run, stateless, empty env); a `ralph` tool that runs fresh-agent iteration loops toward an objective; a `workflow` tool that orchestrates subagents from JavaScript; and `/plan` plan mode, which guides rather than restricts (every tool stays available) and ends with `exit_plan_mode` presenting the plan for approval.
dimensions.tools: A tool is a TypeScript object registered with `ctx.tools.register(defineTool({ name, description, parameters, output: { schema, render }, execute }))`; parameters use a small DSL (string/number/integer/boolean/null/array/object/json/oneOf) compiled to JSON Schema for the wire, which is shared with subagents and MCP, and `execute` returns canonical JSON that `output.render` turns into model-facing content blocks. Execution runs a fixed pipeline: `tools/pre-execute` (extensible allow/deny/ask waterfall) → monotonic `ctx.tools.guard()` guards → `tools/execute` → `tools/post-execute` (inspect/replace) → definition-owned `finalizeContent` → observe-only `tools/result`; invalid input, denials and timeouts become structured errors without ending the turn, and `ctx.tools.restrict(filter)` applies per-agent allow/deny masks. The built-in catalog (docs/tool-catalog.md) is large: `bash`/`pwsh` (+ persistent variants), `str_replace_editor`, `read`/`write`/`edit`/`read_image`, `glob`/`grep` (ripgrep), `web_search`/`web_fetch`, `subagent`, `list_subagent_models`, `send_message`/`interrupt_agent`/`list_agents`, `skill`, `todo_write`, `exit_plan_mode`, `ask_user_question`, `run_code`, `cordis_inspect_list/query`, six `terminal_*` PTY tools, `job_*`, `create/get/update_goal`, `schedule_*`, `lsp`, `ralph`, `workflow`, `present`, `plugin_manager`, three MCP resource tools, five `session_*` history-query tools, and experimental `stagehand_*` browser and agent-team tools; the Minimal preset exposes only `bash` and `str_replace_editor`. Result size is handled by policy plugins rather than a hard-coded cut: the `spill` family stores oversized text outside context and returns a preview plus locator (opt-in via `maxInlineTokens`, keeps the original on storage failure), `compaction-tool-result-pruner` trims old outputs, v0.1.7 notes add "unified token budgeting for tool outputs (text/images)", and PTC output has a worker hard cap. Exact bash byte/timeout limits are not documented in the pages I read.
dimensions.extensibility: Everything is a Cordis plugin: a module exporting `name`, optional `inject = ['tools','llm']`, `apply(ctx, config)` and a Schemastery `Config` schema; registrations go through `ctx.effect()` so unloading reverses side effects, and misconfiguration fails at load time. docs/architecture.md lists the pluggable seams: `ctx.llm` (providers), `ctx.tools`, `ctx.fs` policy, `ctx.sandbox`, `ctx.shell`/`ctx.terminals`, `ctx.agentLoop`, `ctx.commands` (slash commands with no model turn), `ctx.jobs`, `ctx.webhookRuntime`, the `SessionPersistence` storage interface, agent presets (`ctx.agentPresets`) and personas, system-prompt sections, skills, and the Web UI itself. Composition is declarative: named profiles under `$DSH_HOME/profiles/<name>` stack bundles (`dsh-base`, `dsh-web-app`, `dsh-headless`, `sdk-app`, `sdk-minimal`, `acp-app`) declared in package.json's `"dsh"` field, with patches applied profile → `cordis.patch.yml` → home-level → CLI `--patch`, inspectable via `--dump-config` and `--dump-config-schema`. A third party develops locally with `pnpm dsh web --patch ./cordis.yml` (an `insert:` entry pointing at the .ts file), then publishes an npm package named `dsh-<name>` with `"dsh": { "bundle": { "patch": "./cordis.patch.yml" } }`, tags the repo `dsh-plugin`, and users install with `dsh plugin --profile <name> add <pkg | github:user/repo | ./x.tgz>`; since v0.1.6 a Plugin Manager page and `plugin_manager` tool install/unload at runtime. Four shipped agent presets (Standard, Code/PTC, Minimal, Creator, the last adding `cordis_inspect_*` runtime inspection) are themselves plugin bundles. Plugins run in the harness process, which ArceApps flags as an isolation weakness versus Codex's folder-based plugins.
dimensions.context: Context is a projection of the append-only session log (`deriveMessages()`; the invariant "model-visible means logged"), stored as JSONL with optional Zstandard, migration chain v0→v4, and fork/resume/replay. Compaction (`compaction-basic`) auto-condenses when tokens exceed floor(min(W×0.8, W−O−65536)) (`thresholdRatio` 0.8, `headroomTokens` 65536), keeps the newest 16% verbatim (`retainRatio`/`retainTokens`), replaces the oldest span with one `<compacted-summary>` message (intent, files, errors, pending work, next steps), never condenses the system prompt, can use a separate `summarizationProvider/Model`, reuses the provider's warm KV cache, and is also available as `/compact`; tool-result pruning, image offload and spill complement it. Memory files: `agent-instructions` discovers `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` plus `.local.md` overlays from `$DSH_HOME/AGENTS.md` (~/.dsh) then project root (`.git` marker) down to cwd, injects them as one durable user-role message in `<\system-reminder>` framing under a required `maxBytes` budget, and refreshes only after first-party read/write/edit calls (no watcher); skills are SKILL.md files with frontmatter found in `.dsh/skills`, `.agents/skills` and `~/.dsh/skills`. KV-cache friendliness is explicit: the system-prompt assembler canonicalizes section and tool order and leaves nodes untouched when unchanged, `systemPromptUpdate: 'in-history'` appends prompt changes rather than invalidating the prefix, and the pi-ai adapter preserves cache prefixes across config changes; the 97–99.6% hit-rate figure comes from Masood's article, not the repo. Persistent cross-session memory is thin: `ctx.goals` is same-session only, `session_*` tools can search prior sessions, and the MCP docs point to a third-party memory-integration guide, but no native memory store is documented.
dimensions.permissions: Permissions are two knobs bundled into user-facing presets (docs/subsystems/permission-presets.md): sandbox mode (`sandbox/mode`: `read-only` is the sandbox-policy default, `workspace-write`, `danger-full-access`) and approval policy (`approval/policy`: `ask` default, `never`); the shipped presets are `workspace-write`+`ask` and `danger-full-access`+`never`, with derived `custom` and `auto` (Auto review), and every switch is a durable `permission/preset` event. The sandbox (docs/subsystems/sandbox.md) confines file effects only — "network and process visibility are outside this vocabulary" — using bwrap then Landlock on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS and a restricted-token/ACL backend on Windows that is explicitly "partial" (hard links, unconfined reads); policy resolves per call, and it is fail-closed: with no usable backend `ctx.sandbox.confine()` rejects with `SandboxUnavailableError`, "silent unconfined passthrough is never legal". Approval is equally fail-closed: outcomes are `allowed-once` (the only grant), `rejected`, `cancelled`, `unavailable`; a missing or throwing answerer yields `unavailable`, `never` is enforced before any answerer, and `approval/asked`/`approval/decided` are log-only audit events; a sandbox denial offers a one-time escalation retry. Dangerous shell commands are not pattern-matched: `bash` runs under sandbox confinement with denials reported as facts, and `tools/pre-execute` listeners or a PreToolUse hook can deny or ask; no Claude-Code-style allow/deny command rules are documented. SAFETY.md states these controls "do not guarantee isolation or prevent damage", and DataCamp's Windows run saw sandbox failure plus three `danger-full-access` prompts.
dimensions.hooks: Two layers exist. Internally, typed Cordis events are the hook system: waterfalls that must call `next()` — `agent/pre-step`, `agent/request`, `llm/stream`, `tools/pre-execute` (allow/deny/ask), `tools/execute`, `tools/post-execute` (inspect/replace) — plus observe-only `tools/result`, the serial `agent/turn-stopping`, `fs/*` policy events, and monotonic `ctx.tools.guard()` guards; the `guard` family ships `repeat-tool-reminder` (nags on identical repeated calls) and `timeout-policy`. Externally, `hooks-claude-code` and `hooks-codex` run an existing `hooks.json` (via `configPath`) and support 7 of Claude Code's 30 events: SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SubagentStart (in-process only) and SubagentStop (observe only). These can veto: the README says they "can block prompts or tool calls with model-visible messages", PreToolUse can ask for approval, PostToolUse can block the result with feedback, and Stop can force another step; the other 23 events (PermissionRequest, SessionEnd, etc.) are ignored. Exit-code semantics for shell hooks are not documented. Webhooks (`ctx.webhookRuntime`) and scheduled tasks (`schedule_*`, v0.1.7-rc.2) are separate trigger surfaces.
dimensions.subagents: The model calls a `subagent` tool (name configurable) with a task, optional `run_in_background`, and `provider`/`model`/`reasoning_effort` when model selection is enabled (`list_subagent_models` lists routes). Backends: `spawn` (fresh in-process child that sees none of the parent conversation), `fork` (child seeded from the parent's completed history but not the in-flight turn, via `ctx.agents.create({ sessionId, seed, meta: { parentSession, seedLength } })`), and out-of-process `acp`, `codex`, `claude-code` and `dsh-sdk` — so dsh can drive Claude Code or Codex as children. Inheritance is explicit: tools are masked with `toolFilter`, each child can get its own persona, model comes from `agentOptions`, and sandbox/approval resolve per session and per call. The only documented limit is `maxDepth` (Host setting `subagent.maxDepth`, initially 1; 0 forbids delegation); token and concurrency budgets are not documented. Foreground calls return the child's final text (errors map stop reasons to headlines with partial text); background calls return `started background subagent job <id>` or, for continuable children, `started subagent <childId>` controllable via `send_message`/`interrupt_agent`/`list_agents`; children stay visible to the parent and scheduling is logged. Experimental Agent Teams (`ctx.agentTeams`, disabled in dsh-base) add a Lead session, `spawnTeammate()`, a durable mailbox and a revisioned task DAG.
dimensions.providers: The `ctx.llm` seam has two adapters: `llm-deepseek` (native, now "Messages protocol exclusively", with account and API-key plugins; credentials live in `$DSH_HOME/.credentials.yaml`) and `llm-pi-ai`, whose catalog covers OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepSeek, while docs/user/guide/providers.md also lists ids `anthropic`, `openai`, `moonshotai` (Kimi) and `zai` (GLM). Wire protocols are `openai-completions`, `openai-responses` and `anthropic-messages`; a provider entry carries `apiKeyEnv`, `baseURL`, `models`, `retryPolicy`, `reasoningEfforts`, `inputModalities`, `defaultContextWindow` and a `compat` block (`supportsDeveloperRole`, `maxTokensField`) for awkward gateways. Local models (Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp) are added as a "Custom model API" provider with base URL plus protocol and optional `GET /models` discovery, one provider per protocol. The pi-ai README says Bedrock, Vertex, Azure and Codex "authenticate through flows a profile cannot completely describe" and are reachable only through native catalog providers, so New Stack's and DataCamp's "supports AWS Bedrock/Azure/Google" is an overstatement of what a profile can configure. Weak-model handling is not documented (no tool-call repair or prompt simplification described; compaction can use a separate `summarizationModel`), and Composio notes local models are "not out of the box"; `llm-retry` and `token-meter` plugins round out the group.
dimensions.mcp: dsh is an MCP client (`packages/mcp/mcp-client`, docs/subsystems/mcp.md): transports are stdio (child process with environment scrubbing) and streamable-http (URL plus headers); each server needs a `serverName` (1–32 chars) and its tools surface as `mcp__<server>__<tool>` so name clashes coexist; server instructions are added to the system prompt as a scoped, server-attributed section. `mcp-resources` adds `list_mcp_resources`, `read_mcp_resource` and `list_mcp_resource_templates` (URI templates since v0.1.6); images persist when the model accepts them, other media becomes diagnostic text; unsupported are prompt templates, elicitation, task-based execution and resource subscriptions, and discovery uses the SDK's 60 s timeout. Whether dsh can expose itself as an MCP server is not documented. Beyond MCP, `dsh --profile acp` serves the Agent Client Protocol over stdio (create/list/resume/close sessions, attach MCP servers, text and image prompts, answer permission prompts, cancel), `subagent-acp` is the matching client, and `--profile sdk` serves JSON-RPC stdio for the Python SDK. A2A is not documented.
dimensions.evals: The repo's own BENCHMARK.md is a two-line stub: install the Python SDK and run the `jsonrpc-agent` minimal variant with separate workspaces and session IDs per task; the `benchmarks/` directory holds vitest runtime-performance gates (session-open, conversation-fold, terminal-io, agent-continuation, long-session-browser) on synthetic inputs, not model evals. DeepSeek's V4-Pro-0813 model card states code-agent scores were measured "with the minimal mode of DeepSeek Harness" at `max` reasoning, temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95: DeepSWE 62.7, Toolathlon-Verified 74.1, DSBench-FullStack 71.1, DSBench-Hard 67.2 (V4-Flash 54.4/70.3/68.7/59.6), with a caveat that scores may differ under other scaffolds; VentureBeat and datanorth add Terminal-Bench 2.1 = 87.9. The project publishes no harness-vs-model or preset (Minimal vs Standard) ablation. Third parties: DataCamp's same-model (Claude Sonnet 5) test produced a byte-identical patch in 55.0 s for Claude Code vs 125.4 s for dsh on Windows; Composio's 30 hard tasks on V4 Pro gave dsh 20/30 vs Claude Code 19/30 at 88.6k vs 649.9k tokens per task and $0.028 vs $0.074 per success; ArceApps measured ~95k input tokens per task vs 12–22k for OpenCode/Claude Code; dshbase cites an 8-harness V4-Flash run where Claude Code cost ~$0.195 per success vs ~$0.028 for the cheapest.
dimensions.distinctive: Three ideas stand out. First, the loop, storage, sandbox and model adapter are all replaceable plugins on Cordis with reversible effects and declarative profile/patch layering, so you compose a harness rather than configure one, and presets like Minimal (two tools) or Code Mode (`run_code`) are just different plugin trees. Second, "model-visible means logged": the append-only session log is the source of truth from which context is derived, giving fork, replay, keyless deterministic replay tests, and durable `sandbox/mode`, `approval/*` and `permission/preset` events that survive restart. Third, fail-closed safety as first-class vocabulary (`SandboxUnavailableError`, the `unavailable` approval outcome, one-time escalation) plus interop bridges that run Claude Code or Codex as subagents and reuse their `hooks.json`. The loudest criticisms: developer-preview churn with no security audit, PRs not accepted and issues disabled; partial Windows sandboxing (DataCamp's three approval prompts); heavy token use, including a duplicate AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md injection bug worth ~30k tokens (ArceApps); a steep profile/bundle/patch learning curve and slower startup; a raw plugin ecosystem (dshbase: 101 community plugins with install failures; ArceApps: 316 listed, 41 validated); in-process plugins and `cordis_*` self-modification complicating assurance (Composio); and the model card's own admission that its scores are harness-sensitive, measured in Minimal mode rather than the Standard preset users run. Masood additionally cites a Tencent Zhuque study of 25.5% indirect prompt-injection success, from a member-only article I could only partly read.

profiles.name: Claude Code (Anthropic)
profiles.one_liner: Anthropic's closed-source, Claude-only agentic coding harness: one tool-calling loop wrapped in a deep file-based extension layer (CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, subagents, MCP, plugins, workflows), classifier-gated permissions, OS-level sandboxing and cache-first context management, shipped as CLI, IDE extensions, desktop, web and an Agent SDK.

dimensions.identity: Maintained by Anthropic PBC; research preview 24 Feb 2025 alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet, general availability 22 May 2025 with Claude 4 (scriptbyai timeline). LICENSE.md in the GitHub repo reads '© Anthropic PBC. All rights reserved. Use is subject to Anthropic's Commercial Terms of Service' — proprietary, and the anthropics/claude-code repo is an issue tracker, docs and devcontainer, not source. It ships as a native binary (README badge Node.js 18+; the `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` path is now marked deprecated in favour of `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash`, `brew install --cask claude-code`, `winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode`); Winder.ai reports the implementation is TypeScript, which the official docs do not state. Distribution: terminal CLI, VS Code/Cursor and JetBrains extensions, a desktop app, the web at claude.ai/code, GitHub Actions/GitLab CI, Slack, and the Agent SDK (`claude_agent_sdk` for Python, `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` for TypeScript, both bundling the binary). Popularity signal: 148.1k GitHub stars (Sept 2026); latest CLI version in CHANGELOG.md is 2.1.283.
dimensions.loop: A single ReAct-style loop: the model receives the system prompt, tool definitions, history and prompt, emits text and/or tool calls, the harness executes them (read-only tools like Read/Glob/Grep run concurrently, state-mutating Edit/Write/Bash run sequentially), appends the results as a user message and repeats; docs describe this as gather context → act → verify with no separate planner/executor. A turn is one round trip and the loop ends when a response contains no tool calls (stop_reason `end_turn`), yielding a `ResultMessage` with cost, usage and session_id in the SDK. Plan mode is a permission mode, not a different loop: it keeps all tools loaded and uses `EnterPlanMode`/`ExitPlanMode` tools plus an appended system message to preserve the cache prefix. There is no step cap by default in interactive use; `--max-turns` (counts tool-use turns only) and `--max-budget-usd` apply in `-p`/SDK runs and return `error_max_turns`/`error_max_budget_usd`, with the budget covering subagent spend (v2.1.217+); subagents can carry `maxTurns` in frontmatter. A `Stop` hook can refuse the end of a turn (exit 2 or `continue: true`), forcing another cycle. Dynamic workflows are the one code-as-orchestration variant: Claude writes a JavaScript script using `agent()`, `parallel()`, `pipeline()` that a runtime executes outside the conversation.
dimensions.tools: Built-in tools are fixed inside the closed binary; there is no user decorator or manifest for adding a native tool, only MCP servers or the Agent SDK's in-process 'SDK MCP server' custom tool handlers (where an MCP `readOnlyHint` annotation is what permits parallel execution). The built-in set (tools-reference) is Bash, PowerShell, Read, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit, Glob, Grep (ripgrep), LSP, WebFetch, WebSearch, Agent, Skill, ToolSearch, AskUserQuestion, EnterPlanMode/ExitPlanMode, EnterWorktree/ExitWorktree, Monitor, TaskCreate/TaskGet/TaskList/TaskUpdate/TaskStop, TodoWrite (disabled when task tools exist), SendMessage, ListAgents, Workflow, Artifact, CronCreate/CronList/CronDelete, ScheduleWakeup, EndConversation, plus MCP tools named `mcp__<server>__<tool>`. Truncation: Bash keeps ~30KB inline by default (configurable up to 128KB), larger output is saved to a file with 64 MiB truncation and a 5 GB kill limit; Read is ~30KB inline with pagination; Glob is capped at 100 files; MCP tool output is capped at 25,000 tokens (warning above 10,000, `MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS`, per-tool `_meta.anthropic/maxResultSizeChars`) with overflow written under `~/.claude/projects/tool-results/`. MCP tool schemas are deferred by default (Tool Search, v2.1.221+, `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH`), so only names sit in context until `ToolSearch` loads a schema. Permission matching is per tool family: command patterns for Bash, path patterns for Read/Edit, `domain:` for WebFetch, subagent type for Agent.
dimensions.extensibility: The runtime loop itself is not replaceable (DataCamp: it 'packages the built-in loop and lets you extend the workflow around it'); what is pluggable is prompts/knowledge (skills), workers (subagents), lifecycle logic (hooks), tools (MCP), orchestration (workflows), plus output styles, status line and LSP code-intelligence plugins. A skill is `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` (or `~/.claude/skills/`) with frontmatter `name`, `description`, `disable-model-invocation`, `user-invocable`, `allowed-tools`, `model`, `effort`, `context: fork`, `agent`, `paths`, `hooks`, and `$ARGUMENTS`/`$0` substitution and `!`cmd`` shell injection; it supersedes the older `.claude/commands/*.md`. A plugin is a directory with `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` holding `skills/`, `agents/`, `hooks/hooks.json`, `.mcp.json` and `workflows/`, installed from a marketplace (`.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`, `/plugin marketplace add`, `claude plugin install name@marketplace`, e.g. `commit-commands@claude-plugins-official`) or loaded locally with `--plugin-dir`, at user/project/local scope; managed settings can allowlist marketplaces and force-install. Third parties therefore add capability by publishing a git repo with a marketplace.json, never by modifying the harness. Providers and the UI are not pluggable; the Agent SDK exposes hooks, `canUseTool`, system-prompt overrides and `settingSources` for embedding, and `claude mcp serve` exposes Claude Code's own tools to other MCP clients.
dimensions.context: Instruction files load in a fixed hierarchy: managed (`/etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md` on Linux), `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `./CLAUDE.md` or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `./CLAUDE.local.md`, nested subdirectory CLAUDE.md files loaded on demand, `.claude/rules/*.md` with optional `paths:` globs, `@path` imports up to four hops, and since v2.1.277 `AGENTS.md` is read when no CLAUDE.md exists; guidance is under 200 lines per file, `/init` generates one, `/context` shows what loaded, `claudeMdExcludes` prunes monorepos. Auto memory is Claude-written notes in `MEMORY.md` under `~/.claude/projects/`, with the first 200 lines or 25KB injected each session; subagents can have their own via `memory: user|project|local`. Compaction: when context nears `autoCompactWindow` (default ~967K tokens on native-1M models, the 200K boundary otherwise; `/autocompact 500k`, `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW`) Claude Code first clears older tool outputs, then summarises; `/compact <focus>` and a 'Compact instructions' section in CLAUDE.md steer it, `PreCompact`/`PostCompact` hooks fire, and afterwards the system prompt, CLAUDE.md, memory and MCP tool list reload, up to five recently modified files are re-read and invoked skill bodies are re-injected (≤5,000 tokens each); a thrashing guard stops auto-compact after a few failed attempts. KV-cache friendliness is a stated design axis: requests are ordered system prompt → project context → conversation, plan mode and skills append messages rather than mutate the prefix, deferred tool stubs avoid schema churn, the compaction request reuses the same prefix, TTL is 5m or 1h (`promptCacheTtl`, `subagentPromptCacheTtl`, `CLAUDE_CODE_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL`), and `/usage` prints a 'Prompt cache (main)' hit ratio; Anthropic's April 2026 post says cache hit rate is monitored with 'uptime-level' seriousness.
dimensions.permissions: Six modes: `default` (Manual, prompts for edits/commands), `acceptEdits` (auto-approves edits plus mkdir/touch/mv/cp/rm/sed in-scope), `plan` (read-only exploration until a plan is approved), `auto` (a second classifier model reviews each action and blocks escalation, unrecognised infrastructure or hostile-content-driven actions; built-in default for interactive terminal/VS Code from v2.1.283, server-side classifier default from v2.1.278, unsupported on Haiku and pre-4.6 models), `dontAsk` (anything that would prompt is denied) and `bypassPermissions` (`--dangerously-skip-permissions`, refused as root, ask rules still apply). Rules live under `permissions.allow/ask/deny` in managed settings, `~/.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/settings.json` and `.claude/settings.local.json`, with syntax `Bash(npm run *)`, `Edit(/src/**)`, `Read(./.env)`, `WebFetch(domain:example.com)`, `Agent(Explore)`, `Agent(model:opus)`, `mcp__github__get_*`; deny beats allow, ask beats allow, and a bare-name deny removes the tool from context. Bash gating splits on `&&`, `||`, `;`, `|`, `|&`, `&` and newlines and requires every subcommand to match, strips wrappers (timeout, nice, nohup, bare xargs), auto-runs a built-in read-only set (ls, cat, grep, find, read-only git), checks `>`/`<`/`tee` targets against Edit/Read rules, and the docs state plainly that a `Bash(rm *)` deny is not a security boundary because `/bin/rm` or `sh -c` bypass it. The workspace fence is the cwd plus `additionalDirectories`/`--add-dir`, hardened by `permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories`, with protected and critical paths never auto-approved in any mode. Sandboxing: the built-in Bash sandbox uses Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap + socat (optional seccomp) on Linux/WSL2, configured by `sandbox.enabled`, `sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite/denyRead/allowRead`, `sandbox.network.allowedDomains`, credential `deny`/`mask` with proxy-side injection and AWS SigV4 re-signing, `excludedCommands`, and an `allowUnsandboxedCommands` escape hatch (`dangerouslyDisableSandbox`) that can be turned off; whole-process isolation comes from `@anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime`, the reference devcontainer with a default-deny iptables firewall, custom containers/VMs, or Anthropic-hosted cloud VMs.
dimensions.hooks: Over thirty lifecycle events: SessionStart, Setup, UserPromptSubmit, UserPromptExpansion, PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PermissionDenied, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PostToolBatch, Notification, MessageDisplay, SubagentStart/SubagentStop, TaskCreated/TaskCompleted, Stop, StopFailure, TeammateIdle, InstructionsLoaded, ConfigChange, CwdChanged, DirectoryAdded, FileChanged, WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove, PreCompact/PostCompact, PreModelSwitch/PostModelSwitch, Elicitation/ElicitationResult, SessionEnd. Hooks are declared under `hooks` in any settings.json scope, in plugin `hooks/hooks.json`, or in skill and subagent frontmatter, keyed by a `matcher` (tool name, list or regex such as `mcp__.*`) with an optional `if: "Bash(rm *)"` permission-rule filter, `timeout` (600s default), `async`, `once` and `statusMessage`. Five hook types: `command` (JSON on stdin, exec or shell form), `http` (POST JSON, allowlisted by `allowedHttpHookUrls`), `mcp_tool`, `prompt` (single LLM judgment) and `agent` (multi-turn verifier, experimental). Veto power is explicit: exit code 2 blocks a PreToolUse call, rejects a UserPromptSubmit prompt, prevents Stop, blocks PreModelSwitch and fails WorktreeCreate/Remove, while JSON `hookSpecificOutput` can return `permissionDecision: allow|deny|isolate`, rewrite the call with `updatedInput`, inject `additionalContext`, or set `continue`/`systemMessage`; PermissionRequest returns a `decision` object instead. PostToolUse and most other events are observe-only. Organisations can pin behaviour with `allowManagedHooksOnly` and `disableAllHooks`.
dimensions.subagents: Subagents are Markdown files with YAML frontmatter in `.claude/agents/`, `~/.claude/agents/`, plugin `agents/`, managed settings or the `--agents` JSON flag, with fields `name`, `description`, `tools`/`disallowedTools`, `model` (sonnet/opus/haiku/inherit), `permissionMode`, `maxTurns`, `skills`, `mcpServers`, `hooks`, `memory`, `background`, `omitClaudeMd`, `effort` and `isolation: worktree`; built-ins are Explore and Plan (read-only, skip CLAUDE.md) and general-purpose. The parent spawns them through the Agent tool by auto-delegation on `description`, natural language, `@agent-name`, or `claude --agent`; each child gets its own context window and system prompt, loads the CLAUDE.md hierarchy and git status but not the parent's history (a fork copies history), and inherits the parent's tool pool minus Agent-at-depth-limit, AskUserQuestion, EnterPlanMode/ExitPlanMode and similar, with background subagents restricted further. Permissions: if the parent is in bypassPermissions, acceptEdits or auto the child inherits that mode, otherwise its own `permissionMode` applies, and prompts bubble up to the main session. Limits are 3 nesting levels (`CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH`), 20 concurrent (`CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS`), `maxTurns` marks a run partial, combined descriptions are capped at 15,000 tokens, and the SDK budget cap covers children. What returns is the child's final text plus a small metadata trailer; custom subagents are resumable by ID via `SendMessage`. Above subagents sit agent teams (experimental, `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1`: a lead plus peer sessions with a shared task list and JSON mailboxes under `~/.claude/teams/`, no nested teams, roughly 7x tokens) and dynamic workflows (JS scripts, 16 concurrent agents, 1,000 agents per run, 4,096 items per `parallel()`/`pipeline()`, `/deep-research`, the `ultracode` keyword).
dimensions.providers: Claude models only, reached through the Anthropic API, Amazon Bedrock (`CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1`), Google Cloud's Agent Platform/Vertex (`CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX=1`), Microsoft Foundry (`CLAUDE_CODE_USE_FOUNDRY=1`), Claude Platform on AWS, or any LLM gateway set with `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` (LiteLLM is named in the costs doc) with `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_GATEWAY_MODEL_DISCOVERY=1`. Models are chosen by alias (`default`, `best`, `fable`, `opus`, `sonnet`, `haiku`, `opusplan`, `[1m]` suffix) or `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`, with per-provider pins `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL`/`SONNET`/`HAIKU`/`FABLE` and `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` for children. There is no official Ollama, vLLM or llama.cpp support; the only route to a non-Anthropic model is a gateway that speaks the Anthropic Messages API, and DataCamp and Winder.ai both list single-vendor lock-in as the headline limitation. Through a gateway, features degrade: auto mode is unavailable on unsupported models, Tool Search may fall back to upfront schema loading, and cache behaviour depends on whether the gateway forwards `cache_control` markers. Weak-model handling is not documented beyond cost advice (Sonnet for most work, `model: haiku` for simple subagents).
dimensions.mcp: Claude Code is a full MCP client: `claude mcp add --transport stdio|http|sse|ws` or `.mcp.json` (project scope, requires trust approval) and `~/.claude.json` (local/user scope), `${VAR:-default}` env expansion, OAuth 2.0 via `/mcp` or `claude mcp login`, a `headersHelper` for custom auth, MCP resources and prompts surfaced as slash commands, elicitation including URL-mode (v2.1.281), `list_changed` dynamic tool updates, auto-reconnect with backoff, tool calls over two minutes moved to background, and Channels for server-pushed messages. Tool Search defers MCP schemas by default (v2.1.221+), outputs are capped at 25,000 tokens, and two client runtimes exist (MCP TypeScript SDK 1.x and 2.0 at protocol revision 2026-07-28, selected by `MCP_SDK_GENERATION=v2`). It is also an MCP server: `claude mcp serve` exposes its tools over stdio, and the Agent SDK accepts in-process `type: "sdk"` servers. ACP and A2A are not mentioned anywhere in the official docs; web search results show a Zed-maintained adapter (`@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp`) that wraps the Agent SDK to run Claude Code inside ACP editors, but that page was not read and Anthropic does not document it.
dimensions.evals: Anthropic publishes model-level numbers rather than harness-level ones: the Claude Opus 5.5 announcement (22 Sept 2026) reports Terminal-Bench 4.0 66.4% at xhigh effort, FrontierCode v1.1 54.4%, CursorBench 4.0 57.8%, OSWorld 2.0 81.8% and Terminal-Bench-Science 58.7%, with no SWE-bench Verified figure and a note that production safeguards were enabled; the January 2025 SWE-bench engineering post described Anthropic's minimal bash-tool plus string-replace edit-tool scaffold (49% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet) under the philosophy 'keep the scaffolding minimal'. No official Claude-Code-harness versus bare-model ablation is published. Third-party signals: Winder.ai cites a same-model memory benchmark where Letta Code scored 59.1% versus Claude Code 41.6%, and search summaries claim vendor scaffolds run 15-30 points above standardised leaderboards, which I could not verify from a primary source. Internally, the 23 April 2026 postmortem disclosed that Anthropic's evals measured a 3% quality drop from a 25-word brevity instruction and committed to per-line prompt ablations, per-model evals and soak periods. The harness ships its own eval tooling: `claude plugin eval` runs `evals/<case>/prompt.md` against `graders/*.md` of types `regex`, `tool_used`, `tool_order`, `file_exists`, `llm` and `baseline`, three runs per case by default, with a no-plugin baseline reporting WITH, W/OUT and Δ, a `--threshold`, `--judge-model` and HTML report for CI gating.
dimensions.distinctive: Three genuinely distinctive ideas. First, cache-first architecture: every feature is designed to append rather than mutate the prompt prefix (plan mode as tools, deferred tool stubs, compaction forking the same prefix), and cache hit rate is treated as an uptime metric. Second, a layered, git-shareable, file-based extension surface (CLAUDE.md and rules, SKILL.md, agents, hooks, settings, workflows, plugins) in which hooks can veto and rewrite tool calls and a classifier-driven auto mode replaces most permission prompts; Marmelab's Sept 2026 survey credits Claude Code with popularising hooks, subagents, skills and instruction files. Third, an escalation ladder for multi-agent work, subagents to agent teams to script-orchestrated dynamic workflows, in which the harness writes a task-specific harness ('a harness for every task'). The loudest criticisms: closed source and single-vendor lock-in with a non-replaceable loop (DataCamp, Winder.ai); cost and token burn (about $13 per developer per active day in enterprise, agent teams ~7x tokens, compaction and long-context creep, incident write-ups citing four- and five-figure sessions); the March-April 2026 quality regression that Anthropic's own postmortem attributed to a high-to-medium effort default, a thinking-clearing bug that fired every turn and a brevity prompt (fixed in v2.1.116); 'thin on durable memory by design' (Winder.ai); a sprawling configuration surface (30+ hook events, six permission modes, several settings layers) and the docs' own admission that permission rules are not a security boundary without the OS sandbox.

unknowns: Implementation language: the official repo publishes no source; TypeScript is asserted only by Winder.ai (secondary) and inferred from the Node.js 18+ badge and former npm distribution.
Download counts: no npm or installer download figures were found; only the 148.1k GitHub star count.

Harness-vs-model ablation: Anthropic publishes model benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode, CursorBench) but no Claude-Code-scaffold vs bare-model comparison; the '15-30 point vendor scaffold gap' appeared only in search snippets and is unverified.
ACP / A2A: not documented by Anthropic; the Zed ACP adapter was seen only in search results, not read.
Explicit weak-model handling: not documented beyond cost-routing advice and the note that auto mode is unsupported on Haiku and older models.
Exact auto-compact trigger on 200K-context models: docs say 'the 200K boundary' without a percentage.

CHANGELOG coverage: the raw CHANGELOG.md fetch surfaced only versions 2.1.275-2.1.283 without dates, so per-version dates for 2026 features come from the docs' 'requires v2.1.x' notes and the scriptbyai timeline rather than the changelog itself.

profiles.name: OpenAI Codex CLI (openai/codex)
profiles.one_liner: OpenAI's Apache-2.0, Rust-core terminal coding agent (also the engine behind the IDE, desktop and cloud surfaces via its app-server protocol), distinguished by OS-level sandboxing with an orthogonal approval policy, MCP/skills/plugins/hooks extensibility, and a Responses-API-only model loop co-designed with OpenAI's Codex models.

dimensions.identity: Maintained by OpenAI in the openai/codex monorepo. The CLI first shipped on 16 April 2025 as a TypeScript tool and was rewritten in Rust: the engine is the `codex-rs` Cargo workspace (roughly 70+ crates; a March 2026 analysis measured the repo at 95.7% Rust) and the npm package `@openai/codex` is now a thin launcher. The CLI is Apache-2.0; the Codex desktop app is proprietary. Distribution: `curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh`, `npm install -g @openai/codex`, `brew install --cask codex`, plus IDE extensions (VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf), a desktop app (`codex app`), Codex cloud, and SDKs (`@openai/codex-sdk` for TypeScript, `openai-codex` on PyPI for Python 3.10+). Popularity: the README shows 126.5k stars; a third-party tracker reports 125,960 stars, 19,599 forks and 1,125+ releases on 22 Sep 2026 and 79.2M npm downloads in the trailing 30 days. Latest stable release is 0.157.1 (26 Sep 2026).
dimensions.loop: A single ReAct-style tool loop over the OpenAI Responses API: `codex-core` builds the prompt, calls the model, and if the response is a `function_call` it runs the tool through `ToolRouter`, appends the output and calls again; the turn ends when the model emits a final assistant message (`response.output_text.done`) instead of another tool call. Internally it is an async submit/event queue (`Op` in: `UserTurn`, `Interrupt`, `Shutdown`; `EventMsg` out: `TurnStarted`, `AgentMessageDelta`, `ExecCommandBegin/End`, `PatchApplied`, `TokensUsed`), so the TUI, IDE extension and app-server are pure event consumers. There is no documented step or turn cap: issue #12336 asking for `--max-turns` was closed as not planned, and the loop is bounded only by the context budget plus auto-compaction. Planning is a tool (`update_plan`, OpenAI's 'default TODO tool') rather than a planner/executor split; the official prompting guide tells the model to skip plans for the easiest ~25% of tasks, never make single-step plans, and never end a turn with only a plan. The app-server exposes `turn/start`, `turn/steer` (append input mid-turn) and `turn/interrupt`.
dimensions.tools: Tools are Rust handlers compiled into `codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/`, registered in `registry.rs` and dispatched by `router.rs`; there is no decorator, manifest or plugin API for third-party native tools, so external tools arrive only via MCP. The handlers directory shows the built-in set: `unified_exec` (`exec_command` + `write_stdin` PTY sessions, up to 64 live processes), `shell_spec` (`shell_command`), `apply_patch`, `plan` (`update_plan`), `view_image`, `request_user_input`, `request_permissions`, `multi_agents`/`multi_agents_v2`, `mcp` and `mcp_resource`, `tool_search` (deferred tool discovery), `get_context_remaining`, `new_context_window`, `request_plugin_install`/`list_available_plugins_to_install`, `current_time`, `sleep`, `wait_for_environment`, `send_message_to_user_async`, plus hosted `web_search` (`tools.web_search = disabled|cached|indexed|live`, default `cached`). Tools are feature-flagged in config (`[features] shell_tool`, `unified_exec`, `multi_agent`, `memories`, `hooks`). Truncation: `exec_command` takes `max_output_tokens` (default 10,000, ~4 bytes/token) and buffers through a `HeadTailBuffer` capped at 1 MiB that drops the middle; `tool_output_token_limit` in config.toml caps each tool's contribution to context; the cookbook prescribes a 10k-token budget split half head/half tail with a `…N tokens truncated…` marker. `apply_patch` is a bespoke file-oriented diff format the Codex models are trained on, and OpenAI recommends using the exact implementation.
dimensions.extensibility: Everything pluggable is configured through files rather than code: MCP servers (`[mcp_servers.<id>]`), Skills (`SKILL.md` directories under `.agents/skills`, `~/.agents/skills`, `/etc/codex/skills`, invoked with `$skill-name` or implicitly, with optional `agents/openai.yaml` metadata), Plugins (a `.codex-plugin/plugin.json` manifest bundling skills, MCP servers, app connectors and `hooks/hooks.json`, listed in `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json` or `~/.agents/plugins/marketplace.json`, installed with `/plugins` or `codex plugin`), hooks (`hooks.json`), custom agent roles (`.codex/agents/*.toml`), model providers (`[model_providers.<id>]`) and `notify` commands. UIs plug in through the app-server JSON-RPC protocol (`codex app-server`, with `generate-ts` / `generate-json-schema` for bindings), which powers the VS Code extension, desktop app and JetBrains/Xcode integrations; the TypeScript and Python SDKs wrap the same core. Prompts are extensible via AGENTS.md and `experimental_compact_prompt_file`, but the system prompt itself is not user-replaceable. Publishing to the official plugin directory is curated by OpenAI; self-serve distribution is via git-hosted marketplaces. Enterprise admins gate all of it with `requirements.toml` and `policy.installation` (`AVAILABLE`, `INSTALLED_BY_DEFAULT`, `NOT_AVAILABLE`).
dimensions.context: Instructions: Codex reads `~/.codex/AGENTS.override.md` then `AGENTS.md`, then walks from the git root down to cwd taking at most one file per directory (override, `AGENTS.md`, then `project_doc_fallback_filenames`), concatenating until `project_doc_max_bytes` (default 32 KiB) is reached. Compaction: auto-compaction fires at `model_auto_compact_token_limit`, hard-capped at 90% of `model_context_window`; with OpenAI models it uses the server-side `/responses/compact` endpoint, which returns an encrypted opaque summary that preserves reasoning, while non-OpenAI providers fall back to a local summarisation prompt; `/compact [instructions]` triggers it manually, `PreCompact`/`PostCompact` hooks fire, and 0.157.0 resumes threads from the latest compaction boundary. Persistent memory: `[features] memories = true` (off by default) enables a two-phase async pipeline that extracts per-session summaries and consolidates them into `~/.codex/memories/` (`MEMORY.md`, `memory_summary.md`, `raw_memories.md`, `rollout_summaries/`, `skills/`), with secret redaction, `memories.generate_memories` / `use_memories` / `extract_model` / `consolidation_model` / `disable_on_external_context`, and a `/memories` per-chat toggle. KV-cache friendliness: the prompt prefix is kept stable and OpenAI's guidance warns that changing tools, model, sandbox/approval mode or cwd mid-thread breaks the cache; skills load progressively (name+description first, `skills.max_context_tokens` capped at 10,000) and `get_context_remaining` exposes the budget to the model.
dimensions.permissions: Two orthogonal knobs: `sandbox_mode` (`read-only`, `workspace-write`, `danger-full-access`) is what the OS lets the process do, and `approval_policy` (`on-request` default, `never`, or a `{ granular = { sandbox_approval, rules, mcp_elicitations, request_permissions, skill_approval } }` table) is when Codex stops to ask; `untrusted` was removed in 0.149.0 and `on-failure` is deprecated. The OS sandbox is Seatbelt (`sandbox-exec` with generated `.sbpl` profiles) on macOS, Landlock + seccomp-BPF via the `codex-linux-sandbox` helper (or `bwrap`) on Linux/WSL2, and restricted tokens/ACLs with `CodexSandboxOffline`/`CodexSandboxOnline` users on Windows; reads are never restricted, writable roots default to cwd plus temp dirs with `.git` and `.codex` carved out read-only, and network is off by default. Since v0.119–0.121 named profiles `[permissions.<name>]` add per-path `read|write|none` glob rules and a managed `network_proxy` with `mode = "limited"` domain allowlists. Command gating: a command that fails in the sandbox is heuristically detected (`is_likely_sandbox_denied`) and re-offered with escalation; Starlark `prefix_rule(pattern=..., decision="allow|prompt|forbidden")` files in `~/.codex/rules/*.rules` (tested with `codex execpolicy check`) pre-decide commands with strictest-match-wins; `approvals_reviewer = "auto_review"` routes approval prompts to a guardian reviewer agent that denies exfiltration/credential-probing/destructive actions, with a circuit breaker after 3 consecutive or 10 rolling denials. `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` (`--yolo`) removes everything; `codex sandbox <cmd>` runs arbitrary commands inside the same sandbox.
dimensions.hooks: Twelve lifecycle events: `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PermissionRequest`, `PostToolUse`, `PreCompact`, `PostCompact`, `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`, `Stop`, `Interrupt`. Hooks are declared in `~/.codex/hooks.json`, `<repo>/.codex/hooks.json`, inline `[hooks]` tables in `config.toml`, or a plugin's `hooks/hooks.json`; each handler is `type: "command"` (or an MCP tool) with a regex `matcher` (tool names such as `Bash`, `apply_patch`, MCP tool names; `startup|resume|clear|compact` for SessionStart; `manual|auto` for compaction) and a `timeout` (default 600 s; 1 s for `SessionEnd`/`Interrupt`). Handlers get one JSON object on stdin (`session_id`, `cwd`, `hook_event_name`, `model`, plus event fields) and answer with JSON (`continue`, `stopReason`, `systemMessage`, `suppressOutput`, `hookSpecificOutput`). Veto is real: `PreToolUse` blocks with `permissionDecision: "deny"` or exit code 2, `PermissionRequest` can `allow`/`deny` an approval prompt, `UserPromptSubmit` can block a prompt, `PostToolUse` can replace the tool result with feedback via `decision: "block"`, and `Stop`/`SubagentStop` can force continuation; `Interrupt` output cannot prevent the interrupt. `[features] hooks = false` disables them, `allow_managed_hooks_only = true` keeps only enterprise `requirements.toml` hooks, and `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` skips trust review; async hooks are not supported.
dimensions.subagents: The parent model spawns children through tools in `multi_agents_v2` (`spawn_agent`, `send_input`, `wait`, `close_agent`, plus `spawn_agents_on_csv` batch fan-out whose workers must call `report_agent_job_result`); the runtime schedules threads, forwards approvals and collects results, and a unified `SpawnRequest` plus an agent message board landed in 0.157.0. Three built-in roles ship (`default`, `worker`, `explorer`); custom roles are TOML files in `~/.codex/agents/` or `.codex/agents/` with required `name`, `description`, `developer_instructions` and optional `model`, `model_reasoning_effort`, `sandbox_mode`, `mcp_servers`, `skills.config`; project-scoped roles are ignored unless the project is trusted. Children inherit the parent's sandbox policy, permission mode, live `/approvals` overrides, MCP servers and skills unless the role file overrides them. Limits live under `[agents]`: `enabled` (true), `max_concurrent_threads_per_session`, `default_subagent_model`, `default_subagent_reasoning_effort`; community documentation additionally reports `max_threads` (6), `max_depth` (1, so no grandchildren) and `job_max_runtime_seconds` (1800). Children return summaries rather than raw transcripts, and `SubagentStart`/`SubagentStop` hooks wrap them. Subagents went GA in 0.115.0 (16 Mar 2026) and MultiAgentV2 in 0.128.0 (30 Apr 2026), which replaced v1's full-history forks that multiplied token cost per child.
dimensions.providers: OpenAI-first: authentication via ChatGPT-plan OAuth or `OPENAI_API_KEY`/`CODEX_API_KEY`, with GPT-6 Sol/Luna the September 2026 defaults and Amazon Bedrock support added in 0.157.0. Other endpoints are configured under `[model_providers.<id>]` with `base_url`, `env_key`, `query_params`, `http_headers` and `wire_api`, but `wire_api = "responses"` is the only accepted value (Chat Completions support was removed in February 2026), so a provider must speak the Responses API natively or sit behind a translating gateway such as LiteLLM. Local models: `codex --oss` with `oss_provider = "ollama" | "lmstudio"` (defaults to gpt-oss-20b via Ollama), and Ollama's docs show a profile with `base_url = "http://localhost:11434/v1/"`, `wire_api = "responses"` and a recommended context of at least 64k tokens; LM Studio and MLX work the same way. Weak-model handling is not documented; non-OpenAI models lose server-side compaction (local summary path) and hosted web search, and repo issues report gpt-oss-20b emitting fake `apply_patch` calls that never apply (#2064) and a performance regression between 0.55 and 0.73 (#8272).
dimensions.mcp: MCP client is native: `codex mcp add <name> --env K=V -- <cmd>`, `codex mcp list`, `codex mcp login <name>`; `[mcp_servers.<id>]` supports stdio (`command`, `args`, `env`, `env_vars`, `cwd`) and streamable HTTP (`url`, `bearer_token_env_var`, `auth = oauth|chatgpt`, `client_id`, `callback_url`) with `startup_timeout_sec` (10), `tool_timeout_sec` (60), `enabled_tools`/`disabled_tools` and `enabled`; 0.157.0 restricted local servers to stdio descriptors and OAuth endpoints to HTTP(S). MCP resources are readable and `tool_search` defers loading of large tool catalogs. Codex is also an MCP server (`codex mcp-server`) so other orchestrators can drive it. For IDEs OpenAI deliberately rejected MCP and built the app-server protocol (JSON-RPC 2.0 as JSONL over stdio, experimental WebSocket/Unix socket, `thread/start`, `turn/start`, `turn/steer`, server-initiated approval requests). ACP support is via the Zed-originated `codex-acp` adapter (now `agentclientprotocol/codex-acp`, Apache-2.0), not an OpenAI deliverable; A2A exists only as an open feature request (#11980).
dimensions.evals: OpenAI publishes model-level numbers, not CLI-harness ablations: GPT-5.3-Codex scored 56.8% on SWE-Bench Pro (public) and 77.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 (vs 64.0% for GPT-5.2-Codex); GPT-5.5 reached 82.7% on Terminal-Bench 2.0; third-party trackers cite GPT-5.6 Sol at 88.8% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 64.6% on SWE-Bench Pro. Harness-vs-model comparisons come from outsiders: a 21 Sep 2026 analysis puts GPT-5.6 Sol at 78.9% / $0.76 per task inside the Codex harness versus 83.3% / $0.42 inside Pi on Terminal-Bench 2.0; an April 2026 piece notes Codex CLI + GPT-5.4 at 77.3% while using roughly 3–4× fewer tokens than Claude Code or Cursor; `davisbuilds/openbench` runs the same model (gpt-5.5-medium plus open models) through codex, pi, opencode, cursor and devin and finds correctness saturates while wall-clock spread reaches ~4× and token cost ~8×. No OpenAI-published ablation isolating the Codex CLI harness was found.
dimensions.distinctive: Three ideas stand out. (1) Sandboxing as an OS primitive rather than a prompt: `sandbox_mode` and `approval_policy` kept orthogonal, Starlark execpolicy rules, a managed domain-allowlist network proxy, and an LLM guardian (`auto_review`) that adjudicates escalations instead of a human. (2) One Rust core exposed through the app-server JSON-RPC protocol so CLI, IDE, desktop, cloud and third-party clients are thin event consumers, with OpenAI explicitly rejecting MCP for that job. (3) Tight model–harness co-design: a Responses-only wire API, server-side encrypted compaction that keeps reasoning, and an `apply_patch` format the models are trained on, buying low token cost at the price of provider lock-in. Loudest criticisms: repeated sandbox escapes (CVE-2025-61260, where a repo-supplied `.env` redirecting `CODEX_HOME` auto-loaded MCP servers; the August 2026 Overpatch and Heapjack escapes fixed in 0.149.0; a Windows web-search binary-hijack RCE), approval-prompt fatigue that pushes users toward `--yolo`, removal of `approval_policy = "untrusted"` without deprecation (#39973), local-model friction after the Chat Completions removal, subagent roles that initially could not be spawned by name (#14579), and relentless release churn (1,125+ releases).

unknowns: evals: no OpenAI-published harness-vs-model ablation for Codex CLI exists; all harness comparisons are third-party
providers: how weak or small models are handled is not documented (only community issue reports)
subagents: official defaults for nesting depth (max_depth) and per-child runtime budget are not in the config reference; the values 6 / 1 / 1800 s come from community documentation
tools: no documented API for registering a native (non-MCP) tool from outside the Rust tree
loop: no explicit step or turn cap is documented; issue #12336 requesting --max-turns was closed as not planned
mcp: the purpose of the code-mode-protocol / code-mode-host / code-mode-runtime crates is not documented
identity: npm download counts come from a third-party tracker, not from OpenAI

profiles.name: OpenCode (anomalyco/opencode, formerly sst/opencode)
profiles.one_liner: MIT-licensed, TypeScript, provider-agnostic terminal coding agent from Anomaly (ex-SST) built as a client/server harness (TUI, desktop, web, IDE, SDK and ACP are all clients of one embedded HTTP server), with 75+ providers via the Vercel AI SDK and models.dev, file-convention extensibility (AGENTS.md, .opencode/{agents,tools,commands,skills,plugins}), tree-sitter-parsed permission rules, and no OS sandbox.

dimensions.identity: Maintained by Anomaly (GitHub org anomalyco, formerly SST; the repo was renamed from sst/opencode to anomalyco/opencode and the old name now only redirects), led by Dax Raad and Adam Doty. The TypeScript rewrite launched publicly on June 19, 2025 (per the Learn AI wiki) after a dispute with Charm over Kujtim Hoxha's original Go project, whose lineage became Charm's Crush. It is MIT licensed, written in TypeScript (Bun runtime in v1, migrated to Node.js in v2) with a TUI rendered by the Zig-cored OpenTUI. Distribution: CLI/TUI (`curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash`, `npm i -g opencode-ai`, `brew install anomalyco/tap/opencode`), a desktop app (Tauri in v1, Electron in v2), a VS Code/Cursor/Windsurf extension, `opencode web`, `opencode serve` (HTTP server with an OpenAPI 3.1 spec and the `@opencode-ai/sdk` client) and `opencode acp`. Popularity: the README shows 210.1k stars and the homepage claims 208K stars, 950 contributors, 13,000+ commits and "over 16M developers every month"; the Harness Engineering paper calls it "the most-starred dedicated coding agent". Two release lines ship in parallel as of late September 2026: v1.18.32 (Sep 21) and v2.0.18 (Sep 25), and the homepage install script now points at `opencode.ai/v2/install`; npm download counts were not obtainable.
dimensions.loop: A single-agent tool loop, not planner/executor: a hand-rolled `while(true)` in `packages/opencode/src/session/prompt.ts` where the message log doubles as the work queue, so pending subagent spawns and compactions are persisted message parts dequeued one per iteration and the loop is resumable across process restarts. Streaming and tool dispatch are delegated to Vercel AI SDK `streamText` (the only system in the eleven-harness study whose inner LLM plumbing is a third-party SDK); several tool calls in one assistant message execute in parallel, uncapped. A turn ends when the assistant finishes without tool calls; the per-agent `steps` key (legacy `maxSteps`) has no default (Infinity), and when a cap is hit the harness injects `MAX_STEPS_PROMPT` ("MAXIMUM STEPS REACHED", asking for a summary) rather than raising an error, and issue #24505 (Apr 2026) notes the full tools object is still passed, so it is not a hard stop. Stuck detection is a `doom_loop` check: three consecutive identical (tool, args) calls route to a permission ask (default `ask`), which misses A,B,A,B cycles (issue #47759). On context overflow the loop compacts and, in v2, does a one-shot compact-and-retry when the provider classifies the error as overflow.
dimensions.tools: Tools are defined in code with `Tool.define()` (`packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts`) using Zod/Effect schemas plus a sibling `.txt` description file; `registry.ts` filters first by config flags, then at runtime by model and by agent permissions (denying `"*"` for a tool removes it from the LLM's view). The documented built-ins are bash, edit, write, read, grep, glob, lsp, apply_patch, skill, todowrite, webfetch, websearch and question (the source tree also holds plan, code-mode, invalid and external-directory; the paper counts 17 registered first-party tools). The tool surface is model-conditional: GPT-family models receive a port of Codex's `apply_patch` DSL and lose edit/write entirely, while others get SEARCH/REPLACE `edit` with a nine-stage replacer cascade (exact, line-trimmed, block-anchor, whitespace-normalized, context-aware under Levenshtein 0.65), and LSP diagnostics are fed back into edit results when `lsp` is enabled. Truncation is centralized in `truncate.ts`: `MAX_LINES = 2000`, `MAX_BYTES = 50 * 1024`; overflow is written to a file in a truncation directory and the model is told "The tool call succeeded but the output was truncated. Full output saved to: <file>" with a hint to use Grep/Read with offset, or the explore subagent if the task tool is available. `read.ts` uses `DEFAULT_READ_LIMIT = 2000` lines, `MAX_LINE_LENGTH = 2000` chars and a 50 KB byte cap with "(Showing lines a-b of n. Use offset=... to continue.)"; `grep.ts` runs bundled ripgrep with `limit: 100` and appends "(Results truncated. Consider using a more specific path or pattern.)".
dimensions.extensibility: Almost everything is pluggable by file convention or npm. Plugins are listed under `"plugin": ["opencode-helicone-session", "@my-org/custom-plugin"]` or dropped in `.opencode/plugins/*.ts`; a v1 plugin is `async ({ project, client, $, directory, worktree }) => hooks` returning roughly twenty typed hooks, executed sequentially, and can register tools via the `tool` hook. V2 replaces this with `Plugin.define({ id, async setup(ctx) })` exposing `ctx.session.hook`, `ctx.permission.hook`, `ctx.tool.hook`, `ctx.shell.hook` and `ctx.tool.transform(editor => editor.add({...}))`, hot-reloads watched config dirs, and lets one package export both `setup()` (v2) and `server()` (v1). Custom tools need no plugin: any `.opencode/tools/<name>.ts` or `~/.config/opencode/tools/<name>.ts` exporting `tool({ description, args: { q: tool.schema.string() }, async execute(args, ctx) })` from `@opencode-ai/plugin` becomes tool `<name>` (named exports become `<file>_<export>`, and a same-named file overrides a built-in). Agents are markdown in `.opencode/agents/`, slash commands are markdown in `.opencode/commands/` (frontmatter `agent`, `model`, `subtask`; `$ARGUMENTS`/`$1`, shell injection with !`cmd`, `@file`), skills are `SKILL.md` directories, and themes, formatters, LSP servers and providers (any AI SDK package named in the provider's `npm` field, installable at runtime) are all config-driven. The ecosystem page lists community plugins such as opencode-daytona, oh-my-opencode, opencode-supermemory and opencode-vibeguard; there is no official marketplace, which reviewers count as a gap.
dimensions.context: Rules come from `AGENTS.md` in the project (walked upward to the worktree root) and `~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`, with `CLAUDE.md` and `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` as fallbacks (disable via `OPENCODE_DISABLE_CLAUDE_CODE`), plus an `"instructions"` array of paths, globs or URLs (5 s timeout); nested instruction files are injected into tool outputs as `<\system-reminder>` blocks, and `/init` generates AGENTS.md. Compaction is threshold-triggered LLM summarization by a hidden, all-tools-denied `compaction` agent: it fires at `limit.input` minus a reserved output margin using a chars/4 estimate (no tokenizer in the tree), passes the previous summary back in a `<previous-summary>` block and merges it into fixed headings (Objective / Important Details / Work State / Next Move / Relevant Files), keeping a verbatim tail of two user turns. V1 config is `compaction: { auto, prune, reserved }`, where pruning soft-deletes old tool outputs only when more than 20K tokens are reclaimable and always protects the newest 40K; v2 config is `compaction.auto`, `compaction.keep.tokens` (default 15000) and `compaction.buffer` (default 10% of the limit), with manual `/compact` and plugin hooks `experimental.session.compacting` (v1) / `compaction` (v2). There is no built-in persistent memory (the community plugin opencode-supermemory fills that role). For KV-cache friendliness OpenCode emits six providers' cache-control dialects simultaneously and caps the system prompt at two messages (one by default) to match cache breakpoints, exposes `provider.setCacheKey`, and Artificial Analysis measured a 97% cache hit rate; a shadow git repository snapshots the worktree per step for `/undo` and `/redo`.
dimensions.permissions: A `"permission"` block maps actions to `allow`, `ask` or `deny`: read, edit (covers edit/write/patch), glob, grep, bash, task, skill, lsp, question, webfetch, websearch, external_directory and doom_loop, with per-pattern maps such as `"bash": { "git *": "allow", "rm -rf *": "deny" }`, `*`/`?` wildcards, last-match-wins ordering and per-agent overrides; an ask offers once / always / reject. Defaults are permissive: `"*": allow` inside the project, with asks reserved for `external_directory`, `.env` reads and `doom_loop`. The distinctive mechanism is syntax-aware command permissioning: every bash command is parsed with web-tree-sitter (bash and PowerShell grammars), the exact command text becomes the ask pattern, "always allow" grants are scoped by a ~130-entry command-arity dictionary (so `git commit *` rather than blanket approval), and file-argument paths are resolved so out-of-project paths hit `external_directory`. V2 changes the format to an ordered array `permissions: [{ action, resource, effect }]`, states that "Saved approvals are durable, project-scoped allow rules. They never override a configured deny", and drops `doom_loop` and `lsp` as core actions. There is no sandbox: the Harness Engineering paper classifies OpenCode as policy-only ("sandbox" in its code means git worktrees) and Kingy's review says the permission system "is not a kernel-enforced sandbox"; containment is left to community layers (opencode-daytona, Docker Sandboxes via ACP). `experimental.policies` adds `provider.use` allow/deny statements so an org can block providers regardless of credentials.
dimensions.hooks: Lifecycle hooks are delivered through plugins, not a shell-command config. V1 hook names in `packages/plugin/src/index.ts`: `chat.message`, `chat.params` (temperature, topP, maxOutputTokens, options), `chat.headers`, `permission.ask` (set `output.status` to `allow | deny | ask`), `tool.execute.before` (mutate `output.args` or throw to block, e.g. `throw new Error("Do not read .env files")`), `tool.execute.after` (rewrite title/output/metadata), `tool.definition`, `shell.env`, `config`, `auth`, and a catch-all `event` fed by the bus (session.created/idle/compacted/error, file.edited, permission.asked/replied, message.updated, tui.*). Hooks can veto: throwing in `tool.execute.before` aborts the call, and `permission.ask` can auto-deny. V2 hooks are registered per subsystem: `ctx.permission.hook("evaluate", e => { e.effect = "deny"; e.message = ... })`, session hooks `prompt`, `context`, `compaction`, `generate`, `title`, `model.request`, `http.request`, `http.response`, `retry`, `ctx.shell.hook("create.before")` and `ctx.tool.hook("execute.before" | "execute.after")`; v2 hooks veto by setting fields on a mutable event rather than by throwing, and run in registration order. Innfactory notes there is "no standalone hooks system documented" outside plugins.
dimensions.subagents: The `task` tool (params `description`, `prompt`, `subagent_type`, optional `task_id` to resume and `background`) creates a child Session with `parentID` set, running the same loop, titled "<description> (@<agent> subagent)". Built-in subagents are general (broad tools, cannot launch further subagents), explore (read-only code search) and scout (read-only external docs), plus hidden compaction/title/summary agents; custom ones are markdown in `.opencode/agents/` with `mode: subagent`, invoked automatically or via `@name`, and `permission.task` controls which an agent may spawn. A child inherits the parent's model unless it configures its own; `deriveSubagentSessionPermission()` hands it the parent's deny and external-directory rules, and `todowrite` and `task` are denied unless the subagent explicitly permits them. Nesting is capped by `subagent_depth` (default 1, practical max 2). Only the final assistant text returns, wrapped as `<task id="<sessionID>" state="..."><task_result>...`, background results are injected as synthetic user messages, and multiple task calls in one message run concurrently; v2 adds background execution with a UI listing running work and a kill switch. No per-child token budget is documented.
dimensions.providers: 75+ providers through the Vercel AI SDK and the models.dev registry; a provider is declared under `"provider"` with an `npm` package (e.g. `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible`), `options.baseURL`, `options.apiKey: "{env:KEY}"` and `models.<id>.limit.context/output`, and `enabled_providers` / `disabled_providers` allow-list them. Local models use the same pattern: Ollama at `http://localhost:11434/v1`, LM Studio, llama.cpp and any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (the docs example is `"model": "lmstudio/google/gemma-3n-e4b"`). A ~1,400-line per-vendor transform matrix handles release-date-gated reasoning tiers, per-model temperature defaults and six cache dialects, and nine base system prompts are chosen by model-id substring (anthropic.txt, beast.txt for GPT-4.1, codex.txt, gemini.txt, kimi.txt, meta.txt, trinity.txt, gpt-astra.txt for GPT-6, default.txt); the tool surface is also model-conditional. Beyond that prompt/tool matrix there is no documented strategy for weak or small models, only a "models that work well" list and a warning that MCP servers add context. Anthropic blocked Claude Pro/Max OAuth tokens on January 9, 2026 and OpenCode merged PR #18186 "Remove anthropic references per legal requests" on March 19, 2026, so Claude is API-key only, while OpenAI extended Codex subscription support to OpenCode; the project also sells OpenCode Zen (curated models) and Go ($10/mo).
dimensions.mcp: MCP client support lives under `"mcp"`: `{ type: "local", command: ["npx", "-y", ...], environment, cwd }` or `{ type: "remote", url, headers }`, with `enabled`, `timeout` (default 5000 ms for tool fetching), OAuth auto-detected on 401 with RFC 7591 dynamic client registration (`opencode mcp auth <name>`, tokens in `~/.local/share/opencode/mcp-auth.json`, `oauth: false` to disable). MCP tools are exposed as `servername_toolname`, can be disabled with `"tools": { "my-mcp*": false }` and re-enabled per agent; the source covers tools, prompts, resources and resource templates while sampling and elicitation are disabled, and an experimental code mode collapses the MCP catalog into a single `execute` tool that runs model-written scripts. OpenCode does not act as an MCP server. ACP: `opencode acp` runs the agent as a JSON-RPC-over-stdio subprocess for Zed, JetBrains, avante.nvim and CodeCompanion.nvim with full parity except `/undo` and `/redo`. A2A is not native (open issues #3023 and #18021; a third-party a2a-opencode wrapper exists). Agent Skills follow agentskills.io `SKILL.md` and are discovered from `.opencode/skills`, `.claude/skills`, `.agents/skills` and their global equivalents.
dimensions.evals: The project publishes no leaderboard submissions; its own anomalyco/opencode-bench derives tasks from later production commits, runs the agent with a 30-minute timeout and scores with three LLM judges (Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5 Codex, Kimi-k2) across five weighted dimensions (API signature 20%, logic 30%, integration 20%, tests 20%, checks 10%) with a variance penalty (lambda 0.5), but Kingy's August 2026 audit found only one published result (~0.123) and a CLI that ran one episode instead of the promised three. Third-party numbers: Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index scores OpenCode+GLM-5.3 at 54 (DeepSWE v1.1 61%, Terminal-Bench 4.0 40%, SWE-Atlas-QnA 59%, $4.24/task) versus Claude Code+Opus 5.5 at 66. Kingy's fixed-model harness ablation had OpenCode solve 81.0% (34/42) with GPT-5.6 Sol and 70.3% (26/37) with DeepSeek V4 Flash against Claude Code's 81.1%, with no statistically significant differences. The arXiv "Scaffold Effect" paper (June 2026) compared Goose, OpenCode and OpenHands-SDK on identical models and found up to a 40x difference in tokens per solved task with only 0-8 point pass-rate spread. Builder.io's Sonnet 4.5 head-to-head had OpenCode take 78% longer than Claude Code (16:20 vs 9:09 over four tasks) while writing 94 tests to 73.
dimensions.distinctive: Three ideas stand out. First, the client/server harness: an embedded HTTP server with an OpenAPI spec and generated SDK, with TUI, desktop, web, IDE plugin and CI all as clients, and a log-as-queue loop where the transcript is the work queue so runs resume across restarts; the Harness Engineering paper calls it "the corpus's most thoroughgoing client/server architecture" and notes roughly three-fifths of its source is clients rather than harness. Second, syntax-aware command permissioning: tree-sitter parses every shell command and grants are scoped by argument arity, giving policy-as-code rulesets without a sandbox. Third, provider-native optimization from a multi-provider substrate: a nine-prompt model-family matrix, model-conditional tool surface, six-dialect cache fanout, runtime-installable providers and deliberate cross-vendor interop (it reads CLAUDE.md and .claude/skills). The loudest criticisms: no OS-level isolation and allow-by-default permissions ("agent permissions are broad by default"), slower than Claude Code on the same model, bloated prompts (a 171 KB payload on a hello-world call), a step cap that is not a hard stop and doom-loop detection that misses periodic cycles, an edit-tool description that overclaims read-before-edit enforcement, an immature in-house benchmark, two parallel release lines with v1 plugins not working in v2, `/share` pages staying public until unshared, and the Anthropic fallout that removed Claude subscription access.

unknowns: First public release date (June 19, 2025) and monthly-active-user figures come only from secondary sources (Learn AI wiki, homepage claim), not a primary changelog
npm weekly download counts (registry page blocked)
Default value of the per-agent `steps` cap is not stated in the docs; the Infinity default comes from source analysis in the Harness Engineering paper
Whether OpenCode v2.0.x is considered GA or still beta is not stated on the docs or tags pages; both v1.18.x and v2.0.x ship in parallel
Per-subagent token or time budgets: not documented
Any documented strategy for weak or small local models beyond the model-family prompt matrix and model-conditional tool surface: not documented
Official Terminal-Bench or SWE-bench submissions by the project: none found; only third-party measurements exist
A2A support: not native, only feature requests and a third-party wrapper
V2 `subagent_depth` and the v2 task-result format are documented only in v1 docs/source, not in the v2 docs pages read
