profiles.name: SWE-agent and mini-swe-agent (SWE-agent/SWE-agent, SWE-agent/mini-swe-agent)
profiles.one_liner: Princeton/Stanford research harnesses: SWE-agent (2024, NeurIPS) introduced the Agent-Computer Interface with LM-specific tools in YAML tool bundles; its successor mini-swe-agent (2025-26) is a ~100-line, bash-only, linear-history loop that is now the standard scaffold for the official SWE-bench "Bash Only" leaderboard, Terminal-Bench 4.0 (Artificial Analysis) and DeepSWE.

dimensions.identity: Both repos live under the SWE-agent GitHub org, maintained by the Princeton/Stanford SWE-bench team (John Yang, Carlos Jimenez, Kilian Lieret; Ofir Press's group), MIT-licensed, pure Python (pydantic + jinja2 + litellm; mini adds typer/rich/textual). SWE-agent went public in April 2024 (paper v1 6 May 2024, NeurIPS 2024), shipped 1.0 on 13 Feb 2025 and 1.1.0 on 22 May 2025, and its own docs now describe it as maintenance-only with development effort moved to mini-swe-agent; the GitHub page shows ~20.4k stars, 2.2k forks. mini-swe-agent first appeared on PyPI on 23 Jul 2025 (v1.1.0), moved to v2.0.0 on 11 Feb 2026 and is at v2.4.6 (23 Jul 2026) as of Sept 2026; installed as `pip install mini-swe-agent` / `uvx mini-swe-agent` / `pipx install mini-swe-agent`, it ships a CLI (`mini`, `mini -v` textual UI, `mini-extra {config,inspector,swebench,swebench-single}`) plus Python bindings. Its GitHub page read ~8k stars / 1.1k forks in Sept 2026 (a July 2026 third-party review quoted 5.6k), Python >=3.10, extras `full`, `modal`, `contree`, `dev`. The README lists Meta, NVIDIA, IBM, Nebius, Anyscale, Essential AI, Princeton and Stanford as users.
dimensions.loop: mini-swe-agent is a single ReAct-style loop with no planner: `DefaultAgent.run()` seeds `messages` with `system_template` and `instance_template`, then `while True: step()`; `step()` = `query()` (checks `0 < step_limit <= n_calls`, `0 < cost_limit <= cost`, `wall_time_limit_seconds`, then calls the model) followed by `execute_actions()`, which runs every action in `message['extra']['actions']` through `env.execute(action, cwd)` and appends observation messages built by `model.format_observation_messages()`. Control flow is exception-driven: subclasses of `InterruptAgentFlow` (`Submitted`, `LimitsExceeded`, `TimeExceeded`, `RepeatedFormatError`, `UserInterruption`) carry messages that are appended, and the loop exits when the last message has `role == 'exit'`; `run()` returns `{'exit_status', 'submission'}`. The model ends a task by running the standalone command `echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT` (v1 used `MINI_SWE_AGENT_FINAL_OUTPUT`). Defaults: `step_limit: 0` (unlimited), `cost_limit: 3.0`, `max_consecutive_format_errors: 3`; v2 allows parallel tool calls so a step may execute several bash actions. SWE-agent 1.x's `DefaultAgent.forward()` renders templates, queries, parses (`function_calling`, `thought_action`, `xml_thought_action`, `action_only`), runs `bash -n`, checks the blocklist, executes in a persistent SWE-ReX shell, runs a `state_command` returning JSON (`open_file`, `working_dir`) and renders `next_step_template` (`OBSERVATION: {{observation}}`); format/blocked/syntax errors requery up to `max_requeries: 3` then `exit_format`, with other exits `exit_cost`, `exit_context` (autosubmits `git diff`), `exit_command_timeout`, `submission`; a `RetryAgent` can wrap several `DefaultAgent` attempts under a `ScoreRetryLoop`/`ChooserRetryLoop`.
dimensions.tools: mini-swe-agent has exactly one tool, bash. Since v2.0.0 (11 Feb 2026) the default `LitellmModel` sends a native `BASH_TOOL` definition and `_parse_actions()` -> `parse_toolcall_actions()` raises `FormatError` (with `finish_reason`) for any other tool; the legacy `litellm_textbased` / `openrouter_textbased` model classes instead regex-extract a ```mswea_bash_command``` block (renamed from ```bash``` to avoid clashing with examples in prompts). Nothing is installed in the target environment because bash is assumed present. Observations are rendered by a Jinja2 `observation_template` in `mini.yaml`: `returncode` plus `output`, and if output exceeds 10,000 chars it becomes `output_head`/`output_tail` (5,000 chars each) plus `elided_chars`; `LocalEnvironment.execute()` uses `subprocess.Popen(shell=True)` with stdout+stderr merged, `timeout: 30` s default, and on timeout returns partial output, `returncode: -1` and `exception_info`. SWE-agent 1.x instead uses tool bundles: each `tools/<bundle>/` has `config.yaml` (per tool `signature`, `docstring`, `arguments[{name,type,description,required,argument_format}]`, optional `state_command`), `bin/` executables, `install.sh`, optional `lib/`; the repo ships `registry`, `edit_anthropic`, `review_on_submit_m`, `windowed`, `windowed_edit_linting`, `windowed_edit_replace`, `windowed_edit_rewrite`, `search`, `submit`, `forfeit`, `diff_state`, `filemap`, `image_tools`, `web_browser`, `multilingual_setup`, and `config/default.yaml` loads `registry` + `edit_anthropic` + `review_on_submit_m` with `parse_function: {type: function_calling}`. Observations are capped by `max_observation_length: 100000` chars with `next_step_truncated_observation_template`, and empty output is replaced by the no-output template; env vars `PAGER=cat`, `MANPAGER=cat`, `LESS=-R`, `PIP_PROGRESS_BAR=off`, `TQDM_DISABLE=1`, `GIT_PAGER=cat` suppress noisy output in both projects.
dimensions.extensibility: mini-swe-agent has no plugin registry; extension is by Python subclassing against implicit Protocols: `Model` (`query()`, `format_observation_messages()`), `Environment` (`execute(action: dict, cwd: str = '')`) and the agent's control flow. The cookbook's recipe is: pick an agent class (`DefaultAgent`, `InteractiveAgent`), an environment (`LocalEnvironment`, `DockerEnvironment`, ...), a model class, and bind them in a run script; examples override `execute_actions()` (`AgentQuitsOnSubmit`, `AgentWithPythonFunctions`, `ValidatingAgent` with a `forbidden_patterns` config) or subclass `LocalEnvironment` (`EnvironmentWithForbiddenPatterns`). Behaviour is otherwise configured in YAML (`-c` files merge recursively; `agent`, `model`, `environment` sections; Jinja2 `system_template`/`instance_template`), classes are chosen by name (`--environment-class docker|singularity`, model `litellm|openrouter|portkey|litellm_textbased`), and `MSWEA_DEFAULT_RUN` swaps the CLI entry point. Prompts, models, environments and templates are pluggable; UI and tools are not (bash is the only tool by design). SWE-agent 1.x is YAML-first where every config key maps to a CLI flag and pluggable parts are tool bundles (any language, installed into the container by `install.sh`), `history_processors`, `parse_function`, model classes, `AbstractAgentHook`s registered via `agent.add_hook()`, and SWE-ReX deployments; adding a tool means adding a bundle directory, not Python.
dimensions.context: mini-swe-agent deliberately has no compaction or summarisation: history is 'completely linear, every step just appends to the messages', so the trajectory `.traj.json` (OpenAI chat format plus an `extra` field for cost/usage/actions) is byte-identical to what the model sees, which is KV-cache/prompt-cache friendly and why RL groups adopt it; `LitellmModelConfig.set_cache_control` adds Anthropic cache markers. The only context control is per-observation truncation (10k chars, head/tail 5k) plus the `cost_limit`/`step_limit`/`MSWEA_GLOBAL_COST_LIMIT`/`MSWEA_GLOBAL_CALL_LIMIT` caps; context-window errors are non-retryable and end the run. Issue #965 'add compaction?' (opened 22 Sep 2026, citing long-horizon benchmarks) is open with no maintainer response yet. No memory files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md style) or persistent cross-run memory are documented in either project. SWE-agent 1.x manages context with `history_processors`: `LastNObservations(n, polling=1)` replaces older observations with 'Old environment output: (N lines omitted)', `ClosedWindowHistoryProcessor` keeps only the latest file window per file, `CacheControlHistoryProcessor(last_n_messages=2, tagged_roles=['user','tool'])`, `RemoveRegex`, `TagToolCallObservations`, `ImageParsingHistoryProcessor`; `max_input_tokens` is configurable and a `ContextWindowExceededError` triggers autosubmit then `exit_context`.
dimensions.permissions: mini-swe-agent's `InteractiveAgent` (the `mini` CLI) has three modes: `confirm` (default; press Enter to run, type text to reject, and the model receives 'Commands not executed. The user rejected your commands with the following message: ...'), `yolo` (`-y/--yolo`, or `/y`), and `human` (`/u`, user types commands); `whitelist_actions` is a list of regexes that skip confirmation, `confirm_exit: true` asks before finishing. There are no allow/deny rules beyond that whitelist and no workspace fence: `LocalEnvironment` is explicitly 'No isolation', so sandboxing is a choice of environment class: `DockerEnvironment` (`docker exec`), `SingularityEnvironment` (Apptainer for HPC), `BubblewrapEnvironment` (unprivileged, Linux-only, experimental), `ContreeEnvironment` (Nebius, v2.2.0), `SwerexDockerEnvironment`/`SwerexModalEnvironment`; commands run as independent `subprocess.run` calls so `cd`/`export` do not persist. Command gating is DIY via the cookbook's `forbidden_patterns` validating agent/environment. SWE-agent 1.x gates dangerous commands with `ToolFilterConfig`: `blocklist` (prefix match) defaults to `vim, vi, emacs, nano, nohup, gdb, less, tail -f, python -m venv, make`, `blocklist_standalone` (exact) to `python, python3, ipython, bash, sh, /bin/bash, /bin/sh, nohup, vi, vim, emacs, nano, su`, plus `block_unless_regex` and `blocklist_error_template` ('Operation ... is not supported by this environment'); blocked actions requery the model. Isolation comes from SWE-ReX deployments (`docker` with `image`, `docker_args`, `startup_timeout`; `modal`; `local`; `remote`; `dummy`), with `execution_timeout: 30`, `total_execution_timeout: 1800`, `max_consecutive_execution_timeouts: 3`; there is no per-action human confirmation in batch mode (the experimental `ShellAgent` is the human-in-the-loop variant).
dimensions.hooks: mini-swe-agent has no hook/event system; the documented extension points are the `InterruptAgentFlow` exception family (raise `Submitted` etc. from an overridden `execute_actions()` or from an environment's `execute()`) and subclassing. SWE-agent 1.x has `AbstractAgentHook` with `on_init`, `on_run_start`, `on_step_start`, `on_actions_generated(step)`, `on_action_started(step)`, `on_action_executed(step)`, `on_step_done(step, info)`, `on_run_done(trajectory, info)`, `on_setup_attempt`, `on_setup_done`, `on_model_query(messages, agent)`, `on_query_message_added(...)`, `on_tools_installation_started`, registered with `agent.add_hook()`. The source shows every method returns nothing: they are pure observers used for logging/saving and cannot veto or rewrite an action. Vetoing in SWE-agent happens instead through the static `ToolFilterConfig` blocklist and the `bash -n` syntax check inside the step, not through hooks. Run-level hook classes exist but their docs page did not load, so their names are not reported here.
dimensions.subagents: Not documented: neither project has a sub-agent or multi-agent facility; mini-swe-agent is by design a single linear agent, and its `DefaultAgent` has no spawn/delegate method. The closest constructs are SWE-agent's `RetryAgent` (`agent_configs` list of `DefaultAgentConfig`s, `retry_loop` of type `chooser`/`score` with `max_attempts`, `cost_limit`, `min_budget_for_new_attempt`), which runs sequential independent attempts and picks one via a reviewer, and mini-swe-agent's `RouletteModel`/`InterleavingModel` (`models/extra/roulette.py`, `swebench_roulette` config), which randomly switch the model per step within one trajectory. Nothing inherits tools or permissions from a parent, there are no depth budgets, and nothing 'returns to a parent' beyond the retry loop's `best_attempt_idx`. A third-party C++ port (`Yihao23/mini-swe-agent-cpp`) adds sub-agents and MCP but is not part of the official project.
dimensions.providers: Both go through litellm with provider-prefixed model names (`anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929`, `ollama/...`, `hosted_vllm/...`) and `api_base` for any OpenAI-compatible server. mini-swe-agent's model classes are `LitellmModel` (tool calling), `LitellmResponseModel` (OpenAI Responses API), `AnthropicModel`, `OpenRouterModel`, `PortkeyModel`, `RequestyModel`, `DeterministicModel` (tests), `RouletteModel`/`InterleavingModel`, and the `litellm_textbased`/`openrouter_textbased` classes for models without function calling; the default is set by `MSWEA_MODEL_NAME` (`mini-extra config set`), keys by `MSWEA_MODEL_API_KEY`/provider vars, retries by `MSWEA_MODEL_RETRY_STOP_AFTER_ATTEMPT` (default 10). The local-models page shows vLLM via `model_name: hosted_vllm/ricdomolm/mini-coder-1.7b`, `api_base: http://localhost:8000/v1`; Ollama appears in issues (#707, #630) as `ollama/qwen2.5:3b` with `OLLAMA_API_BASE`; unknown-cost models need a `LITELLM_MODEL_REGISTRY_PATH` JSON registry or `cost_tracking: ignore_errors` (`MSWEA_COST_TRACKING`). Weak-model handling is minimal by philosophy: the maintainers chose bash over custom tools because 'tool calling performs poorly with smaller models' (HN, Aug 2025), the `format_error_template` re-explains the `{"command": ...}` format, and `max_consecutive_format_errors: 3` stops runaway loops. SWE-agent's `GenericAPIModelConfig` adds `per_instance_cost_limit: 3.0`, `total_cost_limit: 0`, `per_instance_call_limit: 0`, `temperature: 0`, `retry: {retries: 20, min_wait: 10, max_wait: 120}`, `fallbacks`, `convert_system_to_user`, `max_input_tokens`/`max_output_tokens`, and `HumanModel`, `ReplayModel`, `InstantEmptySubmitTestModel` for testing; 1.0.1 was specifically 'fixes mostly to compatibility with local models'.
dimensions.mcp: Not documented: neither SWE-agent nor mini-swe-agent has an MCP client or server, and no ACP or A2A support is mentioned in READMEs, docs, changelogs or the FAQ. mini-swe-agent's stated position is that bash is the entire tool surface, so external tool protocols are out of scope; a search of the official repos for 'Model Context Protocol' surfaced only the unofficial `mini-swe-agent-cpp` port, which wires MCP servers from `.mini-agent/mcp.json`. SWE-agent's `web_browser` and `image_tools` bundles are bespoke bash tools, not MCP. Integration with the wider ecosystem is instead through litellm (any provider), SWE-ReX (execution backends) and `sb-cli` (SWE-bench evaluation).
dimensions.evals: SWE-bench is the home benchmark: the 2024 paper reported 12.5% pass@1 on SWE-bench and 87.7% on HumanEvalFix with GPT-4 and ACI ablations (linting, 100-line windowed viewer, summarised search); SWE-agent 1.0 + Claude 3.7 was SOTA on full and Verified in Feb 2025; mini-swe-agent hit 65% Verified in July 2025 and the README now claims >74%. Since 2025 swebench.com's 'Bash Only' leaderboard runs every model through mini-swe-agent with one system prompt; the Feb 2026 refresh (v2, tool calling; v1/v2 results 'not necessarily comparable') gave Claude 4.5 Opus 76.8%, Gemini 3 Flash 75.8%, MiniMax M2.5 75.8%, Claude Opus 4.6 75.6%, GLM-5 and GPT-5.2 72.8%. Artificial Analysis runs all 66 Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks 'with the mini-swe-agent harness', pass@1 over three repeats; DeepSWE (Jul 2026, 113 long-horizon tasks) fixes mini-swe-agent across 16 model configs and its n=10 pilot found mini-swe-agent at parity or better than native harnesses (Opus 4.7: 50% vs Claude Code 40%; GPT-5.5: 40% vs Codex CLI 40%; Gemini 3.1 Pro: 40% vs Gemini CLI 20%); ProgramBench (v2.3.0 support) runs it with a $3 cap. Harness-vs-model evidence: SambaNova (Nov 2025) measured DeepSeek-R1-0528 at 30.3% with mini-swe-agent vs 7%/0% single-shot; the Aug 2025 'roulette' post showed GPT-5+Sonnet-4 step-mixing beating either alone (~$0.30/instance); Epoch AI deliberately uses its own loop with `bash`, `text_editor` and `apply_patch` tools and 2M-token budgets rather than mini-swe-agent. `mini-extra swebench --subset verified --split test --workers N` writes `preds.json` for `sb-cli`.
dimensions.distinctive: Three ideas: (1) the Agent-Computer Interface, the claim that LMs are a new class of user needing purpose-built tools, realised as guardrails (linter-gated edits, a 100-line windowed viewer, search that lists only matching files, 'Your command ran successfully and did not produce any output') and shipped as language-agnostic YAML tool bundles installed into the sandbox; (2) mini-swe-agent's radical minimalism as an empirical counter-claim to (1) for frontier models: one bash tool, one `subprocess.run` per action with no stateful shell, and an append-only linear history identical to the trajectory, which made it the neutral 'measure the model, not the scaffold' harness for SWE-bench Bash-Only, Terminal-Bench 4.0, DeepSWE and RL fine-tuning pipelines; (3) exception-as-control-flow (`Submitted`, `LimitsExceeded`) plus Jinja/YAML templates, so a teaching-sized loop stays hackable while cost/step/wall-clock limits are first-class. Loudest criticisms: the HN launch thread objected that '100 lines' hides ~120 lines of prompt YAML, that no `cd`/`export` persistence and no context compaction hurt long tasks, and that generic bash under-serves small models compared to guided tools (the maintainer replied it refutes the original ACI hypothesis for large LMs); a July 2026 review calls it not beginner-friendly, a shell-access risk on `LocalEnvironment`, sparse in UX, and warns SWE-bench success is not daily-driver fit; the v2 pivot to native tool calling quietly retired the 'no tool-calling interface' selling point that the README still advertises; and SWE-agent 1.x is effectively frozen in maintenance mode with hooks that observe but cannot veto.

unknowns: subagents: no sub-agent/multi-agent facility is documented in either project (only RetryAgent and RouletteModel as loose analogues)
mcp: no MCP/ACP/A2A support found in any official README, doc or changelog
hooks (mini-swe-agent): no hook/event system exists; SWE-agent run-level hook class names not verified because swe-agent.com/latest/usage/hooks/ returned 404
context: no memory-file or persistent-memory mechanism documented; compaction status only known from open issue #965 with no maintainer reply
identity: mini-swe-agent star count is inconsistent across sources (~8k on the GitHub page in Sept 2026 vs 5.6k in a July 2026 review); PyPI download counts not found
providers: Ollama configuration is only evidenced in GitHub issue search snippets (#707, #630), not in the official local-models page
evals: exact ACI ablation numbers from the paper were not read (abstract only); the '~2x GPT-4 with ACI vs raw bash' figure comes from a secondary article
loop: SWE-agent release years were inferred (release page rendered month/day only); 1.0 = 13 Feb 2025 per docs

profiles.name: Goose (aaif-goose/goose, formerly block/goose)
profiles.one_liner: Rust-native, MCP-everything agent host (desktop, CLI, ACP server) originally from Block and now governed by the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation: bring your own model (60+ providers incl. Ollama and embedded llama.cpp), bring your own tools (MCP servers), with recipes, subagents, hooks and Code Mode layered on a single tool loop.

dimensions.identity: Created at Block, Inc. and publicly launched as "codename goose" 1.0 on January 28, 2025; donated to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) at the Linux Foundation in December 2025 alongside MCP and AGENTS.md, with the repo and docs moving from block/goose to github.com/aaif-goose/goose and goose-docs.ai on April 7, 2026. Apache-2.0. Core is Rust (crates: goose, goose-agent, goose-cli, goose-mcp, goose-providers, goose-context-management, goose-local-inference, goose-sdk with UniFFI cross-language bindings) plus a TypeScript/Electron desktop app. Distributed as a desktop app (macOS/Linux/Windows, auto-updater since v1.49), a CLI (`curl .../releases/download/stable/download_cli.sh | bash`), an ACP server (`goose acp` over stdio, `goose serve` over HTTP/WebSocket, default port 3284), and forkable "custom distributions". README shows 54.7k stars, 6.3k forks, 5,733 commits (Sept 2026); releases are roughly weekly, latest v1.52.0 on Sept 23, 2026. Download counts are not published.
dimensions.loop: A single ReAct-style tool loop: the user request plus the tool list goes to the provider, tool calls are executed, results are appended, and the loop repeats until the model replies without tool requests; a "context revision" step removes old content along the way. Errors such as invalid JSON or unknown tools are returned to the model as tool responses rather than aborting. Since v1.46.0 (Aug 12, 2026, PR #9574 "Unrolled agent loop") the loop is a re-entrant state machine: "Each call runs from the persisted conversation to the next applied step or client yield; no coroutine state is held between steps", with ordered steps for approval, cooperative execution, unknown-tool recovery and context compaction (the latter with per-reply retry budgets). Step limits: `GOOSE_MAX_TURNS` default 1000 turns without user input (`--max-turns` on `goose session`/`goose run`), `--max-tool-repetitions` to break tool loops, `GOOSE_SUBAGENT_MAX_TURNS` 25, and recipe `settings.max_turns`; hitting the cap is persisted as a message. A turn also ends on cancellation, a client yield (approval/elicitation), or a Stop hook. Headless: `goose run -t/-i/--recipe --no-session --output-format text|json|stream-json`.
dimensions.tools: Every tool is an MCP tool; the built-ins are Rust MCP servers in the goose-mcp crate, runnable standalone via `goose mcp <name>` and enabled with `--with-builtin <id>`. The default-on Developer extension exposes `shell`, `write`, `edit` (exact-text replace), `tree` (directory tree with line counts) and `read_image`; other built-ins are Computer Controller, Memory, Tutorial and Auto Visualiser, and "platform extensions" include Analyze, Apps, Chat Recall, Code Mode, Extension Manager, Skills, Summon (delegate), Todo and Top of Mind. Third-party tools are registered in `config.yaml` under `extensions:` with `type: stdio|streamable_http|builtin`, `cmd`, `args`, `envs`, `enabled` and a per-extension `timeout` in seconds (e.g. 300). Tool results: `GOOSE_MAX_TOOL_RESPONSE_SIZE` (default 200000 characters) is the cutoff beyond which a response "is written to a temporary file instead of being included inline"; `GOOSE_TOOL_CALL_CUTOFF` (computed from context limit and compaction threshold) keeps the N most recent tool calls in full and summarises older outputs; shell output streams while a command runs (v1.46). User-facing verbosity is separate (`GOOSE_CLI_MIN_PRIORITY`, `/r` toggle, `GOOSE_MAX_CODE_BLOCK_LINES` 50).
dimensions.extensibility: Almost everything is pluggable. Tools: any MCP server (stdio or streamable HTTP, OAuth client support since v1.47) added via `goose configure` or `--with-extension`. Providers: declarative JSON in `~/.config/goose/providers/<name>.json` with `engine: openai|anthropic|ollama`, `host`, `models[]` (`context_window`, `supports_tools`, `supports_vision`), `auth` (header/query/oauth) and `extra_headers`, or a Rust `Provider` trait implementation; 47 declarative definitions ship. Prompts: eight Jinja2 templates overridable in `~/.config/goose/prompts/` (system.md, compaction.md, permission_judge.md, subagent_system.md, tiny_model_system.md, session_name.md, apps_*.md). Behaviour packages: hooks and skills bundled as Open Plugins (`plugin.json` + `hooks/hooks.json`, installed with `goose plugin install <git-url>` into `~/.agents/plugins/` or `<project>/.agents/plugins/`), Agent Skills (`SKILL.md` in `~/.agents/skills/`, `.agents/skills/`, with `.claude/skills/` compatibility), custom agents (Markdown+YAML in `~/.agents/agents/`), recipes (YAML), slash commands. UI: any ACP client can drive goose, and organisations can fork a "custom distribution" preconfigured via `init-config.yaml` (providers, bundled extensions, branding, allowlist).
dimensions.context: Two-tier context management: auto-compaction fires at `GOOSE_AUTO_COMPACT_THRESHOLD` 0.8 of the context limit (0.0 disables), and if the limit is still exceeded `GOOSE_CONTEXT_STRATEGY` applies `summarize|truncate|clear|prompt` (prompt is the interactive CLI default, summarize the headless default, Desktop is summarize-only); `/compact` triggers it manually, the summary prompt is `compaction.md`, `GOOSE_CONTEXT_LIMIT` overrides the window (128k or model-specific), and `GOOSE_TOOL_CALL_CUTOFF` summarises old tool outputs first. Memory files: goose reads `AGENTS.md` then `.goosehints` by default, globally from `~/.config/goose/.goosehints` and hierarchically from cwd up to the repo root (local wins on conflict); `CONTEXT_FILE_NAMES` (JSON array) adds `CLAUDE.md` or `.cursorrules`. Persistent memory comes from the Memory extension (`remember_memory`, `retrieve_memories`, `remove_memory_category`, `remove_specific_memory`, stored in `.goose/memory/` locally and `~/.config/goose/memory/` globally), plus Chat Recall, Top of Mind, per-turn "persistent instructions" and progressively-loaded Skills (names/descriptions at session start, body on demand). KV/prompt-cache friendliness is explicit since v1.46: "cache-safe request assembly with append-only turn context and declared cache semantics", `GOOSE_CACHE_TTL` 5m|1h for Anthropic (headless always 5m), and per-message token/cost/TTFT/tok-per-s tracking.
dimensions.permissions: Four modes via `GOOSE_MODE`, `goose configure` > goose settings > goose mode, or `/mode`: `auto` (the documented default: "goose can modify files, use extensions, and delete files without requiring approval"), `smart_approve` (risk-based, uses the `permission_judge.md` prompt plus tool annotations), `approve` (confirm every tool), `chat` (no tools). Per-tool overrides of Always Allow / Ask Before / Never Allow layer on top (`goose configure` > Tool Permission or Desktop settings). Extra gates: adversary mode (create `~/.config/goose/adversary.md` with plain-language rules and an independent reviewer on the same model returns ALLOW/BLOCK before every tool call; errors fail open), prompt-injection detection (`SECURITY_PROMPT_ENABLED` default false, `SECURITY_PROMPT_THRESHOLD` 0.8, pattern plus optional ML classifier on tool parameters, warns with Allow Once/Deny), `GOOSE_ALLOWLIST` URL restricting which MCP server commands may be installed (corporate), a "Trust and Execute" consent dialog for recipes, and since v1.49 "per-turn model tool allowlists". Sandboxing: there is no built-in OS sandbox or workspace fence; `--container <id>` runs the extensions (not the agent) inside a Docker container, and isolation is otherwise delegated to Container Use MCP, devcontainers or third-party wrappers. MCP roots share the cwd but the docs "do not address file access restrictions". Open issue #12448 (Sept 22, 2026) argues the `GooseMode::Auto` default silently auto-approves every tool on a fresh install.
dimensions.hooks: Lifecycle hooks follow the Open Plugins hooks spec (shipped v1.46, Aug 2026; blog May 14, 2026). Twelve events: SessionStart, SessionEnd, Stop, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PreToolUseResult, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, BeforeReadFile, AfterFileEdit, BeforeShellExecution, AfterShellExecution. Config lives in `~/.agents/plugins/<name>/hooks/hooks.json` or `<project>/.agents/plugins/<name>/hooks/hooks.json` as `{"hooks": {"Event": [{"matcher": "<unanchored regex>", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "${PLUGIN_ROOT}/x.sh", "timeout": 30, "on_failure": "allow|block"}]}]}}`, with the event payload (including `tool_input`) on stdin. Veto is real but limited: only PreToolUse and Stop can block, by exiting 2 (reason from stderr) or printing `{"decision":"block","reason":"..."}`; exit 0 with empty stdout allows, and `on_failure: block` denies when the hook itself crashes (default `allow`). Hooks cannot modify tool input.
dimensions.subagents: Children are spawned three ways: the model may "autonomously decide to use subagents" in auto mode, a recipe's `sub_recipes: [{name, path, values}]` each become a tool that "executes the subrecipe in a separate session with its own context", or a custom agent is invoked with "Delegate to code-reviewer: ..."; the `summon` platform extension supplies the `delegate` tool. By default subagents inherit all extensions from the parent session (restrictable by prompt or recipe), run under the `subagent_system.md` prompt, and a recipe can pin `settings.goose_provider`/`goose_model`. Limits: `GOOSE_SUBAGENT_MAX_TURNS` 25 (overridable by recipe `settings.max_turns`), a 5-minute default timeout, and no nesting ("subrecipes cannot define their own subrecipes"; subagents are blocked from spawning subagents, managing extensions or schedules, and v1.51 "Enforce subagent platform guards"). Execution is sequential by default, parallel on request. The parent receives structured JSON: `execution_summary` {total_tasks, successful_tasks, failed_tasks, execution_time_seconds} and `task_results[]` {task_id, status, result}; a failed or timed-out subagent yields no output.
dimensions.providers: 60+ providers selected with `GOOSE_PROVIDER`/`GOOSE_MODEL` (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry, Mistral, Groq, DeepSeek, xAI, OpenRouter, LiteLLM, many regional gateways), plus ACP providers that wrap Claude Code, Codex, Amp and Pi subscriptions. Local: Ollama (`OLLAMA_HOST`, `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH`), LM Studio, Ramalama, Docker Model Runner, vLLM/KServe through the OpenAI-compatible `OPENAI_HOST`, and since April 2026 a built-in Local provider that embeds llama.cpp in-process (goose-local-inference crate, GGUF from HuggingFace, `goose local-models`, with Gemma 4 recommended for native tool calling). Weak-model handling: `GOOSE_TOOLSHIM=true` (default false) routes text-formatted tool calls through an interpreter model (`GOOSE_TOOLSHIM_OLLAMA_MODEL` default mistral-nemo; `GOOSE_TOOLSHIM_BACKEND` ollama|local|llama.cpp), the `tiny_model_system.md` prompt emulates tools mostly via shell, and the docs warn that goose "relies heavily on tool calling capabilities and currently works best with Claude 4 models". The 2025 lead/worker split (`GOOSE_LEAD_MODEL`) "has been removed from goose"; multi-model today means `/model` switching and per-subagent models.
dimensions.mcp: Goose is an MCP client host end to end: stdio, streamable HTTP and builtin transports, OAuth for extensions (v1.47), MCP elicitation (form mode, 5-minute timeout), MCP roots (a single root = session cwd, updated on directory change), MCP Apps, and Code Mode which wraps MCP tools as callable TypeScript functions; the built-in extensions are themselves MCP servers exposed by `goose mcp <name>`. ACP: goose is a native ACP server (`goose acp` stdio, `goose serve` HTTP/WebSocket with `GOOSE_SERVER__SECRET_KEY`) used by Zed and JetBrains, and discussion #7309 (Feb 18, 2026) makes ACP "the primary interface for all goose clients" with a plan to move the desktop to ACP and retire goosed/goose-cli; goose is also an ACP client through ACP providers, passing its extensions to the remote agent as MCP servers. "MCP remains the protocol for extensions." A2A support is not documented.
dimensions.evals: The project publishes no SWE-bench or Terminal-Bench numbers; issue #895 (Jan 2025) asking for benchmarks closed without a published result, and no goose entry was found on tbench.ai leaderboards. The only first-party evaluation is the "Goose Vibe Check" blog (Mar 31, 2025): 8 tasks x 3 runs across 32 models, claude-3-5-sonnet 1.00, best open model qwen2.5-coder:32b 0.80, and "none of the models configured with the toolshim greater than a 41% success rate". The strongest third-party measurement is "The Scaffold Effect" (arXiv 2607.22585, Jul 28, 2026): on a 50-task Terminal-Bench Pro subset with Qwen 3.6 Plus / MiniMax M2.5, Goose scored 48%/38% vs OpenCode 50%/46% and OpenHands-SDK 50%/46%, but used 28,142 / 36,950 tokens per solved task (OpenCode ~40x more), 0.2-0.3 no-action turns, REASON-dominated failures ("stops rather than commit to a wrong solution"), 38% vs OpenHands 69% on fresh-implementation tasks, and is characterised as a "heavyweight IDE agent with eager file-tree pre-injection". A secondary review's "~75% SWE-bench" claim is unsourced. No harness-vs-model ablation is published by the project itself.
dimensions.distinctive: Distinctive ideas: (1) the host inversion, "you bring the model, you bring the tools, and Goose orchestrates them", taken to the limit: built-in tools are MCP servers, providers are JSON manifests, prompts are templates, and ACP is becoming the client interface, so goose is a protocol hub rather than a product; (2) Code Mode, where the model writes TypeScript executed by the Deno-based pctx runtime against three meta-tools (`list_functions`, `get_function_details`, `execute_typescript`), collapsing many tool calls into one step and keeping tool definitions out of context; (3) recipes as shareable YAML agents (instructions, prompt, extensions, parameters, `sub_recipes`, `response.json_schema`, `retry.checks`, `settings`, goose:// deeplinks, scheduler) plus adversary mode, an LLM reviewer that vetoes tool calls. Loudest criticisms: the auto-approve default (issue #12448; vibecodinghub Aug 2026), recipe supply-chain risk (issue #10325 Jul 2026 showed a shared recipe's stdio `cmd` ran with no consent, fixed in PR #12094 and v1.52 "Require recipe consent"; Block's own red team planted an infostealer via a hidden-Unicode poisoned recipe, The Register Jan 12, 2026), no built-in sandbox, polish and inner-loop speed "a notch below the most refined commercial agents" and extension configuration friction (dev.to Jun 2026), setup burden and diluted non-coding scope, and the Scaffold Effect finding that it gives up early and lags on fresh-implementation tasks.

unknowns: Download/install counts (only GitHub stars/forks are public)
Exact algorithm behind smart_approve risk classification (beyond the permission_judge.md prompt and tool annotations)
Whether multiple tool calls in one model turn are dispatched in parallel
Whether MCP roots impose any file-access restriction (docs say they do not address it)
Any official Terminal-Bench or SWE-bench submission (none found)
Per-direction (input/output) token accounting exposed by the harness (the Scaffold Effect paper notes goose reports totals only via Harbor)
A2A or other non-MCP/ACP integration standards (not documented)

profiles.name: Cursor CLI, Amp, Pi, Crush, Qwen Code, Kimi Code CLI (group profile of six second-tier harnesses)
profiles.one_liner: Six terminal coding-agent harnesses that bracket the design space in Sept 2026: two closed, vendor-hosted products (Cursor CLI, Amp), one radically minimal open toolkit whose whole thesis is "no permission system, everything is an extension" (Pi), one TUI-first open Go agent (Crush), and two model-vendor harnesses that ship Claude-Code-shaped feature sets around their own models (Qwen Code, Kimi Code CLI; the Python "Kimi CLI" was archived in 2026 and replaced by the TypeScript "Kimi Code CLI").

dimensions.identity: Cursor CLI: Anysphere/Cursor; beta launched 7 Aug 2025 (`curl https://cursor.com/install -fsS | bash`, command `agent`, originally `cursor-agent`); proprietary, closed source, works only with a Cursor subscription; distributed as CLI + IDE + Cloud Agents; no public repo or star count. Amp: Amp Inc. (spun out of Sourcegraph on 2 Dec 2025, led by Quinn Slack and Beyang Liu); public preview May 2025; closed source, hosted service; CLI via shell installer/Homebrew/npm plus web app, macOS/iOS apps and VS Code extension (JetBrains deprecated); Hobby tier free, Individual $20/mo, no markup on provider token prices; no star count. Pi: Mario Zechner (badlogic), now under Earendil (`earendil-works/pi-mono`, repo moved 7 May 2026 with v0.74.0; old badlogic URL redirects); monorepo begun Aug 2025, design write-up 30 Nov 2025; MIT; TypeScript; npm `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` (v0.85.1, 5 Sep 2026) plus `pi-agent-core`, `pi-ai`, `pi-tui` libraries and a TypeScript SDK; 109.5k stars / 13.9k forks; a Sept 2026 review cites ~1.53M weekly npm downloads for the CLI and 5.12M for pi-tui. Crush: Charm (`charmbracelet/crush`); descends from Kujtim Hoxha's TermAI/OpenCode (Apr-May 2025), rebranded Crush in July 2025; FSL-1.1-MIT; Go single binary; 28.3k stars; v0.96.1 released 21 Sep 2026. Qwen Code: QwenLM/Alibaba; launched July 2025 alongside Qwen3-Coder, originally a fork of Gemini CLI v0.8.2 and independent since v0.1; Apache-2.0; TypeScript; npm `@qwen-code/qwen-code` plus VS Code/Zed/JetBrains plugins, Telegram/DingTalk/WeChat/Feishu integrations and TS/Python/Java SDKs; 28.1k stars; v0.24.6 released 26 Sep 2026. Kimi Code CLI: Moonshot AI; the original Python Kimi CLI (Apache-2.0) shipped as a technical preview on 27 Oct 2025 and is now archived (11.4k stars; its 1.52.0 release turned `uv tool install kimi-cli` into an installer for the successor); the TypeScript rewrite `MoonshotAI/kimi-code` is MIT, single-binary, first changelog entry 0.14.0 on 10 Jun 2026, latest 2.1.1 on 24 Sep 2026, 7.7k stars, installed via `npm install -g @moonshot-ai/kimi-code` or `code.kimi.com/kimi-code/install.sh`.
dimensions.loop: All six are single-agent tool-calling loops (no planner/executor split, no code-as-action); differences are in queueing, budgets and modes. Pi documents it most plainly: "A submitted message is added to the active branch. Pi builds a model request from the system prompt, active branch, available tools, and model settings... If tool results or queued messages require another model request, Pi starts another turn. Otherwise, the run ends"; steering messages (Enter) land after the current assistant turn, follow-ups (Alt+Enter) after the agent finishes; no step limit is documented. Crush runs a `SessionAgent` on the `charm.land/fantasy` provider abstraction, executes every tool call of a step before the next model call, and evaluates its auto-summarize stop condition only between steps (issue #3620); it has two named agent prompts, `coder.md.tpl` and `task.md.tpl`, managed by a Coordinator. Qwen Code inherits the Gemini CLI loop and is the only member with explicit run budgets: `--max-session-turns N` (exit code 53), `--max-tool-calls N` (exit 55), `--max-wall-time 5m`, plus `QWEN_CODE_UNATTENDED_RETRY=1`; its own SWE-bench harness runs with `max_iterations=500`. Kimi Code CLI "chooses the next step based on the feedback it receives", auto-runs read-only tools, confirms edits/commands, records each agent's turn as `agents/*/wire.jsonl`, and allows `Ctrl-S` mid-stream injection and `Shift-Tab`/`--plan` Plan mode. Cursor CLI has Agent/Plan/Ask modes (`--mode=plan|ask`, Shift+Tab), lets you steer a running turn by typing, and since Aug 2026 "single-turn runs wait for their subagents" before `-p` exits; `&` hands the thread to a Cloud Agent. Amp fixes a Dial mode (`low/medium/high/ultra`, `Ctrl+S`) per thread that cannot be changed later, `amp -x` "waits until the agent ends its turn, prints its final message, and exits", and a plugin `agent.end` handler may return `{ action: 'continue', userMessage }` to auto-chain another turn.
dimensions.tools: Pi: built-ins listed in the `defaultTools` setting are `read, bash, powershell, edit, write, grep, find, ls` (the original four were read/write/edit/bash); extension tools are registered in-process via `pi.registerTool()` with a TypeBox schema and `execute()`; tool-output truncation limits are not documented in the pages read. Crush: each tool is a `.go` file plus a `.md` description in `internal/agent/tools/` (bash, edit, multiedit, view, write, grep, glob, ls, fetch, web_fetch, web_search, sourcegraph, diagnostics, download, todos, question, `lsp_definition/symbols/call_hierarchy/rename/replace_symbol`, `job_output/job_kill`, `list_mcp_resources/read_mcp_resource`); bash output is capped by `const MaxOutputLength = 30000` with head+tail retention, a `"... [%d lines truncated] ..."` marker and spill to file, and commands running past `DefaultAutoBackgroundAfter = 60` seconds are moved to a background job. Qwen Code: `run_shell_command`, `monitor` (long-lived streaming commands), `web_fetch`, `web_search`, `todo_write`, `agent`, `exit_plan_mode` plus file tools, external tools via `tools.discoveryCommand`/`tools.callCommand`; truncation is governed by `tools.enableToolOutputTruncation` (true), `truncateToolOutputThreshold` (25,000 chars) and `truncateToolOutputLines` (1,000) for Shell/Grep/Glob/ReadFile/ReadManyFiles. Kimi Code CLI: `Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, ReadMediaFile, Bash, WebSearch, FetchURL, EnterPlanMode/ExitPlanMode, TodoList, Agent, AgentSwarm, AskUserQuestion, NotifyUser, Skill, TaskList/TaskOutput/TaskStop/WaitFor, CronCreate/CronList/CronDelete`; `Read` returns 100,000 chars by default (max 500,000), `Grep` `head_limit` 250, `Glob` 100 entries. Cursor CLI exposes tool families only through its permission syntax (`Shell(...)`, `Read(...)`, `Write(...)`, `WebFetch(...)`, `Mcp(server:tool)`); no full list or truncation rule is documented. Amp: the list is obtained by `amp tools list`; named tools include Oracle, Librarian, Painter, Search and Read Thread, tools can be hidden with `amp.tools.disable`, and plugins add tools via `amp.registerTool({ name, title, description, inputSchema, execute })` returning a string or text/image content blocks; truncation is not documented.
dimensions.extensibility: Pi is the purest plugin model: an extension is a TypeScript module `export default function (pi: ExtensionAPI)` in `~/.pi/agent/extensions/` or `.pi/extensions`, and it can register tools, `/` commands (`pi.registerCommand`), shortcuts, flags, providers (`pi.registerProvider`) and message renderers, subscribe to lifecycle events, and is complemented by skills (SKILL.md), prompt templates (`~/.pi/agent/prompts`), themes, `SYSTEM.md`/`APPEND_SYSTEM.md`, and installable packages listed in the `packages` setting. Amp's Plugin API is the closed-source analogue: TypeScript/JS plugins in `.amp/plugins/` or `~/.config/amp/plugins/` export a default function receiving `PluginAPI`, with `amp.on()` events, `registerTool`, `registerCommand`, `registerSkill`, `createAgent`/`registerAgentMode`, `amp.ai.ask()` yes/no classification and `createWebhook`; precedence is project > system > personal > workspace, and skills are read from `.agents/skills`, `.claude/skills`, `~/.config/agents/skills` and `amp.skills.path`. Crush has no plugin API; it is extended through the Bash-based `crushrc` (`provider add`, `model add`, `lsp add`, `mcp add`, `permissions allow|deny`, `option`), MCP servers, LSP servers, Agent-Skills-standard skills (`.agents/skills`, `.crush/skills`, `.claude/skills`, `.cursor/skills`), JSON themes and a single PreToolUse hook. Qwen Code extensions are directories with a `qwen-extension.json` manifest (`name, version, mcpServers, contextFileName, commands, skills, agents, workflows, settings`) installed with `qwen extensions install <git|npm|path|archive>` into `~/.qwen/extensions`, alongside `.qwen/skills/SKILL.md`, hooks and Markdown subagents. Kimi Code CLI plugins carry a `kimi.plugin.json` (`skills, agents, commands, mcpServers, systemPrompt(Path), sessionStart.skill, hooks`) installed by `/plugins install <github-url|path>` into `$KIMI_CODE_HOME/plugins/managed/<id>/`. Cursor CLI is extended by rules (`.cursor/rules/*.mdc` with `description/globs/alwaysApply`, `AGENTS.md`), skills, `hooks.json`, `.cursor/agents/` subagents, MCP, and installed plugins whose hooks run in the CLI (Aug 2026 changelog).
dimensions.context: Pi loads `AGENTS.override.md`, `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` from the agent dir, the cwd and its parents; sessions are JSONL trees (each entry has an id and parent) navigated with `/tree`, `/fork`, `/clone`; compaction "inserts a summary entry that replaces older messages in subsequent model requests" while keeping the originals, tuned by `compaction.enabled/reserveTokens/keepRecentTokens/modelOverrides` and `branchSummary.*`, with `cacheWarming` and `showCacheMissNotices` settings for KV-cache hygiene; a Sept 2026 review measured a 1,358-token context floor versus Claude Code's 31,012. Crush reads `~/.config/crush/CRUSH.md`, `~/.config/AGENTS.md` and a project `AGENTS.md` (created by `crush init`, name set by `option initialize-as`, extra paths via `option context-path`), persists sessions in SQLite, and has `option auto-summarize`; issue #3620 documents a flat 20,000-token `largeContextWindowBuffer` above a 200k window, and issues #2551/#3867 document summary-as-task loops. Qwen Code uses `QWEN.md` (`~/.qwen/QWEN.md`, project root, `.qwen/QWEN.local.md`, `@path` imports, `context.fileName`), an Auto-Memory store in `~/.qwen/projects/<project>/memory/` with `/remember`, `/forget`, `/dream` (dedup) and `/memory`, manual `/compress`, `context.autoCompactThreshold` (default 0.85) and `model.chatCompression.maxRecentFilesToRetain` (default 5); fork subagents share the parent's exact system prompt to preserve prompt-cache prefixes. Kimi Code CLI follows the AGENTS.md convention (`~/.kimi-code/AGENTS.md`, `~/.agents/AGENTS.md`, project and subdirectory `AGENTS.md`, detection order AGENTS.md > .cursorrules > KIMI.md), compacts automatically near the window limit with `/compact [hint]` and `/fork`, and stores `state.json` + `wire.jsonl` under `~/.kimi-code/sessions/`. Cursor CLI loads `.cursor/rules`, nested `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`, offers `/summarize` or `/compress`, a `preCompact` hook and `@` mentions, and advises rules under 500 lines. Amp searches `AGENTS.md` from the cwd up to `$HOME`, pulls subtree `AGENTS.md` when files there are read, adds `~/.config/amp/AGENTS.md` and `/etc/ampcode/AGENTS.md`, falls back to `AGENT.md`/`CLAUDE.md`, supports `@`-mentions gated by `globs` frontmatter and `AMP_IGNORE_GUIDANCE_FILES`; threads live server-side at `ampcode.com/threads/T-…`, and instead of in-place compaction the idiom is "Handoff and …" to a fresh thread, with cheaper "system models" doing summarisation.
dimensions.permissions: Pi: none by design; "Pi can read, change, and execute files with the permissions of the account that started it, and it does not ask for approval before every tool call"; the docs point to Docker (`pi-sandbox` Dockerfile), Docker Sandboxes (`sbx run --kit docker.io/sbx/pi-kit:latest pi`), the Gondolin micro-VM extension and NVIDIA OpenShell; project trust only gates loading `.pi/` extensions/settings and "does not limit what tool calls can access"; print mode takes `--approve`/`--no-approve`. Crush prompts per tool call by default, `permissions allow <tools>` pre-approves, `permissions deny` hides tools, `--yolo` skips everything; the bash tool hard-bans 54 commands (curl, wget, ssh, sudo, apt, npm…) with `ArgumentsBlocker` rules and a `safeCommands` bypass only when no command chaining; no sandbox. Qwen Code: `tools.approvalMode` = `plan|default|auto-edit|auto|yolo` (Shift+Tab, `/approval-mode`), `permissions.allow`/`permissions.deny` rules (replacing `tools.allowed/exclude`), an Auto Mode LLM classifier "biased toward blocking when uncertain" with `permissions.autoMode.hints` and a fallback to manual after three consecutive blocks; sandboxing via `-s/--sandbox`, `QWEN_SANDBOX=true|false|docker|podman|sandbox-exec`, six macOS Seatbelt profiles (`permissive-open` default) and `tools.executionSandbox { filesystem: read-only|workspace-write, network: open|closed, backend: auto|bwrap }`. Kimi Code CLI: `default_permission_mode = manual|yolo|auto` (`--yolo` = "Ask When Needed", `--auto` = "Never Ask"), `[[permission.rules]]` with `decision = allow|deny|ask` and `pattern = "Bash(rm -rf*)"`, MCP tools matched as `mcp__<server>__<tool>`; Auto mode blocks shutdown/reboot/rm -rf (0.40.0) and 2.1.0 blocks symlink escapes from the workspace; no container sandbox documented. Cursor CLI: `permissions.allow/deny` in `~/.cursor/cli-config.json` and `<project>/.cursor/cli.json` using `Shell()/Read()/Write()/WebFetch()/Mcp()` (deny wins); run modes Allowlist / Auto-review / Run Everything (`approvalMode: allowlist|auto-review|unrestricted`), an OS sandbox (`sandbox.mode`, `sandbox.networkAccess`, `sandbox.json` for network policy and extra paths, read-access boundary added Aug 2026), a classifier steered by `permissions.json` `allow_instructions/block_instructions`, `--force`/`--yolo`, `--trust`, `--approve-mcps`, and sudo passwords passed over IPC so "the AI model never sees it". Amp: "does not ask for approval before running tools" by default; policy is a plugin `tool.call` handler returning `allow | reject-and-continue | modify | synthesize | error` (the docs' example uses `amp.ai.ask()` to classify destructive git commands), plus `amp.mcpPermissions`, mandatory `amp mcp approve` for workspace MCP servers, and Orbs as per-thread isolated remote machines.
dimensions.hooks: Cursor: `hooks.json` (`~/.cursor/hooks.json`, `.cursor/hooks.json`, `"version": 1`) with events `sessionStart/sessionEnd, preToolUse/postToolUse/postToolUseFailure, subagentStart/subagentStop, beforeShellExecution/afterShellExecution, beforeMCPExecution/afterMCPExecution, beforeReadFile, afterFileEdit, beforeSubmitPrompt, preCompact, stop, afterAgentResponse, afterAgentThought, workspaceOpen`; permission hooks return `permission: allow|deny|ask` with `user_message`/`agent_message`, exit code 2 blocks, invalid JSON blocks, other failures fail open unless `failClosed: true`, `loop_limit` defaults to 5, and `type: prompt` hooks let an LLM judge. Qwen Code: `hooks` key in settings.json with 20+ events (`PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PostToolBatch, SessionStart/End/Delete, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStart/Stop, PreCompact/PostCompact, PermissionRequest, Notification…`), hook types command/http/function/prompt, veto via `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision: "deny"` or exit 2. Kimi Code CLI: `[[hooks]]` entries in `config.toml` (`event, matcher, command, timeout` 1-600s default 30) over 20 events, of which `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse` and `Stop` can block (exit 2 = block, other non-zero = fail-open) using the same `permissionDecision` JSON. Crush: only `PreToolUse` ("with plans to support the full gamut") in `crush.json` with regex `matcher`, `command`, `timeout`; exit 2 blocks the call, exit 49 halts the turn, output `decision` allow/deny plus `context` and shallow-merge `updated_input`, explicitly "broadly compatible with Claude Code hooks". Pi: in-process typed events `session_start, session_shutdown, before_agent_start, tool_call (can mutate input or block), tool_result, turn_end, agent_end, context, provider_stream_event, input`. Amp: plugin events `session.start, agent.start, agent.end, tool.call, tool.result, changes.prompt`, with `tool.call` as the veto point. All six can veto a tool call; only Cursor, Qwen Code and Kimi Code also veto at prompt-submit or stop.
dimensions.subagents: Cursor: Markdown agents in `.cursor/agents/` (also reads `.claude/agents/`, `.codex/agents/`, `~/.cursor/agents/`) with frontmatter `name, description, model (inherit|id), readonly, is_background`; built-in Explore, Bash and Browser subagents; invoked by a Task tool or `/name`, run in parallel, inherit all parent tools including MCP, have their own context, "the main agent only sees the final summary", background state is written to `~/.cursor/subagents/`, and nesting is capped: a subagent launched by a subagent cannot launch further ones. Amp: Search, Oracle, Librarian, Read Thread and Painter run in isolated context windows, "can't communicate with each other", start only with what the parent gives them and return a final summary; plugins add custom subagents with `amp.createAgent`. Qwen Code: `.qwen/agents/*.md` or `~/.qwen/agents/` with `name, description, tools, disallowedTools, model (inherit|fast|id), approvalMode (default|plan|auto-edit|yolo|bubble)`; built-in Explore (`agents.builtin.exploreModel`) and general-purpose; dispatched via the `agent` tool; `subagent_type: "fork"` inherits parent history (`fork_turns`), shares the parent's system prompt for cache hits, runs detached, and is scoped with `fork_tools`/`fork_profile`; regular subagents cannot recurse; completions arrive as notifications (queue of 20) and agents stay addressable via `list_agents`/`send_message`; experimental Agent Teams (`experimental.agentTeam`, `/coordinate`) allow up to three workstreams with one writer in a leader-owned git worktree. Kimi Code CLI: built-in `coder`, `explore` (read-only) and `plan` (no shell), custom Markdown+YAML agents (`name, description, tools, disallowedTools, override, subagents`), `Agent` and `AgentSwarm` tools, parallel execution, "always allow" rules propagate to children, built-ins cannot dispatch further subagents, and "only the final result appears in the main Agent's context". Crush: no merged subagent system as of Sept 2026; PR #3098 (open) proposes Markdown agents with `permissionMode: default|bypassPermissions` dispatched through an `agent` tool with a dynamic `subagent_type` enum. Pi: deliberately none ("a black box within a black box"; "If you need pi to spawn itself, just ask it to run itself via bash"), with community packages filling the gap.
dimensions.providers: Pi is provider-agnostic through its `pi-ai` package: bundled providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Groq, xAI, Mistral, OpenRouter, Bedrock, Ollama and more), custom endpoints in `~/.pi/agent/models.json` with `api` kinds such as `openai-completions` (docs example `"ollama": { "baseUrl": "http://localhost:11434/v1", "api": "openai-completions" }`, stated to cover Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, SGLang and proxies), a `/llama` command that drives the llama.cpp router, `/model`, `Ctrl+P` and `/thinking` for mid-session switching, and credential precedence `--api-key` > `auth.json` > `models.json` > env vars. Crush ships the widest local list: providers Hyper, Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Vercel AI Gateway, OpenRouter, Bedrock, Vertex, Azure, generic `openai-compat`/anthropic-compat, and local types `ollama`, `llamacpp`, `lmstudio`, `omlx`, `litellm` with model auto-discovery (`discover_models`), plus a Catwalk catalog and mid-session model switching. Qwen Code speaks OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini and Qwen APIs and "any third-party provider or local model (Ollama / vLLM)", with `model.name`, `fastModel` and `advisorModel` roles; Winder.ai (Aug 2026) calls it "the best harness we have used for Qwen models and the worst for anything else" because of parsing bugs with other models. Kimi Code CLI defines `[providers.<name>] type = kimi|anthropic|openai|openai_responses|google-genai|vertexai` with `base_url`/`api_key_env`, so any OpenAI-compatible server (the docs name DeepSeek and Qwen) works, plus `/provider`, `kimi provider` and models.dev registries; models carry `max_context_size` and `capabilities`. Cursor CLI routes only through Cursor's backend (Auto with Cost/Balance/Intelligence, Composer 2.5, Grok, Claude, GPT, Gemini, Kimi K, GLM, Muse Spark); no BYO key or local model is documented for the CLI. Amp picks models per Dial mode but Model Routing lets users add connections to Anthropic, Google AI Studio, Meta, OpenAI, xAI, OpenRouter, Vercel AI Gateway, Cloudflare AI Gateway, Ollama Cloud or a Custom URL with mapping patterns like `anthropic/*`. None of the six documents a weak-model regime (retries, output repair, reduced tool sets); the Pi review notes it is the natural home for DeepSeek/Qwen/vLLM users.
dimensions.mcp: Cursor: `.cursor/mcp.json` and `~/.cursor/mcp.json`, transports stdio, SSE and Streamable HTTP, OAuth, approval before MCP tool use by default, `Mcp(server:tool)` permission rules, `--approve-mcps`; it is also an ACP server (`agent acp`, stdio JSON-RPC 2.0, used by Zed, JetBrains and avante.nvim) exposing agent/plan/ask session modes. Amp: `amp.mcpServers` in `~/.config/amp/settings.json` or `.amp/settings.json` (`command/args` or `url/headers`), remote definitions via `amp mcp remote`, `amp mcp approve` for workspace servers, `--mcp-config` in execute mode, skills that bundle `mcpServers` and hide their tools until loaded, and an enterprise MCP Registry Allowlist; no ACP documented. Pi: no native MCP or ACP; the community `pi-mcp-adapter` package bridges MCP (197,718 weekly downloads per the Sept 2026 review). Crush: `mcp add` with stdio/http/sse, `--timeout`, `--disabled-tools`, `--header`, OAuth and `sessionless`, plus `list_mcp_resources`/`read_mcp_resource` tools; ACP server support (`crush acp`, PR #2450) has been open since Mar 2026 and a community `crush-acp` bridge exists. Qwen Code: `mcpServers` in settings and inside extensions; ACP via `qwen --acp`, listed in Zed's ACP agent registry. Kimi Code CLI: `~/.kimi-code/mcp.json` and `.kimi-code/mcp.json`, stdio/http/sse, `/mcp-config` (AI-native interactive config), `/mcp` status, `/mcp-config login <server>` OAuth, tools named `mcp__<server>__<tool>`; ACP via `kimi acp` (the Oct 2025 Python CLI already shipped ACP).
dimensions.evals: Qwen Code is the only member that publishes a harness-level table: SWE-bench_Verified (500 cases, 3 trials per harness version, 1,500 jobs across seven versions) with Qwen 3.7 Max at `temperature=1, top_p=0.95, reasoning_effort=high, context_1m=true, max_tokens=64,000, max_iterations=500`; v0.22.0 scores 77.33% avg / 84.4% pass, the best version 0.0.14 scores 77.80% / 84.6%, and the range across versions is 76.40-77.80%, which is effectively a harness-version ablation on a fixed model. Cursor publishes model results measured in its own harness: Composer 2.5 (18 May 2026) at 79.8% SWE-Bench Multilingual, 69.3% Terminal-Bench 2.0 and 63.2% CursorBench v3.1, with no CLI-vs-IDE or harness-vs-model ablation. Pi has no official benchmark; the 6 Sep 2026 heyuan review ran three identical tasks and reports pi at $0.10-0.31 per task versus Claude Code at $0.61-1.16 with Claude Code consuming 1.8-2.5x the input tokens, attributing the gap to harness overhead rather than tool capability. Kimi's numbers (K2.6 at ~80.2 SWE-bench Verified) come from Moonshot's in-house SWE-agent-derived scaffold, not from Kimi Code CLI. Amp and Crush publish no benchmarks.
dimensions.distinctive: Pi: the thesis is that four tools and a loop are enough, that permission prompts are "security theater" once an agent can write and run code ("As soon as your agent can write code and run code, it's pretty much game over"), and that everything else (guards, MCP, subagents, plan mode) belongs in in-process TypeScript extensions; the tree-structured JSONL session with `/fork` is its second idea, and it has become infrastructure other agents build on (pi-tui downloads exceed the CLI's). Criticisms: no sandbox or guardrails for newcomers, a 449 MB install that contradicts "minimal", silent context inflation from auto-discovered skills, and no cost display in text mode. Cursor CLI: the Auto-review run mode (allowlist first, OS sandbox second, a classifier subagent third) and the sudo-over-IPC design are the distinctive safety ideas, and its hooks surface is the richest of the six; criticism centres on lock-in to Cursor-routed models with no local option and on a permissions.json/allowlist interaction that users report as contradicting the docs. Amp: the Dial (task difficulty instead of model names), Orbs (a fresh remote machine per thread), server-side shareable threads with "Handoff" instead of compaction, and a no-approval-by-default stance where policy is a plugin `tool.call` hook; criticisms are cost ("You pay per token and it's not cheap"), a "no backcompat, no legacy features" culture that killed toolboxes and `amp.permissions`, and a manual now behind sign-in. Crush: a Bubble Tea TUI with LSP-informed tools, a Bash-scripted `crushrc`, the broadest local-provider list (ollama/llamacpp/lmstudio/omlx/litellm), and multi-client shared workspaces via `crush serve`; criticisms are the FSL licence, a hooks system stuck at PreToolUse, no merged subagents or ACP, and auto-summarize bugs (fixed 20k buffer, summary-as-task loops). Qwen Code: the richest Claude-Code-style feature set in open source (Auto-Memory with `/dream`, fork subagents that preserve prompt cache, Agent Teams, Seatbelt/bwrap sandboxes, run budgets with exit codes) and a published harness-version ablation; the loudest criticism is that it is tuned for Qwen models and breaks on others. Kimi Code CLI: single-binary TypeScript rewrite with video input, AI-native `/mcp-config`, ACP from day one, `AgentSwarm` and cron tools, and TOML permission rules like `Bash(rm -rf*)`; criticisms are the churn of archiving the Python CLI within a year, thin sandboxing (workspace-fence hardening only), and documentation that lags the release cadence (2.1.1 on 24 Sep 2026).

unknowns: Pi: tool-output truncation limits (not in how-pi-works.md, settings.md, usage.md); exact first-release month (repo begun Aug 2025 per secondary sources, one profile says Nov 2025)
Pi: any official benchmark or harness ablation (none published; only a third-party 3-task cost comparison)
Cursor CLI: full built-in tool list, per-turn step limits, tool-result truncation, licence text (proprietary inferred from absence of source), any popularity metric
Cursor CLI: whether the CLI can use BYO API keys or local models (models page silent; treated as not supported)

Amp: built-in tool list (docs defer to `amp tools list`), tool-result truncation, step limits, popularity signal, ACP support, and the permissions/subagents manual pages (now behind sign-in; profiled from /docs pages and Aug 2026 secondary coverage)
Crush: auto-summarize default threshold (only the 20k buffer above 200k windows is documented in issue #3620); subagents and ACP exist only as open PRs (#3098, #2450)
Crush: benchmarks (none published)

Qwen Code: exact first-release date (July 2025 per launch coverage, not confirmed from the releases page); Agent Teams internals beyond the user doc; tool-output truncation defaults taken from the settings reference as surfaced by search, not from a page fully read
