profiles.name: cornac
profiles.one_liner: A from-scratch, provider-agnostic Python agent harness (this repo, ~4k LOC, 440 tests) whose thesis is "the agent isn't the model, it's the harness": a single ReAct-style tool loop with fail-closed permissions, vetoing hooks, a workspace path fence, privilege-preserving sub-agents, and weak-model scaffolding that lifted a frozen local qwen3.5:4b-class lineup from 12/27 to 26/27 on its own coding spike.

dimensions.identity: Maintainer: spv (Sripadha), solo learning project at github.com/sripadha/cornac (remote exists; plan Week 6 still says 'flip the repo public', so it is private today). First commit 2026-06-18 ('Week 1: walking skeleton'); no tagged release, pyproject version 0.1.0, NOT on PyPI (the name `cornac` is taken by a recommender-systems package; the `ankus` rename was cancelled 2026-09-07 and is unresolved). License MIT (LICENSE file + pyproject). Language: Python >=3.10, hatchling build, deps anthropic>=0.40, httpx, ddgs, pyyaml. Distribution: library only (`pip install -e .`, `from cornac import Agent, ToolRegistry, Policy, HookBus`); pyproject declares a console script `cornac = cornac.cli:main` but cornac/cli.py does not exist. Popularity: none measurable (private repo, 0 stars, 0 downloads). Test suite: 16 files, 329 `def test_` functions, 440 collected with parametrization.
dimensions.loop: Single synchronous ReAct-style tool loop in `Agent.run(user_message) -> RunResult` (cornac/core/agent.py). Shape: `for _ in range(max_steps)` (default 20): `provider.complete(self.messages, self.registry.schemas())`, append the assistant Message, fire on_assistant_message; if `not response.wants_tools` the turn ends with `RunResult(stop_reason='done')`; otherwise every ToolCall runs sequentially through `_handle_call` (hook gate -> policy -> approver -> `registry.execute`) then `_note_repeats`, and each result is appended as a role='tool' Message. Hitting max_steps returns `RunResult(text=None, stop_reason='max_steps')`, explicitly never a fabricated answer. Two weak-model branches inside the same loop: (1) the continue nudge: if the reply has no tool calls but its LAST non-blank line matches `_ANNOUNCES` ('let me', "let's", 'i will', "i'll", "i'm going to", 'now i', 'next,', 'next step', with exclusions for 'let me know/summarize/explain'), the loop appends `NUDGE_MESSAGE` as a user message and continues, bounded by `max_nudges=1` and never on the last permitted step; (2) the repeated-call note: keyed on (tool name, sorted-JSON args), when the same call returns byte-identical content again, `REPEAT_NOTE` ('[cornac] This exact call was already made {n} times...') is appended to the result, advisory only, never blocked. No planner/executor split, no code-as-action (plan lists CodeAct as optional stage 6), no parallel tool execution, no streaming. RunResult fields: text, stop_reason ('done'|'max_steps'), steps (provider calls), duration, usage (summed Usage), nudges, children. `self.messages` persists across run() calls on one Agent.
dimensions.tools: Definition: `Tool` ABC (cornac/tools/base.py) with class attrs name/description/input_schema (JSON Schema) and `run(arguments: dict) -> str`; raising is allowed and converted to an error result. Convenience: `@tool(name=, description=)` decorator builds a `_FunctionTool`, inferring properties from signature annotations via `_PY_TO_JSON` (str/int/float/bool/list/dict -> string/integer/number/boolean/array/object, unknown -> string), required = params without defaults, description = docstring. Registration: `ToolRegistry([tools])` (registry.py), `add()` raises ValueError on duplicate names, `schemas()` emits neutral {name, description, input_schema} in registration order (each provider reshapes), `execute(call)` never raises: unknown tool -> error listing available names, exception -> `ToolResult(is_error=True, content='ExcType: msg')`. Built-ins (11, via `default_tools(workspace)` in builtin/__init__.py): read_file, write_file, edit_file, list_dir, grep (files.py, class-based, Workspace-confined), run_bash (shell.py), run_python (python_exec.py), web_search (ddgs/DuckDuckGo, no key), web_fetch (httpx, follow_redirects, FETCH_TIMEOUT 20s), get_current_time (clock.py, @tool), spawn_agent (spawn.py). Result truncation: `truncate_head_tail(text, head, tail, label)` (_truncate.py) keeps both ends with a '... [output truncated: N chars omitted; showing first H and last T] ...' notice; run_bash/run_python use HEAD_CHARS=40_000 + TAIL_CHARS=10_000 on combined stdout+stderr; read_file and grep cap at MAX_BYTES=100_000 (head only); web_fetch MAX_FETCH_CHARS=20_000; sub-agent reply 4_000 head+tail. Execution safety: `run_with_timeout` (_subprocess.py) runs children with start_new_session=True and on timeout `os.killpg`s the whole group, drains pipes for PIPE_DRAIN_TIMEOUT=1.0s, and returns partial output; DEFAULT_TIMEOUT=30s for both bash and python; run_bash prefixes '(exit code N)'; run_python runs a stashed source file through `_pyrunner.RUNNER_SOURCE` which echoes a trailing bare expression like a notebook cell and keeps tracebacks on the model's line numbers. Coding scaffolding in files.py: `_syntax_refusal` compile()s any .py content BEFORE write_file/edit_file and refuses with the SyntaxError line if it fails (file untouched); write_file reports 'created/overwrote X: 404 -> 179 chars; REMOVED top-level: def clamp, def mean' via ast; edit_file replaces one exact snippet, falls back to dedent/reindent matching (`_match_reindented`), refuses old==new, preserves CRLF/BOM, refuses non-UTF-8, and gives difflib 'closest match' hints bounded by HINT_MAX_LINES=5000/HINT_MAX_LINE=200; grep has a GREP_TIMEOUT=10s SIGALRM `_time_limit`. The loop rewrites any '[cornac]' inside tool output to '[cornac?]' (`_neutralise_marker`) so only the harness speaks behind the bare marker.
dimensions.extensibility: In-process Python objects only, no plugin manifest, no entry points, no dynamic discovery, no config-driven loading. Pluggable seams: (1) providers, subclass `Provider` and implement `complete(messages, tools) -> Message` (providers/base.py); (2) tools, subclass `Tool` or use `@tool`, then pass into `ToolRegistry([...])` at construction; (3) approver, any `Callable[[ToolCall, Policy], Decision]` passed as `Agent(approver=...)` (`cli_ask` is the default; docstring names a web UI or Slack bot as alternatives); (4) policy, a dict or YAML via `Policy.from_yaml(path)` (examples/cornac.policy.yaml); (5) hooks, `HookBus.on(event, callback)` passed as `Agent(hooks=bus)`. A duck-typed optional tool protocol (`bind_parent(agent)` called by Agent.__init__, `reset_for_run()` called by Agent.run) lets a tool talk to its agent, used by SpawnAgent; `SpawnAgent` is subclassable and `_child_spawner` uses `type(self)` so subclasses propagate down the tree. Not pluggable: prompts (system_prompt is a bare string; `Workspace.describe()` is the only supplied prompt fragment), UI (none), context management (none), CLI (none). A third party adds a tool by constructing it in Python and including it in the registry list before building the Agent.
dimensions.context: None beyond append-only. `Agent.messages` is an append-only list that grows across run() calls; there is no compaction, no summarisation, no tool-result clearing (docs/plan.md §3 defers 'context compaction / tool-result clearing at token-limit' to v2), no CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md-style memory file, no persistent cross-session memory (v2+). KV-cache friendliness is an explicit design rule (plan §4.2 'Append-only context, stable prefix: never rewrite history, never reorder tools, volatile info goes last'): the nudge is appended as a user message rather than editing the system prompt, tools are emitted in registration order, and the repeat note is appended to the result rather than rewriting history. Window control is provider-side only: `OllamaProvider(num_ctx=8192)` set explicitly because Ollama's 2048 default silently truncates, `num_predict=2048` per reply; the spike runner records 'ctx overflow' when prompt+output >= num_ctx. AnthropicProvider does not use prompt caching. The only context-management mechanism is sub-agent isolation (a child has an empty context and returns <=4000 chars).
dimensions.permissions: `Policy` + `Decision` str-Enum {ALLOW, DENY, ASK} in cornac/permissions/policy.py; no named modes (no plan/auto-accept/bypass), just a policy object plus an optional approver. Rules per tool: a plain 'allow'/'deny'/'ask', or a rich dict {deny: [...], allow: [...], default, argument}. Matching is deliberately asymmetric: deny = substring over EVERY argument value (`_argument_text`), checked first, deny wins; allow = word-boundary prefix (`_prefix_matches`) on the ONE executed argument (`COMMAND_ARGUMENT`: run_bash->'command', run_python->'code', or `argument:` in the rule), skipped entirely if the string contains any `SHELL_METACHARS` (; && || | & ` $( > < newline) or if the call has any extra argument (`_executed_text` returns None). Config is validated at construction (unknown keys, non-list patterns, allow patterns containing metacharacters, allow list without a known argument -> ValueError). `DEFAULT_RULES`: read_file/list_dir/grep/get_current_time/web_search/web_fetch/spawn_agent allow; write_file/edit_file/run_python ask; run_bash deny-list ['rm -rf','sudo','mkfs',':(){','dd if='] + default ask; global default ask. Session overrides via `Policy.remember()` from the `cli_ask` prompt '[y]es / [n]o / [a]lways / nev[e]r': 'never' wins outright, 'always' only converts ASK->ALLOW and never overrides a configured DENY; EOF on stdin -> DENY. In `Agent._handle_call` ASK with no approver => DENY (headless safety), and the tool runs ONLY on an explicit `Decision.ALLOW` (None, ASK, 'yes' all refuse). Sandboxing: `Workspace.resolve()` (tools/workspace.py) joins to root, `.resolve()`s, and raises `WorkspaceError` unless root is the path or one of its parents, blocking ../ and absolute escapes for file tools; run_bash/run_python are pinned to cwd=workspace root and killed by process group on timeout, but can read anything the user can. Explicitly NOT an OS sandbox: no containers, seccomp, bubblewrap, Landlock (plan §3 acknowledges 'subprocess + Workspace is non-production'). No network egress control; web tools default to allow.
dimensions.hooks: `HookBus` (cornac/hooks/bus.py), an in-process pub/sub: `on(event, callback)`, `fire(event, *args)` returns one entry per callback in registration order (a raising callback prints '[cornac] hook ... raised' to stderr and contributes None, never crashing the loop), and `gate(event, *args)` is identical except a raising callback contributes the `HOOK_FAILED` sentinel. Events fired by Agent: on_user_message(message), on_assistant_message(message), on_nudge(text, n), pre_tool_use(call), on_permission_decision(call, decision), post_tool_use(call, result), on_stop(final_text or None). Fired by spawn_agent on the parent's bus: on_spawn(task, depth), on_spawn_done(RunResult or None, depth). Veto: yes, a pre_tool_use callback returning `Decision.DENY` (or the bare string 'deny', since Decision is a str Enum) vetoes; it is fired through gate() so a callback that crashes counts as a veto (fail closed); the veto is checked BEFORE the policy and approver so a vetoed call never prompts the human; the model receives 'Vetoed by hook: X was blocked by a pre_tool_use hook.' as an error result. Hooks cannot mutate the call or the result, cannot inject context, and are Python callables only (no shell-command hooks, no settings-file hooks, no matchers). examples/hook_trace.py shows a tracer.
dimensions.subagents: `SpawnAgent` tool (cornac/tools/builtin/spawn.py), model-facing name `spawn_agent`, schema {task (required), system_prompt, tools: [names]}. Spawning: the parent's loop calls the tool inside `registry.execute`, the tool builds an ordinary `Agent` and runs `child.run(task)` synchronously (v1: children run one at a time, no parallelism, no background). Inheritance: the parent's provider, the SAME `Policy` object (session always/never included), the SAME approver, the parent's `max_nudges`, and the parent's pre_tool_use veto via `_child_bus` (pre_tool_use forwarded as a gate returning DENY if the parent's hooks deny or crash; on_permission_decision/post_tool_use/on_spawn/on_spawn_done forwarded; on_user_message/on_assistant_message/on_nudge/on_stop stay local). Context: a FRESH message list with system prompt = given persona or `DEFAULT_CHILD_PROMPT` ('You are a focused sub-agent...') plus `Workspace.describe()` if any tool is workspace-bound. Tools: the requested subset of the parent's tools BY REFERENCE (default all shareable), minus any agent-bound tool (`bind_parent`/`reset_for_run`), plus its own deeper SpawnAgent while depth allows; unknown or bound names are refused with the available list. Limits: `max_depth=2` (last level gets no spawn tool at all), `max_children=5` shared across the WHOLE tree via one `_ChildBudget` object reset per run only by the root tool, `child_max_steps=10`, `max_reply_chars=4000` head+tail. Returns to parent: 'Sub-agent reply:\n' + truncated final text (header is unforgeable since everything after it is the child's); a child that hit max_steps returns 'Error: sub-agent gave up after N steps without a final answer'; an empty answer or a raising child return 'Error: ...'. Accounting: `parent.absorb_child(usage)` folds child tokens (including grandchildren) into `RunResult.usage`; `RunResult.children` counts direct children; steps/nudges stay per-agent; duration is wall-clock so it includes children. No agent-to-agent messaging, no shared task list, no named/persistent agent definitions, no parallel workers (plan §3 defers A2A/teams).
dimensions.providers: `Provider` ABC (cornac/providers/base.py) with a single method `complete(messages: list[Message], tools: list[dict]) -> Message` plus a `name` property; the loop never imports a vendor SDK. Neutral types in core/messages.py: Message(role system|user|assistant|tool, text, tool_calls, tool_call_id, name, is_error, usage, stop_reason kept verbatim from the backend), ToolCall(id, name, arguments), ToolResult, Usage(input_tokens, output_tokens, __add__). Two implementations: `AnthropicProvider` (providers/anthropic.py, Messages API through the anthropic SDK, DEFAULT_MODEL 'claude-haiku-4-5-20251001', max_tokens 2048, SDK max_retries=3, hoists system messages into the `system` param, folds role='tool' into user `tool_result` blocks, drops empty assistant turns, reads usage and stop_reason) and `OllamaProvider` (providers/ollama.py, raw httpx POST to /api/chat, DEFAULT_MODEL 'qwen3.5:4b', timeout 300s, num_ctx 8192, seed 42, temperature 0, num_predict 2048, presence_penalty 0 forced on every request to override the Ollama Modelfile's baked-in 1.5, `think=False` automatically for any tag containing 'qwen3', `extra_options` merged last, exponential-backoff retries (max_retries 3, backoff 0.5s doubling) on 5xx/httpx.TransportError while 4xx raise immediately with the daemon's own error text via `_with_daemon_reason`, synthesizes tool-call ids, `request_options()` returned for benchmark logging). No OpenAI-compatible provider, no direct llama.cpp/vLLM provider (they would work only through an Ollama-shaped endpoint), no streaming, no multimodal. Weak-model handling is the project's thesis and is measured: the continue nudge, repeated-call note, edit_file + syntax gate, write_file change report, notebook-style expression echo, Workspace.describe() cwd hint, presence_penalty override, and a tool-call probe in benchmark/spike/run_spike.py that disqualifies models that cannot emit tool calls through Ollama.
dimensions.mcp: none. No MCP client, no MCP server, no ACP, no A2A. docs/plan.md §3 names `MCPToolAdapter` ('mount any MCP server's tools into the registry') as the first v2 item and states the `Tool{name, description, input_schema, run()}` ABC is 'deliberately MCP-shaped'; a grep of cornac/ for 'mcp' finds nothing.
dimensions.evals: No public benchmark (no SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench, etc.). Own coding spike in benchmark/spike/ (run_spike.py, results/, results_round2/, results_round2b/, results_round3/): 3 tasks (swe: fix a failing test; swe2: boundary bug hidden in a helper module; swe3: mutable default argument) x k=3 runs, temperature 0.3 with seeds 42/43/44, graded by cheat-resistant verify.py (test file must be AST-identical, pytest must report exact 'N passed', plus a behaviour check on unseen inputs; verifiers checked against pristine/hand-fixed/edited-test/conftest-cheat/hardcoded variants). Model selection (round 2, docs/observations.md 2026-09-22): Unsloth Qwen3.5-4B Q8_0 9/9 at 98 s/run; Ollama qwen3.5:4b Q4_K_M 7/9 at 25 s; qwen3:4b-instruct-2507 4/9; qwen3:8b 1/9; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B 0/9 (failed the tool-call probe). Round 2b: forcing presence_penalty 0 took qwen3.5:4b to 9/9 at 20.5 s/run, 100% on a 6 GB RTX 2060; model frozen. Harness ablation (round 3, same tasks/seeds/prompts, ONLY cornac changed): 12/27 -> 26/27 total (qwen3:4b-instruct-2507 4/9 -> 9/9, qwen3:8b 1/9 -> 8/9, qwen3.5:4b 9/9 -> 9/9); attribution: edit_file used in 25/27 runs (round 2 had 13 broken whole-file writes, round 3 zero), nudge fixed 5/5 stalls (qwen3:8b announce-then-stop 8 -> 0), syntax gate and removed-functions report never fired, repeated-call note fired 8 times and changed behaviour 0 times. Sub-agent probe (2026-09-23, n=1 at temperature 0): told to delegate the model spawned one read-only child (6 steps, 35.8 s, 17.8k tokens); left alone it used grep and did not delegate (8 steps, 19.1 s, 21.7k tokens). Planned but NOT built: the 6-stage capability ladder (examples/stage_0..5, zero exist) and a 15-task benchmark (benchmark/tasks/ is empty) with rows Haiku bare / Haiku+cornac / qwen3.5:4b+cornac. Caveat stated in the notebook: n=9 per cell cannot separate 9/9 from ~70%.
dimensions.distinctive: Distinctive ideas: (1) Fail-closed gates as a system property, not a setting: a crashing pre_tool_use hook is a veto (`HOOK_FAILED`), an approver returning anything but ALLOW is a refusal, ASK with no approver is DENY, and the allow/deny asymmetry (deny = sloppy substring over all args; allow = word-boundary prefix on the single executed argument, skipped on any shell metacharacter or extra argument) is derived from real holes it found ('ls' in 'false', decoy-argument bypass). (2) Weak-model scaffolding justified by transcript counts and an ablation: the bounded continue-nudge on the last line only, the repeated-call note, edit_file with dedent fallback, compile-before-write syntax gate, 'REMOVED top-level: def clamp' change report, notebook echo, and the cwd hint, each tied to a count from 45 spike transcripts and to the 12/27 -> 26/27 result; the lab notebook also records what did NOT work ('advisory text does not stop a determined loop'). (3) Sub-agents as privilege-preserving context isolation: the child shares the parent's Policy/approver/veto objects by reference so delegation can never escalate, one budget counts the whole tree, tokens roll up, and the '[cornac]' marker neutralisation plus 'Sub-agent reply:' header keep harness text unforgeable by file contents or child models. Also notable: honest RunResult (text=None on max_steps), process-group kill on timeout with partial output, head+tail truncation, provider seam small enough that Ollama support is one file. Loudest criticisms (mostly self-acknowledged in docs/plan.md §3 and docs/observations.md): no context compaction, summarisation, or memory of any kind; no MCP; no OS-level sandbox (path fence only; run_bash reads anything the user can; web_fetch is allow by default with prompt-injection handled only by policy); no CLI or UI (cli.py declared in pyproject but missing), no streaming; sequential-only tools and children; the repeat note is advisory and did not break a single loop; the '[cornac]' marker is spoofable in principle; evidence is thin (n=9 per cell, 3 tasks, one GPU); the ladder and 15-task benchmark that carry the thesis are unbuilt; PyPI name collision unresolved and the repo is private with no external users.

unknowns: mcp: none (no MCP client/server, ACP or A2A; MCPToolAdapter is a v2 plan item)

profiles.name: Hermes Agent (Nous Research)
profiles.one_liner: Nous Research's MIT-licensed, Python "self-improving" personal agent harness: one AIAgent core serving a CLI/TUI, ACP editor server and a 20+ platform messaging gateway, with 69-70 self-registering tools, seven terminal backends, SKILL.md skills the agent writes for itself, SQLite/FTS5 session memory, a four-flavour hook system and a policy floor that survives --yolo; ~249k GitHub stars as of 2026-09-26.

dimensions.identity: Maintained by Nous Research (github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent), MIT license, Python primary (TypeScript for the website, desktop and TUI; ~14 languages per repowise). The GitHub API shows the repo created 2025-07-22; the public launch is triangulated to February 2026 (TechCrunch 2026-07-13: released "weeks after" OpenClaw went viral in January 2026; a 2026-04-14 review dates v0.9.0 to 2026-04-13 "two months after the initial launch") but no primary first-release tag was reachable, so the exact date is an unknown. Distribution is a CLI entry point `hermes` installed by `curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash` (PowerShell `install.ps1`, a signed Termux APT repo with stable and canary channels), plus macOS/Windows desktop apps, an editor server (`hermes acp`), an embeddable `run_agent.AIAgent` class, and a paid cloud tier ($20/$100/$200 per month). Releases are SemVer internally (`v0.21.5` = release tag `v2026.9.24`, 2026-09-24, described as ~460 PRs since v0.21.4) with a daily canary build at 06:41 UTC. Popularity on 2026-09-26: 249,072 stars, 52,842 forks, 43,742 open issues, star-history global rank #19 at ~2.4k new stars/week; TechCrunch reported Nous raising at a $1.5B valuation on the back of it.
dimensions.loop: A single synchronous tool-calling (ReAct-style) loop: `run_agent.py` exposes the `AIAgent` facade, the body is `agent/conversation_loop.py::run_conversation()` and each turn is split into phase modules `agent/turn_*.py` (iteration_prep, api_call, api_error, overflow, truncation, recovery) with `agent/tool_executor.py` executing tool calls (parallel via ThreadPoolExecutor, results re-inserted in original order). Per turn it appends the user message, builds/caches the three-tier system prompt, runs a preflight compression check (>50% of context), converts history to one of three API modes (`chat_completions` / `codex_responses` / `anthropic_messages`), injects ephemeral layers (budget warnings, context pressure), makes an interruptible API call, and loops while tool calls are returned. An `IterationBudget` bounds the loop: the agent-loop doc says default 500 via `agent.max_turns` (the configuration page says "default: unlimited", a documented inconsistency); at 100% the agent stops and returns a work summary. A turn ends when the model answers with no tool calls, the budget is exhausted, or the user interrupts (`/stop`, signal). The stop is guarded: a built-in verify-on-stop guard plus the `pre_verify` hook fire once per turn when code was edited, and a hook may return `{"action":"continue","message":...}` which is injected as a synthetic user turn, capped by `agent.max_verify_nudges` (default 3); the arXiv source study labels this "Budgeted Loop with Stop-Guards".
dimensions.tools: Tools are plain Python modules in `tools/*.py` that self-register at import via `registry.register(name, toolset, schema, handler, check_fn=, requires_env=, is_async=, emoji=)`, producing a `ToolEntry` in the singleton `ToolRegistry._tools` (`tools/registry.py`); `discover_builtin_tools()` AST-scans the directory for top-level register calls so there is no hand-maintained list, and `model_tools.get_tool_definitions()` filters by enabled toolsets and cached `check_fn` results before emitting OpenAI-format schemas. Dispatch is `model_tools.handle_function_call()` -> `registry.dispatch()`; handlers take an args dict and return a string (or JSON error) with dual-level error wrapping, and four agent-level tools (todo_list, memory, session_search, delegate_task) bypass the registry to touch agent state. `toolsets.py` groups ~28 toolsets with platform presets (`hermes-cli`, `hermes-telegram`, `hermes-acp`), toggled via `hermes tools` or `hermes chat --toolsets "web,terminal"`. The built-in set (README says 40+, architecture doc 70+, the arXiv corpus table counts 69) includes `terminal`, `process_manage`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `patch`, `search_files`, `web_search`, `web_extract`, `x_search`, twelve `browser_*` tools, `vision_analyze`, `image_generate`, `video_*`, `todo_list`, `memory`, `session_search`, `clarify`, `execute_code` (Python scripts that call tools over RPC), `delegate_task`, `cronjob_manage`, `skill_manage`/`skill_view`/`skills_list`, fourteen `kanban_*`, `computer_use`, Home Assistant `ha_*`, and dynamic `mcp_<server>_<tool>` entries. Documented result limits: `read_file` ~100K chars with `next_offset` pagination, `web_extract` 15,000-char budget returned as head+tail (max 5 URLs), files >10 MB refused as binary, subagent results bounded to 32k chars, context files truncated 70% head / 20% tail / 10% marker; a general tool-result cap lives in `agent/turn_truncation.py` but its limit is not documented. For large MCP/plugin catalogs, Tool Search defers schemas behind `tool_search`/`tool_describe`/`tool_call` bridge tools (`threshold_pct: 5`, `listing_max_tokens: 4000`, tiers 0-2).
dimensions.extensibility: Plugins are discovered from bundled `plugins/`, user `~/.hermes/plugins/`, project `.hermes/plugins/`, and the pip entry-point group `hermes_agent.plugins`, and are managed with `hermes plugins`. A native plugin is a directory with a `plugin.yaml` manifest (name, version, `provides_tools`, `provides_hooks`, `python_dependencies`, `requires_env`, `config_schema`, `capabilities` such as `tools.override`) and an `__init__.py` exposing `register(ctx)`; the `PluginContext` offers `register_tool(name, schema, handler)`, `register_hook(event, cb)`, `register_command` (slash), `register_cli_command` (`hermes <name>`), `register_platform_handler`, `register_memory_provider`, `register_provider`, `get_config/set_config`, and `dispatch_tool`. Pluggable surfaces therefore cover tools, hooks, middleware, slash and CLI commands, model providers, messaging platform adapters (25+ bundled), memory providers (single-select: Honcho, Mem0, Supermemory, RetainDB, ByteRover, OpenViking, Holographic), context engines that replace the compressor (`context.engine: lcm`), terminal-environment backends, image/video/web-search providers, secret sources and a desktop plugin SDK. Non-Python extension points are MCP servers in `config.yaml`, gateway hooks (`HOOK.yaml` + `handler.py` in `~/.hermes/hooks/`), shell hooks, and skills pulled from `hermes skills tap add owner/repo` or skills.sh/ClawHub with security scanning. Plugins load after built-ins so overrides win, hooks take `**kwargs` for forward compatibility, and compatibility is behaviour-based (deprecated behaviour kept for two minor releases with migration notes).
dimensions.context: The system prompt (`agent/prompt_builder.py`) is assembled in three ordered tiers for cache stability: stable (SOUL.md identity, tool and coding guidance), context (`.hermes.md`/`HERMES.md` > `AGENTS.override.md` > `AGENTS.md` chained from git root to cwd > `CLAUDE.md` > `.cursorrules`, each capped by a dynamic `context_file_max_chars` between 20,000 and 500,000 chars and scanned for injection), and volatile (skills index, `MEMORY.md`, `USER.md`); ephemeral content bypasses the cached prompt entirely, and subdirectory context files are appended to tool results rather than the prompt. Persistent memory is two frozen files in `~/.hermes/memories/`, `MEMORY.md` (2,200 chars, ~800 tokens) and `USER.md` (1,375 chars, ~500 tokens), edited via the `memory` tool's add/replace/remove and hard-capped so an over-limit write returns an error that forces consolidation (`memory_char_limit`, `user_char_limit`, `write_approval`). Cross-session recall is `session_search` over SQLite FTS5 (`hermes_state_fts.py`, `hermes_state_search.py`) with LLM summarisation, plus optional external memory providers. Compaction (`agent/context_compressor.py`, the default `ContextEngine`) triggers at `compression.threshold: 0.50` of the window (absolute `threshold_tokens: 256000`, per-model overrides), keeps the first 3 messages, summarises the middle into a structured goals/progress/decisions/files document, and protects a tail of 20% of the threshold with `protect_last_n: 20` and `min_tail_user_messages: 1`; `in_place: true` soft-archives old rows (active=0, compacted=1) on the same session id instead of rotating ids, the "lineage compaction" the arXiv study names, while a gateway hygiene pass fires at 85%. Optional micro-compaction (`compression.micro_compact: true`, off by default) absorbs one exchange per turn and re-summarises at 2,000 tokens, explicitly at the cost of breaking the prefix cache every turn. KV-cache friendliness is a stated principle ("system prompt doesn't change mid-conversation"): `agent/prompt_caching.py` applies Anthropic `cache_control` with a `system_and_3` strategy (one breakpoint on the system prompt, rolling markers on the last three messages) which the docs claim cuts input cost ~75%, and `auxiliary.compression.model` can route summarisation to a cheaper model.
dimensions.permissions: Approval is configured under `approvals:` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`: `mode: smart | manual | off` (smart, the default, has an auxiliary LLM auto-approve low-risk and auto-deny clearly dangerous commands, escalating only uncertain ones), `timeout: 300` (deny on expiry), `cron_mode`/`single_query_mode`/`unattended_mode: deny`, and user `deny:` fnmatch globs such as `"git push --force*"`. `tools/approval.py` flags ~30 dangerous patterns (`rm -r`, `chmod 777`, `mkfs`, `dd if=`, `DROP TABLE`, `> /etc/`, `kill -9`, `curl | sh`, `docker stop`) and a hardline blocklist (`rm -rf /`, fork bombs, `dd of=/dev/sd*`, malformed quoting) that survives `hermes --yolo`, `/yolo` and `HERMES_YOLO_MODE=1`, as do `approvals.deny` rules, which the arXiv study calls "A Policy Floor That Survives YOLO". CLI prompts offer once / session / always / deny (default), with "always" persisted to `command_allowlist`; file tools block protected paths (`~/.ssh/`, `~/.aws/`, `/etc/sudoers`, `.env`, `vault/`, `mcp-tokens/`) and `HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT` fences writes to a directory (Docker sets `/opt/data`). Sandboxing is the `terminal.backend` choice among local, docker, ssh, singularity, modal, daytona and vercel; the Docker backend drops all capabilities except DAC_OVERRIDE/CHOWN/FOWNER, sets no-new-privileges, `--pids-limit 256`, nosuid tmpfs, and `container_memory` 5 GB / `container_disk` 50 GB defaults, with `terminal.cwd` as a soft workspace fence. Secrets matching KEY/TOKEN/SECRET/PASSWORD/CREDENTIAL/AUTH are stripped from `terminal` and `execute_code` children and MCP subprocesses get a minimal env; URL tools enforce SSRF blocks on RFC1918, loopback, link-local and cloud metadata ranges (`security.allow_private_urls`, `security.website_blocklist`), context files are scanned for injection and rewritten to `[BLOCKED]`, and Tirith pre-exec scanning catches homograph URLs and pipe-to-interpreter. For messaging, gateway users pass an ordered allowlist check (`TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USERS`, `GATEWAY_ALLOWED_USERS`) or DM pairing (8-char code, 1 h TTL, 5-attempt lockout, `unauthorized_dm_behavior: pair|ignore|decline`).
dimensions.hooks: There are four hook systems: gateway hooks (`HOOK.yaml` + `handler.py` dropped in `~/.hermes/hooks/<name>/`, gateway only), plugin hooks (`ctx.register_hook(event, cb)`, CLI and gateway), shell hooks (a `hooks:` block in `config.yaml` pointing at external scripts, CLI/gateway/desktop), and signed outbound webhooks (`hooks.outbound`, fire-and-forget, cannot block). Lifecycle events include `pre_tool_call`, `post_tool_call`, `pre_llm_call`, `post_llm_call`, `pre_verify`, `pre_gateway_dispatch`, `on_session_start`/`on_session_end`, `agent:start`/`agent:step`/`agent:end`, kanban task events, and transform hooks `transform_tool_result`, `transform_terminal_output`, `transform_llm_output`, `transform_api_error_classification`. Hooks can veto: `pre_tool_call` returns `{"action":"block","message":"..."}` (a non-empty message is required and is short-circuited back to the model as the tool error) or approves/modifies arguments; `pre_verify` can force the loop to continue with a synthetic user turn (capped by `agent.max_verify_nudges`, default 3); `pre_gateway_dispatch` can skip or rewrite inbound messages; the Claude Code shape `{"decision":"block","reason":...}` is accepted for compatibility. Post hooks are observe-only, request middleware chains so each callback sees the payload as rewritten by earlier ones, and `gateway/hooks.py` plus `gateway/builtin_hooks/` handle discovery and always-on hooks.
dimensions.subagents: Children are spawned by the `delegate_task` tool (`tools/delegate_tool.py`, backed by the `agent/subagent_lifecycle` API and its `SubagentLaunchRequest`, with states PENDING, STARTING, RUNNING, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, INTERRUPTED, CANCEL_REQUESTED, CANCELLED). Each child starts a completely fresh conversation (only the `goal` and `context` fields are passed, no parent history) with its own terminal session, inherits the parent's enabled toolsets minus `delegate_task` (unless `role="orchestrator"`), `clarify`, `memory`, `send_message` and `cronjob`, keeps `execute_code`, may only be narrowed by `allowed_toolsets` (broadening is rejected and the unsafe-tool block stays enforced), uses the parent's model and credential pool unless `delegation.model` overrides it, and has the workspace's `.hermes.md`/`AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`/`.cursorrules` embedded; `delegation.worktree_isolation` gives each child a git worktree. Limits are `delegation.max_concurrent_children` (10 per batch), `delegation.oneshot_max_children` (2), `delegation.max_spawn_depth` (default 1, i.e. flat; 2 enables orchestrator children) and `delegation.max_iterations` (the delegation page says 250, the agent-loop page says 50, an inconsistency). Only the child's final report returns to the parent: `status` (completed/failed/interrupted), `summary`, exit reason, files modified, issues, and optional `schema_valid`/`schema_errors`, bounded to 32k chars, immutable with a result hash and kept in-process for one hour. Two further primitives sit alongside it: Kanban, a durable SQLite task board where the dispatcher spawns named-profile workers as full OS processes (`kanban.max_in_progress`, `.worktrees/<id>/`, `--completion-contract OWNER/REPO` gating on GitHub required checks), and Mixture-of-Agents, a virtual provider where reference models advise an aggregator once per user turn. Nous's September 2026 post reports an orchestrator dispatching 1,393 subagents (peak 218 concurrent, three levels deep) over git worktrees to cut non-test Python from 1,063,826 to 698,363 lines in ~19 hours for ~$19,300.
dimensions.providers: Provider-agnostic by construction: `hermes_cli/auth.py` holds `PROVIDER_REGISTRY` and `runtime_provider.resolve_runtime_provider()` maps a `(provider, model)` pair to `(api_mode, api_key, base_url)` across 18+ providers and three wire formats, `chat_completions`, `anthropic_messages` and `codex_responses` (with `agent/anthropic_adapter.py` doing format conversion). Named providers include OpenRouter, Nous Portal (OAuth), OpenAI and Codex, Anthropic native, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Alibaba DashScope, Z.AI, Kimi/Moonshot, MiniMax, xAI, NVIDIA NIM, AWS Bedrock, Azure Foundry, Hugging Face, GitHub Copilot, Vercel AI Gateway, Ollama Cloud and LM Studio, switched with `hermes model` or `/model provider:model`. Local models run through any OpenAI-compatible server (Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp, SGLang, LM Studio) via `model.provider: custom` and `model.base_url: http://localhost:11434/v1` (the FAQ's example is `qwen3.5:27b`) or `OPENAI_BASE_URL`; the FAQ warns that `model.context_length` must be set by hand because Ollama reports the model maximum rather than `num_ctx`, and `HERMES_STREAM_READ_TIMEOUT` covers slow local generation. Fallback provider chains, OpenRouter `provider_routing` (`sort: price|throughput|latency`, `only`, `ignore`, `order`), credential pools with key rotation and `auxiliary.*` models for compression/vision/review round out routing. Handling of weak models is only partly documented: native tool calling is assumed (no XML or text tool-call fallback is described), `approvals.mode: smart` and compression can be pushed to cheaper auxiliary models, and the internal `evals/toolperf_abeval` harness reports that tool-layer fixes cut turns 21%, tool calls 29% and errors to zero on weaker models while strong models were at parity.
dimensions.mcp: Hermes is both an MCP client and an MCP server. As a client, servers are declared under `mcp_servers` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml` with stdio, HTTP (optional mTLS) and SSE transports plus OAuth 2.1 token management; tools appear as `mcp_<server>_<tool>` through `tools/mcp_tool.py`, per-server `include`/`exclude` globs filter large surfaces, resources and prompts get `list_resources`/`read_resource`/`list_prompts`/`get_prompt` wrappers, `/reload-mcp` is guarded by `approvals.mcp_reload_confirm`, MCP subprocesses receive only a safe environment, and Tool Search defers MCP schemas out of the prompt. As a server, `hermes mcp serve` (`mcp_serve.py`) exposes Hermes's messaging capabilities to other agents, with `SamplingHandler.max_tokens_cap` bounding sampling requests. For editors it implements ACP (Agent Client Protocol) as a stdio JSON-RPC server in `acp_adapter/` (`hermes acp`, `hermes-acp`, `python -m acp_adapter`) used by VS Code, Zed, JetBrains and Buzz Desktop, with once/session/always approval tiers and a reduced `hermes-acp` toolset. Other standards it adopts: the agentskills.io SKILL.md format, reading `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md`/`.cursorrules`, Claude Code-compatible hook return shapes, and an OpenClaw importer (`hermes claw migrate`). A2A is not documented.
dimensions.evals: No published SWE-bench or Terminal-Bench score for Hermes Agent was found in the README, docs site, landing page or Nous blog index; the repo's `batch_runner.py` and `mini_swe_runner.py` (default `--max_iterations 15`) generate ShareGPT-style trajectories for training rather than scoring. The arXiv source-code study (2609.00006, 2026-07-15) that includes Hermes explicitly does not benchmark and removed self-reported SWE-Bench Verified figures from its table because they were "obtained on different model generations and configurations". The one harness-vs-harness ablation the project publishes is `evals/toolperf_abeval` (README + `ab_eval.py`, `run_all.sh`): 9 production-derived error tasks x 2 models x 2 arms x 3 reps (108 runs, ~2.5 h) measuring LLM turns, tool calls, errors, retries, result bytes and wall-clock, reporting -21% turns, -29% tool calls, errors to 0 and -23% wall time on weaker models with parity on strong ones. The Mixture-of-Agents docs cite "HermesBench" (a claude-opus-4.8 aggregator over a gpt-5.5 reference scores 0.8202 vs 0.7607 for Opus alone and 0.7412 for gpt-5.5 alone) but the benchmark's methodology is not documented anywhere I could reach. The `evals/` directory otherwise holds ~35 regression probes and ~35 subdirectories (compaction, memory, prompt_footprint, tool_search, provider_fallback, subagent_process_handoff) aimed at the harness itself, not model ranking.
dimensions.distinctive: Three ideas stand out. First, the self-improving skills loop: SKILL.md documents under `~/.hermes/skills/` are progressively disclosed (`skills_list` ~3k tokens, `skill_view`, then reference files), the agent creates and patches them itself via `skill_manage` after complex tasks or `/learn`, an optional `skills.write_approval` stages writes for review, and hub installs from skills.sh/ClawHub/GitHub taps are security-scanned. Second, a layered permission floor: LLM-assessed smart approvals sit above a dangerous-pattern list, `approvals.deny` globs and a hardline blocklist that no `--yolo` can lift, plus `HERMES_WRITE_SAFE_ROOT`, secret-stripping and SSRF fences, which the arXiv study singles out as "A Policy Floor That Survives YOLO". Third, a persistent personal agent rather than a coding session: one `AIAgent` serves CLI, ACP, cron, batch and a 20+ platform gateway, with frozen `MEMORY.md`/`USER.md` blocks, FTS5 session recall, in-place lineage compaction and Anthropic cache breakpoints all tuned to keep the prompt prefix stable; the verify-on-stop `pre_verify` guard is a smaller but unusual fourth. The loudest criticisms are footprint and sprawl: Tencent Cloud's August 2026 comparison puts the system prompt near 20k tokens and flags the "larger footprint"; the codebase was ~1.06M non-test Python lines before Nous's own September 2026 refactor (the arXiv study estimates 600K+ LoC, repowise scores defect risk 6.1/10 with `gateway/run.py` at 34,847 lines and `cli.py`/`main.py` as "bug magnets"), and the repo carries 43,742 open issues; reviewers question the auditability of self-modifying skills ("Will you really check which Skills Hermes edited every day?"); a dev.to deep dive flags memory rot, cache-busting from dynamic prompt content and inconsistent reasoning-trace handling; and the docs themselves disagree on basics (max_turns 500 vs unlimited, delegation.max_iterations 50 vs 250, six vs seven terminal backends, 40+ vs 69 vs 70+ tools). Comparison pieces (deepseekagent.io, 2026-08) accordingly file it under "personal automation across channels" rather than coding-first.

profiles.name: GitHub Copilot CLI (GitHub/Microsoft)
profiles.one_liner: GitHub's closed-source, multi-model terminal coding agent (npm @github/copilot, GA 2026-02-25) whose engine also serves as the JSON-RPC backend for the MIT Copilot SDK and as an ACP server, customised almost entirely through Markdown/JSON (instructions, skills, .agent.md agents, JSON hooks, plugins, MCP), with OS-level sandboxing, BYOK for Ollama/vLLM-style endpoints, and a cross-model-family critic ("rubber duck") measured on SWE-Bench Pro.

dimensions.identity: Maintained by GitHub (Microsoft) as the terminal surface of the Copilot coding agent; public preview 2025-09-25 (release tags start at 0.0.328, 2025-09-26), GA 2026-02-25 as v1.0, latest stable 1.0.88 on 2026-09-22 with 1.0.89 prereleases three days later, i.e. a near-daily cadence. Proprietary: LICENSE.md is the "GitHub Copilot CLI License" granting a "non-exclusive, non-transferable, royalty-free license to install and run" with no modification or derivative rights, and github/copilot-cli holds only README.md, changelog.md, issues and release binaries. Open-sourcing requests (#83, 2025-09-27; #3241, 2026-05-11) remain open with no maintainer response. Implementation language is not disclosed; the npm package @github/copilot (Node 22+) is a 13 KB npm-loader.js bootstrap depending only on detect-libc, and the CLI also ships as native executables via `curl -fsSL https://gh.io/copilot-install | bash`, `brew install --cask copilot-cli` and `winget install GitHub.Copilot`. The same engine is exposed to the MIT-licensed github/copilot-sdk (Node, Python, Go, .NET, Rust, Java; 10.5k stars) over JSON-RPC and to editors as an ACP server. Popularity: 11.2k stars / 1.9k forks on the issues-only repo, ~1.21M npm downloads for 2026-09-18..24, and it is bundled with every Copilot plan (Free, Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, Enterprise).
dimensions.loop: A single main-agent tool-calling loop (ReAct-style, no separate planner process): the model calls tools until it emits a final message, at which point stopReason "end_turn" fires the agentStop hook and the SDK raises session.idle. No hard per-turn step cap is documented; the only cut-offs are that an agentStop hook may "block" the stop to force another cycle but "the CLI now ends the turn after 8 consecutive blocks" (v1.0.72), and autopilot "pauses after 5 automatic continuation messages" (--max-autopilot-continues). Shift+Tab cycles three modes: standard (approve each mutating tool), plan (clarify, build a plan, wait for approval, then execute) and autopilot (/autopilot, --autopilot: runs until "the agent determines that the task is complete", a blocker occurs or the user intervenes). Text typed mid-turn is "steering" folded into the running task between tool calls, while Ctrl+Enter queues it as the next turn. The model itself can change inside a turn: the "auto" tier "adapts model selection as your task evolves" (v1.0.75), and at checkpoints (after a plan, after complex implementation, after writing tests) the loop calls the rubber-duck critic through the task tool. Each prompt takes a conversation snapshot, so Esc-Esc rewinds conversation and optionally files (skipping files over 10 MB and turns that touched more than 500 files).
dimensions.tools: Built-in tools live in the closed binary; docs and the reverse-engineered wiki name bash/shell (with paired read/list/stop shell tools), view, edit, create, grep, glob/search, web_fetch, task (spawn subagent) and read_agent, plus LSP-backed navigation when lsp-config.json is present. Agent files address tools via case-insensitive aliases (execute->bash/powershell, read->view, edit, search->Grep/Glob, agent->Task, web->WebSearch/WebFetch, todo) and MCP tools as "server/tool" or "server/*". Third parties never register into the built-in set: they add tools through MCP servers, through out-of-process JavaScript extensions, or via the SDK's defineTool({name, description, parameters as JSON Schema or Zod, handler}). Results: "tool output larger than 20 KiB is saved to a temporary file" and the model receives the path plus a preview (COPILOT_LARGE_OUTPUT_THRESHOLD_BYTES, disable/redirect settings since v1.0.69); the Sept 2026 cost post adds "selective output compaction" that strips repetitive install/build/test/lint noise (-5.5% cost) and removed line-number prefixes from view output (~-5%). postToolUse hooks may replace a result via modifiedResult.textResultForLlm, and hook output is bounded at 10 MiB per invocation. The Task subagent returns "brief summaries on success or full output on failure"; a secondary source claims Codex models are handed apply_patch while Claude gets Edit/Write, which GitHub has not documented.
dimensions.extensibility: Customization is Markdown/JSON-first: instructions (.github/copilot-instructions.md, .github/instructions/**/*.instructions.md with applyTo, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, ~/.copilot/copilot-instructions.md, COPILOT_CUSTOM_INSTRUCTIONS_DIRS), skills (SKILL.md, `copilot skill add`), custom agents (.agent.md), hooks (.github/hooks/*.json), MCP (mcp-config.json), LSP (lsp-config.json, .github/lsp.json) and BYOK providers (providers.json). Plugins bundle skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers, LSP servers, slash commands and extensions behind a plugin.json manifest (Agent Plugins 1.0 schema at agent-plugins.org; legacy .claude-plugin/plugin.json also read), installed with `copilot plugin install OWNER/REPO|marketplace|git-url|path` into ~/.copilot/installed-plugins/, and pinnable by enterprise via enabledPlugins / extraKnownMarketplaces. Extensions (experimental; /experimental on) are the only code-level plug point: "a small Node.js module that runs as a separate process" at .github/extensions/NAME/extension.mjs|cjs|js or ~/.copilot/extensions/NAME/, JavaScript only, contributing "tools that Copilot can call" and "slash commands that you run yourself", with permission handlers that can approve subagent tool requests. /extensions mode selects Load & Augment, Load Only or Disabled; the exact registration API is not in public docs beyond "the SDK that ships with the CLI". Providers are pluggable via BYOK, prompts via instructions/skills/agents, hooks via JSON, but the UI is limited to settings (theme, editorMode vim, sidebar.*) and to whatever editor speaks ACP. Full embedding goes through the SDK: createSession({model, tools, systemMessage, mcpServers, customAgents, hooks, onPermissionRequest}).
dimensions.context: The window holds system prompt, instruction files, tool schemas and history; /context breaks usage down by bucket. Auto-compaction "starts compacting the context in the background" at ~80% (keeping a 20% buffer for in-flight tool work), pauses the agent if ~95% is hit first, writes a structured summary (goals, done, key technical details, files, next steps) and since v1.0.85 saves a numbered checkpoint listed by /session checkpoints; /compact [FOCUS-INSTRUCTIONS] forces it and preCompact hooks fire first. Tool search keeps schemas out of the prompt: above roughly 30 tools, non-built-in tools are deferred and fetched by a search call (mcp-config deferTools: auto|never, agent frontmatter deferred-tool-loading: true, settings toolSearch: false), supported on Claude Haiku 4.5+/Sonnet 4+/Opus 4+ and GPT-5.4+; other models get every tool up front. Persistent memory is server-side "Copilot Memory": repository facts stored with code citations that are re-validated against the current branch plus user preferences, shared with the cloud agent and code review, deleted after 28 unused days, and refreshed in long sessions after 30 minutes. Instruction files combine rather than override (duplicates deduplicated, no precedence order), and a dynamicRetrieval setting controls embeddings-based retrieval per category. Subagents run in separate windows, oversized outputs go to files, /ask asks without touching history, and 1M-token models are offered; KV-cache/prompt-cache friendliness is not documented.
dimensions.permissions: Default two tiers: read-only operations (search, file reads, read-only shell) run automatically; mutating tools prompt Yes / "approve TOOL for the rest of the running session" / No, and a directory-trust dialog gates the workspace (trustedFolders in config.json; /add-dir widens it). Rules: --allow-tool / --deny-tool with patterns shell, 'shell(git:*)', 'shell(git commit)', 'write(.github/copilot-instructions.md)', 'url(github.com)', 'MyMCP(create_issue)'; --available-tools/--excluded-tools remove tools outright; --allow-all-tools, --allow-all-paths, --allow-all-urls or --yolo/--allow-all lift gates; "deny rules always take precedence over allow rules, even when --allow-all is set"; decisions persist in ~/.copilot/permissions-config.json and allowedUrls/deniedUrls in settings.json. Local sandboxing (public preview; sandbox.enabled default false; /sandbox enable|status|policy) confines shell, MCP and LSP child processes with filesystem policies (cwd read/write, repo read, PATH dirs read-only, deniedPaths, "the more specific path wins") and network policy (allowedHosts, blockedHosts, allowLocalNetwork; since v1.0.82 sandboxed commands cannot reach localhost, egress via proxy), while built-in file tools remain "software-only" safeguards. Linux sandboxing requires slirp4netns, nsenter and iptables (namespace-based), Windows requires an Insiders build, and macOS mechanics are not documented. Enterprise floors: MDM/managed settings can force sandbox and set permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode="disable" (always wins), policy hooks in /etc/github-copilot/policy.d cannot be disabled, MCP registry/allowlists apply, and --cloud runs the entire session in a hosted sandbox. Autopilot with "limited permissions" auto-denies gated tools, and --max-ai-credits / "/limits set max-ai-credits N" (minimum 30, each credit $0.01) caps spend.
dimensions.hooks: Hooks are external commands, HTTP calls or prompts declared as {"version":1,"hooks":{event:[{type, bash, powershell, cwd, env, timeoutSec, matcher}]}} in .github/hooks/*.json, ~/.copilot/hooks/*.json, .github/copilot/settings.json, plugins, managed /etc/github-copilot/policy.d/*.json and cross-tool .claude/settings.json. Events: sessionStart, sessionEnd, userPromptSubmitted, userPromptTransformed, preToolUse, postToolUse, postToolUseFailure, agentStop, subagentStart, subagentStop, errorOccurred, preCompact, notification and permissionRequest (CLI only). Veto is explicit: preToolUse returns {permissionDecision: allow|deny|ask, permissionDecisionReason, modifiedArgs, additionalContext}, permissionRequest returns {behavior: allow|deny, message, interrupt}, agentStop/subagentStop return {decision: block|allow, reason, modifiedResponse}, and postToolUse can rewrite the result. Command preToolUse hooks are fail-closed on crash or non-zero exit (exit 2 = deny) but "timeouts are always fail-open"; default timeout is 30 s, matcher is a regex compiled as ^(?:PATTERN)$, and output is capped at 10 MiB. Hooks receive OpenTelemetry trace context (v1.0.81), and repeated agentStop blocks end the turn after 8. The SDK exposes the same contract as createSession({hooks:{onPreToolUse: async (input) => ...}}).
dimensions.subagents: Children are spawned by the model via the task tool (or explicitly with /agent, --agent NAME, /fleet, /research, /security-review, /rubber-duck); each gets "its own context window", streams subagent.started/completed/failed events and subagentStart/subagentStop hooks, and hands back text the parent folds into its response. Built-ins: Explore (read-only search), Task (build/test runner with "access to all of the tools the parent agent can use... with the same permissions granted or denied", returning summaries on success and full output on failure), General-purpose, Code-review, Research, Rubber-duck (different model family, read-only), Security-review and Plan. Custom agents are .agent.md files in .github/agents/, ~/.copilot/agents/ (user wins on a name clash), the org .github repo or enterprise .github-private, with frontmatter description (required), name, tools (default all, [] none, "server/*"), model, mcp-servers, user-invocable, disable-model-invocation (infer retired), include-custom-instructions and deferred-tool-loading; the reference caps an agent prompt at 30,000 characters. Limits: the default maximum nesting depth was lowered "from 6 to 4 to curb runaway recursive sub-agent delegation" (changelog, June 2026) and concurrency/depth are tunable in /settings for usage-based-billing accounts; the default concurrency value is not published. /fleet (or --fleet) decomposes a prompt into independent parallel subtasks with a documented warning that it burns more AI credits; GitHub's June 2026 retune of when the main agent delegates cut tool failures 23% per session. Cloud hand-off is separate: /delegate or an "&" prefix commits to a branch and lets the Copilot cloud agent open a draft PR that /resume can pull back locally.
dimensions.providers: GitHub-hosted and multi-vendor: /model or --model (COPILOT_MODEL) selects Anthropic Claude Opus/Sonnet 4.6 and Haiku 4.5, OpenAI GPT-5.x/GPT-5.3-Codex/GPT-5.4, or Gemini 3 Pro within enterprise model policy; model "auto" routes and re-routes mid-task and effortLevel low|medium|high|xhigh sets reasoning. BYOK is first-class: COPILOT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL plus COPILOT_MODEL, with COPILOT_PROVIDER_TYPE openai|azure|anthropic, COPILOT_PROVIDER_API_KEY or _BEARER_TOKEN, _WIRE_API, _MODEL_ID, _WIRE_MODEL, _MAX_PROMPT_TOKENS, _MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS, _AZURE_API_VERSION, or a ~/.copilot/providers.json registry, and COPILOT_OFFLINE=true. The openai type explicitly covers "OpenAI, Ollama, vLLM, Foundry Local, and any other OpenAI Chat Completions API-compatible endpoint", so llama.cpp's server works by the same route. "Models must support tool calling ... and streaming", and GitHub recommends a context window of at least 128k tokens. Weak-model handling is thin: unsupported models just get every tool loaded up front, the cross-family rubber duck depends on GitHub-hosted models, and nothing documents retries or schema repair for models that mis-format tool calls. A secondary source describes per-model tool dialects (apply_patch for Codex, Edit/Write for Claude) that GitHub itself has not documented.
dimensions.mcp: MCP client support is central: the GitHub MCP server is built in (read-only tools on by default), and more servers come from ~/.copilot/mcp-config.json, repo-level .mcp.json or .github/mcp.json (found walking up to the repo root; .vscode/mcp.json is ignored), /mcp add, `copilot mcp add`, or the experimental /mcp search registry. Schema: type local|stdio|http|sse, command/args/env, url/headers, tools ("*", list or ""), timeout, deferTools auto|never and slowConnectionThresholdMs; remote servers support OAuth with configurable scopes (v1.0.89) and enterprise registry URL/allowlist policies apply. MCP tools are gated like any other ("--allow-tool=MyMCP(create_issue)"), run inside the sandbox, and are deferred by tool search. The CLI is also an ACP (Agent Client Protocol) server: `copilot --acp --stdio` or `--port N` exposes sessions, --available-tools/--excluded-tools, --effort, skills as commands and subagent IDs to editors, minus UI-bound commands (/diff, /resume, /settings, /undo). The same engine runs as a JSON-RPC server (`copilot --headless --port 4321`) for the SDK. A2A is not documented and the CLI does not advertise itself as an MCP server.
dimensions.evals: GitHub publishes no leaderboard score for Copilot CLI on SWE-bench Verified or Terminal-Bench, and I found no Terminal-Bench entry for it. Its engineering posts do publish harness-level ablations: the rubber-duck critic (2026-04-06) was measured on SWE-Bench Pro, where "Claude Sonnet 4.6 paired with Rubber Duck running GPT-5.4 ... clos[ed] 74.7% of the performance gap between Sonnet and Opus" and gained +3.8% on 3+ file / 70+ step problems. The delegation retune (2026-06-12) was production A/B tested: -23% tool failures per session, -27% search failures, -18% edit failures, -5% P95 wait, no quality regression. The cost post (2026-09-02) reports selective output compaction -5.5%, view line-number removal ~-5% offline / -3% online, task-tool prompt compression ~1,300 tokens per turn (-2.9% cost per active hour) and background-result batching -2.3%, validated on unnamed "agentic coding benchmarks" plus online experiments. A secondary comparison quotes model-level SWE-bench Verified (~74% GPT-5 vs 87.6% Claude Opus 4.7), which is not a harness measurement; a model-vs-harness ablation for the CLI itself is not documented.
dimensions.distinctive: Cross-model composition inside one harness: the loop can re-route models mid-task (auto tier), applies per-model features (tool search only where the model was trained for it), and deliberately pairs the orchestrator with a critic from another vendor (Claude session, GPT-5.4 rubber duck) with measured SWE-Bench Pro gains, which a May 2026 essay frames as honest "model-harness fit" routing. Engine-as-a-server: one runtime is the JSON-RPC backend of the MIT SDK, an ACP server for editors, a session mirrored to GitHub.com/Mobile for remote approval, and a --cloud / "&"-delegated cloud job, with out-of-process JS extensions and enterprise floors (policy.d hooks, MDM sandbox, disableBypassPermissionsMode). Deliberate compatibility with rivals: it reads CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md and AGENTS.md, .claude/settings.json hooks, .claude-plugin/plugin.json and Claude-style tool aliases (Read/Edit/Grep/Task), so a repo configured for Claude Code works unchanged. Loudest criticism is the closed binary: issues #83 (2025-09) and #3241 (2026-05) call it "a total blackbox" with near-daily releases and say "no serious developer will implement copilot cli in headless agent workflows"; neither has a maintainer reply. Reviewers describe it as an "interactive companion" with "looser, more conversational" approval gates that trails Claude Code on long-horizon multi-file work. Other complaints: per-subagent and /fleet credit burn, experimental JavaScript-only extensions, Windows-Insiders-only sandboxing, and no per-scope MCP governance like Claude Code's user/project split.

unknowns: Implementation language of the CLI binary (closed source; only the Node bootstrap and native-binary distribution are visible)
Hard per-turn tool-call/iteration limit (only the agentStop 8-consecutive-blocks cutoff and autopilot's 5 continuations are documented)
Sandbox OS mechanism on macOS and Windows (only Linux dependencies slirp4netns/nsenter/iptables and the Windows Insiders requirement are documented)
Default subagent concurrency value (depth default 4 is documented; concurrency default is not)
KV-cache / prompt-cache friendliness of the prompt layout
Any published Terminal-Bench or SWE-bench Verified score for Copilot CLI as a harness
A2A protocol support
Exact extension registration API (tool/slash-command function names) for CLI extensions; only the SDK's defineTool is documented
Per-model tool dialects (apply_patch for Codex vs Edit/Write for Claude) are asserted only by a secondary source
Explicit weak-model handling (retries, schema repair, nudges) beyond the tool-search fallback

profiles.name: Kilo (Kilo Code extension + Kilo CLI, Kilo-Org/kilocode)
profiles.one_liner: MIT-licensed, multi-surface coding agent (VS Code, JetBrains, TUI, cloud) in which every client talks to one `kilo serve` runtime forked from OpenCode; born as a Roo Code/Cline fork in March 2025, rebuilt on the OpenCode core in April 2026, and acquired by Anaconda in July 2026.

dimensions.identity: Maintained by Kilo-Org (Kilo Code; CEO Scott Breitenother), acquired by Anaconda on 15 Jul 2026 with the "open source and source-available codebase" stated to continue. The repo was created 10 Mar 2025 as a fork of Roo Code (itself a Cline fork); the first GitHub release was v4.6.0 on 24 Mar 2025 (version numbers continued Roo's), `@kilocode/cli` first hit npm on 13 Oct 2025 (0.0.1), and the rebuilt extension on the OpenCode core went public beta 10 Mar 2026 and GA 2 Apr 2026. License MIT; TypeScript on Bun with the Effect library in a Turborepo monorepo where `packages/opencode/` is the engine (README FAQ: "Kilo CLI is a fork of OpenCode"; `.opencode-version` pins upstream v1.18.26). Distribution: VS Code extension (1,573,440 installs, 4/5 stars from 211 reviews), JetBrains plugin, CLI (`npm install -g @kilocode/cli`, curl, brew, AUR, release binaries; ~119.6k npm downloads in the last month), Cloud Agent at app.kilo.ai, Slack and mobile. Popularity on 26 Sep 2026: 27,423 stars, 3,200 forks, 537 GitHub releases, 613 open issues, current release v7.8.1 (25 Sep 2026); Anaconda claims 3M+ developers and ~10T tokens/month routed, kilo.ai claims "5M+".
dimensions.loop: A single ReAct-style tool-calling loop per session, described in CONTEXT.md as a "Session Drain": promote the pending prompt, run a provider turn, settle tool calls, repeat until no continuation remains; tool calls inside one assistant step execute concurrently (the migration guide notes "Tool calls now run concurrently rather than sequentially"). The step limit is per agent via the `steps` frontmatter/config field (`const maxSteps = agent.steps ?? Infinity` in `session/prompt.ts`); when `step >= maxSteps` a `MAX_STEPS_PROMPT` user message is injected forcing a text-only reply. `session/processor.ts` sets `DOOM_LOOP_THRESHOLD = 3`: three consecutive calls with identical tool name and input raise a `doom_loop` permission ask (default "ask"), a `malformedToolGuard` aborts after repeated malformed tool calls (#14143), and schema-invalid arguments return an `InvalidArgumentsError` telling the model to "rewrite the input". The processor returns `"compact" | "stop" | "continue"`; a turn ends when the provider finishes without tool calls, on a denied permission or error, or after compaction it auto-continues (pluggable via `experimental.compaction.autocontinue`). An optional CodeMode (experimental flag or config toggle, `packages/codemode`) adds code-as-action: one `execute` tool runs a confined tree-walking JS interpreter over a schema-described tool tree with at most eight concurrent nested calls, so dependent tool chains skip model round-trips.
dimensions.tools: Tools are Effect-based TypeScript definitions: `Tool.define(id, { description, parameters (Effect Schema), execute(args, ctx) })` in `packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts`, where `ctx` carries `sessionID`, `agent`, `abort`, `messages`, `metadata()` and `ask()` (the permission request), and each description lives in a sibling `.txt` file. `tool/registry.ts` merges built-in, Kilo-specific, plugin (`@kilocode/plugin` `tool()` with Zod args) and MCP tools and filters them per agent, model, permission ruleset and network-restricted state. Built-ins: `read`, `glob`, `grep`, `list`, `edit`, `write`, `apply_patch`, `bash`, `webfetch`, `websearch`, `task`, `question`, `todowrite`/`todoread`, `plan` (plan_enter/plan_exit), `skill`, `lsp`, `repo_clone`; Kilo adds `kilo_memory_recall`/save, `repo-overview`, `semantic-search`, `notify_user`, `suggest`, `board` (Swarm), `agent_manager`, `background-process`, `browser-open`, `schedule-wakeup`/cron, `read-docx`/`xlsx`, `generate-image`, `chart` and `notebook_*`. Output truncation is centralised in `tool/truncate.ts`: `MAX_LINES = 2000`, `MAX_BYTES = 50 * 1024` (overridable via `tool_output.max_lines`/`max_bytes`), with the full text written to a managed tool-output file kept 7 days and a hint to Grep/Read it or delegate to the `explore` subagent; compaction pruning later replaces tool outputs older than 40k tokens with "[Old tool result content cleared]". Issue #10497 measured ~37.7k chars (~9k tokens) of built-in tool descriptions on every request (bash 10.3k, todowrite 9.2k), a known overhead.
dimensions.extensibility: Plugins follow the OpenCode model: a module exporting `{ id, server: async ({ client, project, directory, worktree, $, serverUrl }) => Hooks }` typed by `packages/plugin/src/index.ts`. Pluggable surfaces are custom tools (`tool` map via `tool()` with Zod args, or standalone files in `.kilo/tool/` whose filename becomes the tool name; same-name overrides a built-in), auth flows (`auth` hook, OAuth or API key), model catalogs (`provider` hook), system-prompt and message transforms, the compaction prompt, workspace adapters (`experimental_workspace.register`), and TUI plugins via a `./tui` export (SolidJS API for commands, routes, slots, dialogs, keybinds). Load order is built-ins, then the `plugin` array in `~/.config/kilo/kilo.json`, `~/.config/kilo/plugin/`, the project config array, and `.kilo/plugin/`; `kilo plugin <module>` patches config and `KILO_PURE=1` disables externals. Prompt-level extension is file-based: agents as Markdown with YAML frontmatter in `.kilo/agents/*.md` (fields `description`, `mode`, `model`, `temperature`, `top_p`, `permission`, `steps`, `hidden`, `color`, `disable`), commands/workflows in `.kilo/commands/*.md` invoked as `/name`, and Agent-Skills-spec `SKILL.md` folders. A community Kilo Marketplace (github.com/Kilo-Org/kilo-marketplace) distributes agents, skills, MCP servers and plugins via `PLUGIN.yaml`, installable at project (`.kilo/`) or global (`~/.config/kilo/`) scope.
dimensions.context: Instructions come from `AGENTS.md` (or `AGENT.md`) at the project root plus nested per-directory AGENTS.md files loaded when the agent reads files there, `.kilo/rules/`, and the `instructions` config key; precedence is agent prompt > project `instructions` > AGENTS.md > global `instructions` > skills, and AGENTS.md edits are write-protected behind a prompt. Compaction is configured under `compaction`: `auto` (default true), optional `threshold_percent`, `prune` (default true), `tail_turns` 2, `preserve_recent_tokens` 2k-8k, `reserved` about min(20k, model max output); `/compact` triggers it manually, a separate `agent.compaction.model` can be pinned, and `KILO_DISABLE_AUTOCOMPACT=1`/`KILO_DISABLE_PRUNE=1` switch it off. Persistent memory is Kilo Memory (off by default, `/memory on`, per project only): `project.md`, `environment.md`, `corrections.md` plus session digests under `~/.local/share/kilo/memory/<project-slug>-<sha1-12>/`, with only a compact index injected at session start and detail fetched on demand through `kilo_memory_recall` (modes search/typed/digest/catalog); the old rules-based Memory Bank is deprecated, and an embeddings-based codebase index powers a semantic-search tool. KV-cache friendliness is an explicit design goal in CONTEXT.md: a "Context Epoch" keeps the rendered Baseline System Context as the immutable provider-cache baseline, changed context sources are appended as Mid-Conversation System Messages at a Safe Provider-Turn Boundary instead of mutating the system prompt, and only compaction starts a new epoch. Open issue #9494 reports "Compaction exhausted: context still exceeds model limits after 3 attempts" on small-window models.
dimensions.permissions: One allow/ask/deny rule model under the `permission` key in `kilo.jsonc`, shared by VS Code, JetBrains and CLI (the VS Code Auto Approve tab writes the same file). Known keys in `packages/core/src/v1/config/permission.ts`: `read`, `edit`, `glob`, `grep`, `list`, `bash`, `task`, `external_directory`, `markdown_source`, `todowrite`, `question`, `webfetch`, `websearch`, `lsp`, `doom_loop`, `skill`, `agent_manager`, `notebook_read/edit/execute`, plus MCP tools as `{server}_{tool}` and any other key; values are glob-pattern maps (`"bash": { "*": "ask", "git *": "allow" }`), the last matching rule wins, and an unmatched check defaults to `ask`. Bash compound commands need every sub-command allowed, `.env`/`.env.*` always ask (except `.env.example`), per-agent overrides make Ask read-only and let Plan edit only `.kilo/plans/*.md`, and `permission.task` whitelists which subagents may be spawned; `kilo run --auto` auto-approves everything a rule does not deny. A separate OS sandbox (`sandbox.enabled` default false, `sandbox.network` default deny, `allowed_hosts`, `writable_paths`) uses Seatbelt (`/usr/bin/sandbox-exec`) on macOS and Bubblewrap (system or bundled SHA-256-verified `bwrap`) with seccomp and a Unix network relay on Linux; writes are confined to the workspace and Kilo runtime dirs, `.git` is always read-only so mutating git needs explicit escalation, and Windows is unsupported. The docs draw the line explicitly: permissions decide whether a call runs, the sandbox decides what an allowed call can change or connect to, and plugin hooks and MCP clients run as trusted host integrations outside the sandbox. Agent Manager adds git-worktree isolation per session.
dimensions.hooks: Lifecycle hooks are the plugin `Hooks` interface in `packages/plugin/src/index.ts`: `event` (every internal bus event), `config`, `chat.message`, `chat.params` (temperature/topP/topK/maxOutputTokens), `chat.headers`, `permission.ask`, `command.execute.before`, `tool.execute.before`, `tool.execute.after`, `tool.definition`, `shell.env`, `experimental.chat.messages.transform`, `experimental.chat.system.transform`, `experimental.session.compacting`, `experimental.compaction.autocontinue`, `experimental.text.complete`, `experimental.provider.small_model`, and `dispose`. Veto is possible: `permission.ask` receives `output.status` and can set it to `"allow"`, `"deny"` or `"ask"`, `tool.execute.before` can rewrite `output.args` or throw (the docs example throws "reading .env files is blocked"), and `tool.execute.after` can rewrite title/output/metadata. Hooks are in-process TypeScript, not shell commands; the sandbox page warns they "can run before a tool's internal permission check" and run outside the sandbox. There is no dedicated on-stop hook; session lifecycle is observed through `event`. Nested MCP calls made from CodeMode also pass through `tool.execute.before/after`.
dimensions.subagents: Children are spawned with the `task` tool (`subagent_type`, `prompt`, `description`, optional `task_id` to resume a prior child session, `background`, and per-task `model`/`provider`/`variant` now on by default); any agent with `mode: subagent` or `all` defined in `.kilo/agents/*.md` or the `agent` config is a valid target, with built-ins `general` (full tools except todo) and `explore` (read-only) and Kilo's opt-in `scout`, and `@agent-name` invokes one manually. A child runs in its own session with fresh history but shares the parent's worktree (no file isolation), inherits the parent model unless overridden, cannot ask the user questions, and gets a ruleset built by `agent/subagent-permissions.ts`: its own permissions plus the parent's `deny` and `external_directory` rules, with `todowrite` and `task` denied unless it explicitly has them. Depth is governed by `subagent_depth` (default 1; `task.ts` fails with "Subagent depth limit reached"), background mode requires `KILO_EXPERIMENTAL_BACKGROUND_SUBAGENTS=true`, and the parent receives a `<task id=... state=...><task_result>` block containing the child's single final message plus a resumable task_id, with costs propagated upward. Parallelism comes from issuing several task calls in one step, Kilo Swarm adds a shared `board` tool so a session and its descendants exchange findings, and the deprecated Orchestrator mode is replaced by delegation from any full-tool agent. Beyond the task tool, Agent Manager (VS Code) runs up to 4 parallel worktree implementations and "each request can start up to 20 tasks", and Gas Town (cloud) orchestrates polecats (default 2 per rig), a refinery reviewer and a mayor coordinator over beads/convoys. Issue #11708 notes a foreground task blocks the TUI with no cancel path.
dimensions.providers: Provider-agnostic by design: docs list 30+ direct providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Vertex, Bedrock, DeepSeek, Mistral, xAI, Groq, Cerebras, OpenRouter, Requesty, Cloudflare AI Gateway, Eden AI and more) alongside Kilo Gateway, an OpenAI-compatible endpoint with 500+ models at provider rates (a secondary review notes a 5% fee on credit purchases) and encrypted BYOK, plus `kilo-auto/frontier|efficient|free` routing tiers. Local models: Ollama (`provider.ollama.baseURL: http://localhost:11434/v1`, model `ollama/qwen3-coder:30b`), LM Studio (port 1234), Atomic Chat (port 1337), Anaconda Desktop, and any OpenAI-compatible server such as vLLM or SGLang; unlisted models register under `provider.<id>.models`, and `disabled_providers`/`enabled_providers` prune the catalog. The Ollama page is candid about weak models: they "are much more likely to get stuck in loops, fail to use tools properly or produce syntax errors", need `num_ctx` of at least 32k, and benefit from short conversations and disabling MCP tools; recommended picks are `qwen3-coder:30b` or `devstral:24b`. Runtime accommodations include the `InvalidArgumentsError` schema feedback, the malformed-tool-call guard, the doom-loop ask, an `apply_patch` tool "used with certain models", the `experimental.provider.small_model` hook, and an Enhance Prompt button. Credentials live in `~/.config/kilo/auth.json` (mode 0600) and provider model lists are cached five minutes.
dimensions.mcp: MCP client only: servers go under the `mcp` key in `kilo.jsonc` (legacy `.kilocode/mcp.json` is migrated) as `type: "local"` (command array, `environment`, `enabled`, `timeout` default 10s) or `type: "remote"` (`url`, `headers`, `oauth`, `timeout` default 15s), over stdio or streamable HTTP with SSE deprecated. `kilo mcp add|list|auth|logout|debug` manage servers, `/mcps` toggles them in-session, and remote OAuth (including client-metadata documents and dynamic registration) is handled by the CLI runtime so editors never hold MCP credentials. Tools are namespaced `{server}_{tool}` and gated by the same allow/ask/deny rules (glob `github_*`), server instructions are injected into context unless all its tools are denied, and resource-capable servers expose `list_mcp_resources`, `list_mcp_resource_templates` and `read_mcp_resource`; the marketplace can install an MCP server together with companion skills. Kilo exposing itself as an MCP server is not documented. ACP is supported: `kilo acp` starts an Agent Client Protocol server (`packages/opencode/src/acp/`) for ACP-capable editors, though the JetBrains plugin uses its own native Kilo Core runtime rather than ACP. Skills implement the Agent Skills spec and also read `~/.claude/skills` and `~/.agents/skills`; A2A is not documented.
dimensions.evals: No public SWE-bench or Terminal-Bench leaderboard score is published. The repo's own `contributing/features/benchmarking.md` is marked "Partial": a Harbor-facing smoke eval in `.github/workflows/smoke-test.yml` checks out the private `Kilo-Org/kilo-bench` repo and runs two tasks (`hello-world` and `log-summary-date-ranges` from a `terminal-bench-sample`), uploading trajectories, while Harbor/ATIF/Opik adapters are "unverified roadmap". That page explicitly frames two comparisons, model-vs-model with a fixed Kilo agent and agent-vs-agent (or Kilo version) with a fixed model, so a harness-vs-model ablation is planned rather than published. Internally, Kilo Bench runs deterministic pass/fail tasks whose per-model, per-task success rate and cost populate the routing table behind `kilo-auto/efficient`; custom pool entries are benchmarked on demand (10 per owner per 24h). The one quantified public result is the Kilo Swarm post (23 Sep 2026): on Terminal-Bench 4 `rs-archive-clone` with GPT-6 Astra, five trials per arm, cost fell from $41.14 to $25.00 (-39.2%, CI [-25.12, -6.35]) with 10/10 passes, wall-clock 2,375s to 1,138s and ~75% fewer main-agent reasoning tokens, while single-trial results across the broader suite are called inconclusive. Third-party numbers are editorial (standardcompute: quality 7.5, autonomy 7.0, ease of use 8.5).
dimensions.distinctive: Three genuinely distinctive ideas: (1) one engine, many clients: TUI, VS Code, JetBrains, Cloud and Agent Manager are all `@kilocode/sdk` clients of a `kilo serve` HTTP+SSE runtime that hosts directory-keyed instances (worktrees) in one process, so config, permissions and sessions are identical across surfaces; (2) a two-layer safety story, fine-grained allow/ask/deny rules plus an optional Seatbelt/Bubblewrap sandbox with `.git` read-only and network deny-by-default, that documents its own gaps (plugins and MCP run outside it); (3) a cache-aware context architecture (Context Epoch, System Context Registry) layered with per-project Memory, the Swarm shared board, CodeMode and benchmark-driven Auto Model routing. The loudest criticisms centre on the April 2026 v7 rebuild on OpenCode: issues #8108 and #8364 (29 combined reactions) describe lost settings and custom providers, a migration that only imported logged-in providers, removal of Architect/Orchestrator modes, an alleged silent reset to the public gateway, and users pinning 5.12 or moving to Roo (which itself shut down in May 2026). Other recurring complaints: compaction failing on small-context models (#9494), ~9k tokens of tool-description overhead per request (#10497), a foreground subagent freezing the TUI (#11708), "zero markup" messaging versus a 5% credit fee and token burn in multi-agent runs, no Windows sandbox, and roadmap uncertainty after the Anaconda deal. Structurally, Kilo carries a permanent merge burden: every Kilo edit to shared OpenCode files must be annotated with `kilocode_change` markers and CI enforces it.
