profiles.name: Pydantic AI Harness (pydantic/pydantic-ai-harness)
profiles.one_liner: Pydantic's MIT-licensed Python capability library that turns any Pydantic AI v2 agent into a coding/research harness by composing 50+ self-contained "capabilities" (FileSystem, Shell, Coder, SubAgents, Compaction, Memory, CodeMode...) via `Agent(capabilities=[...])` — a library you embed, not an application you run.

dimensions.identity: Maintained by Pydantic (Pydantic Services Inc.), the same org behind pydantic-ai (20.2k stars); the harness repo has 932 stars, 146 forks and 107 dependent repositories as of late September 2026. First PyPI release was 0.1.1 on 13 April 2026 (a DeepWiki snapshot from 11 Apr 2026 and forks named `pydantic-harness` suggest it launched under that name and was renamed); current release is 0.36.0 on 25 Sept 2026, with eight releases in September alone (0.28.1 → 0.36.0), and the README states it stays on 0.x versioning. License is MIT, implementation is Python 3.10–3.14, installed with `uv add "pydantic-ai-harness[coder]"` on top of `pydantic-ai-slim`, with 30+ extras (`[coder]`, `[researcher]`, `[codemode]`, `[acp]`, `[anthropic]`...). Distribution is primarily a library, plus a terminal entry point (`uvx --with "pydantic-ai-harness[coder]" clai -a pydantic_ai_harness.coder:coder_agent -m anthropic:claude-fable-5`), an in-repo TUI `pydantic-clai2` (`uv run --project pydantic-clai2 clai2`), and experimental ACP serving to editors like Zed. pypistats reports ~2.55M downloads in the last 30 days (121k/day), a figure likely inflated by CI and by pydantic-ai's own extras, so treat it as a rough signal.
dimensions.loop: The loop is inherited from Pydantic AI core: a single ReAct-style tool loop executed as a pydantic-graph state machine (UserPromptNode → ModelRequestNode → CallToolsNode → End), drivable node-by-node via `agent.iter()`; there is no separate planner/executor, but Planning, CodeMode and DynamicWorkflow layer plan-tracking and code-as-action on top. A turn ends when the model produces final output, governed by `end_strategy` whose default changed in v2.0.0 from `'early'` to `'graceful'` (tools still run but results are not fed back; `'exhaustive'` runs everything). Hard limits live in `UsageLimits(request_limit, tool_calls_limit, input_tokens_limit, output_tokens_limit, per_request_input_tokens_limit, cost_limit)` which raise `UsageLimitExceeded`; the harness adds soft steering via `WarnNearLimits(max_iterations, max_context_fraction, max_total_tokens)` that injects URGENT/CRITICAL tail warnings, and `SpendLimits(budgets=[Budget(usd=..., window='run'|'day'|'month', scope=...)])` which refuses to start requests once exhausted (`SpendLimitExceeded`). Recoverable tool errors surface as `ModelRetry` against a per-tool `retries` budget so the model self-corrects rather than aborting. The prebuilt `Coder('.')` composes FileSystem + Shell + RepoContext + SubAgents + ClearToolResults + WarnNearLimits + ToolOutputLimits + RepairToolArguments with a short instruction layer ("autonomous investigation and completion, focused changes and verification, pragmatic DRY/YAGNI/SOLID").
dimensions.tools: Tools are contributed by capabilities: a class subclassing `AbstractCapability` returns an `AbstractToolset`/`FunctionToolset` from `get_toolset()` (functions registered with `@toolset.tool` / `@tool_plain`), or the declarative `Capability` shorthand bundles tools plus `instructions`; capabilities can also be declared in YAML agent specs (`capabilities: - FileSystem: {root_dir: ./workspace}`) loaded with `Agent.from_spec(custom_capability_types=[...])`. The Coder harness exposes seven tools: `read_file(path, offset, limit)`, `write_file`, `edit_file(path, old_text, new_text)` or `edit_file(path, replacements=[...])` (each `old_text` must match exactly once, batch is checked in memory before writing), ripgrep-backed `list_files(path, glob)` and `grep`, `shell(command, mode='foreground'|background, timeout=270)`, and `delegate_task`; the raw FileSystem capability has eight default tools plus optional `list_files`/`grep`, Shell has `run_command`/`start_command`/`check_command`/`stop_command`, and other capabilities add `run_code`, `run_workflow`, `write_memory`/`search_memory`, `write_plan`/`update_task_status`, `ask_user_question`, `advisor`, `search_tools`. Result size is controlled at the source: FileSystem caps `max_read_lines=2000` (Coder sets `max_read_chars=60000`) and lists/searches at 1,000 entries, Shell keeps the tail of `max_output_chars=50_000`, and Coder caps any tool result at 64,000 characters. `ToolOutputLimits` applies size bands, default `Band(over=10_000, action=Spill(then=Truncate()))`: Truncate does head/tail/head+tail clamps, Spill writes the payload to a `LocalFileStore` (mode 0700) and hands the model a preview plus `read_tool_result(handle, offset, limit, from_end, pattern)`, Summarize spends one LLM call; the reduction is persisted once rather than recomputed per request, and `ModelRetry`/errors bypass it so the model always sees full error text. `ClearToolResults(keep_pairs=3)` later blanks old tool results while preserving call/return pairing.
dimensions.extensibility: Everything is one primitive: "a capability, a self-contained unit of agent behavior you add to `capabilities=[...]`" that can provide tools, lifecycle hooks, instructions, model settings and native tools; core Pydantic AI ships capabilities needing deep provider integration (Thinking, WebSearch, MCP, ToolSearch, Compaction base), the harness ships the rest. The repo's `agent_docs/core-boundary.md` codifies the seam: "If a feature is mostly a policy decision over existing hooks/toolsets/messages, build it in harness"; anything needing loop or provider changes goes to core first. A third party subclasses `AbstractCapability[DepsT]`, overrides `get_toolset()`/`get_instructions()`/`get_model_settings()` and decorated hooks (`@before_model_request`, `@wrap_tool_execute`...), sets a stable `id` (required when `defer_loading=True`, which collapses the capability to a one-line catalog entry until the model loads it), optionally `get_ordering()` → `CapabilityOrdering(position='outermost')` and `combine()` for duplicate-id merging, implements `get_serialization_name()`/`from_spec()` for YAML specs, publishes under the `pydantic-ai-<name>` prefix and opens a PR to the third-party page (eight are listed, e.g. `pydantic-ai-shields`, `pydantic-ai-backend`, `haiku.rag`). Also pluggable: models/providers (`Model`/`WrapperModel`), toolsets (`WrapperToolset`), agents (`WrapperAgent`), UI (CLI, web chat UI, frontend adapters, ACP), durable backends (Temporal, DBOS, Prefect, Restate, Kitaru, Airflow, AWS Lambda) and Protocol-based stores for Memory/Planning/Spend. `CapabilityCreation(directory=Path('.authored'))` even lets the agent write `<name>.py` + `manifest.json` capabilities at runtime, activated on the next run via `creation.store.load_active()`. Contribution policy: open a capability-request issue first, community upvotes gauge interest, and PRs touching `pyproject.toml`/`uv.lock` are auto-closed; `make testcov` enforces 100% branch coverage.
dimensions.context: Compaction is a menu of `Capability` classes that edit message history before requests and persist the edit into `message_history`: zero-LLM `ClampOversizedMessages`, `ClearToolResults(keep_pairs=3, min_clear_tokens=...)`, `DeduplicateFileReads(file_key=...)`, `SlidingWindowCompaction(keep_messages=40)`; LLM-based `SummarizingCompaction(incremental=True, keep_messages=20, tool_return_max_chars=500, bridge_prefix=True)`; and composites `TieredCompaction(tiers=[...], target_fraction=...)` (the recommended default) and `FallbackCompaction`, all triggered by window-relative `max_fraction` (falls back to `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW`=200K for unknown/local endpoints, ~4 chars/token heuristic unless a `tokenizer` is passed), with provider-native OpenAI/Anthropic compaction as an alternative and `pin(content)` marking state that no strategy may drop. Memory files: `RepoContext` loads `CLAUDE.md` then `AGENTS.md` from `workspace_dir` walking up to `home_dir`, inventories `.claude/.agents/.codex/.grok` assets, and injects once at run start as static instructions; `Skills('.agents/skills')` loads `SKILL.md` on demand through `load_capability`. Persistent memory is `Memory(FileStore('.agent-memory'))` (also `SqliteMemoryStore`, `PostgresMemoryStore`, per-tenant `namespace=lambda ctx: ctx.deps.user_id`) holding a Markdown `MEMORY.md` injected within `max_tokens=2000`/`max_lines=200` plus `write_memory`/`search_memory` tools, and `ConversationSearch` runs BM25 over stored history. KV/prompt-cache friendliness is a first-class constraint: Planning, `SystemReminders` and `WarnNearLimits` append ephemeral `UserPromptPart`s at the request tail behind a `CachePoint` and never persist them ("every reminder would bust the cached prefix"), compaction docs warn that every rewrite invalidates cache from the edit point and `min_clear_tokens` skips clears that would not pay for the cache-write, and `WarnOnCacheBusts(collapse_ratio=0.5, min_prefix_tokens=1024, cache_ttl_seconds=300)` emits a `CacheBustWarning` when `cache_read_tokens` collapses. `CodeMode`/`ToolSearch` keep intermediate results and unused tool schemas out of context altogether.
dimensions.permissions: There are no named permission modes; gating is per-capability configuration plus human-in-the-loop deferral. `FileSystem(root_dir='.')` is a workspace fence: relative paths resolve from `cwd`, anything escaping via `..`, absolute paths or symlinks is rejected (symlinks resolved with `os.path.realpath` before authorization), `protected_patterns` defaults to `.git/*`, `.env`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `**/secrets*` (read-only), with `allowed_patterns`/`denied_patterns` globs, `read_only=True`, hidden dotfiles, binary detection and `expected_hash` optimistic concurrency; write/edit/create emit a cancellable `FileChangeRequestEvent` so listeners can veto before disk I/O. `Shell` has `allowed_commands` (allowlist), `denied_commands` (default `rm, rmdir, mkfs, dd, format, shutdown, reboot, halt, poweroff, init`), `denied_operators`, `allow_interactive=False` (blocks `vi`/`sudo`/`ssh`), `default_timeout=30`, and `denied_env_patterns` with `LLM_API_KEY_ENV_PATTERNS` to strip provider credentials; a denied command returns a `ModelRetry`, and the docs are explicit that "`allowed_commands` is a guardrail against accidents, not a security boundary", recommending containers or `ModalSandbox(image='python:3.12-slim', sandbox_timeout=300, default_command_timeout=60.0)` for untrusted work. Notably the prebuilt `Coder` is permissive by design (`Shell(denied_commands=[], allow_interactive=True, default_timeout=270)`, "Commands are unrestricted and can outlive runs. Use an OS sandbox", optional `unrestricted_filesystem=True`), and `pydantic-clai2` ships `Coder(unrestricted_filesystem=True)`. Dangerous tools are gated with `requires_approval=True` or `raise ApprovalRequired`, which pauses the run returning `DeferredToolRequests`; the caller resumes with `DeferredToolResults(approvals={id: ToolApproved(override_args=...) | ToolDenied('...')})` and the prior `message_history`, and ACP surfaces the same flag to the editor. Layered on top: `ToolGuardrail(guard=..., result_guard=..., tools=['write_file'], hidden=['delete_all'])` returning `GuardrailResult.block/replace/retry/approve`, `PromptInjectionDefender(block_high_risk=True)` on tool results, and `SpendLimits` budgets per run/day/month/tenant.
dimensions.hooks: Lifecycle hooks come from Pydantic AI v2 core and follow a before/after/wrap/error pattern at every stage: `before_run`/`after_run`/`wrap_run`/`run_error`, `before_node_run`/`after_node_run`/`wrap_node_run`, `before_model_request`/`after_model_request`/`wrap_model_request`/`model_request_error`, `before_tool_validate`/`after_tool_validate`/`wrap_tool_validate`, `before_tool_execute`/`after_tool_execute`/`wrap_tool_execute`, output validate/process hooks, `prepare_tools`, `deferred_tool_calls`, `run_event_stream` and `event`. They are registered either as decorated methods on a capability (`@before_model_request`) or via the `Hooks(before_model_request=fn)` capability / `@hooks.on.before_model_request` decorator, with optional `tools=['name']` targeting and a `timeout` (raises `HookTimeoutError`); ordering is `before_*` in capability order, `after_*` reversed, `wrap_*` nested middleware with the first capability outermost. Hooks can veto: raise `SkipModelRequest(response)` to skip the model call, `SkipToolValidation(args)` or `SkipToolExecution(result)` to short-circuit a tool, `ApprovalRequired`/`CallDeferred` from `after_tool_validate` to pause for a human, `ModelRetry` to send a retry prompt, or `ToolFailed` to report failure without spending the retry budget; error hooks use "raise-to-propagate, return-to-recover" semantics. Capabilities additionally emit typed `CapabilityEvent`s (`FileChangeRequestEvent` is cancellable, `DelegationStartEvent`/`DelegationEndEvent`, `PlanUpdatedEvent`, `SpendRecordedEvent`, `ContextUsageEvent`) via `await ctx.emit()` and subscribe with `@on_event(EventClass)`. This is exactly how harness features like Guardrails, PromptInjectionDefender (`after_tool_execute`) and RepairToolArguments (`before_tool_validate`) are built.
dimensions.subagents: `SubAgents(agents=[SubAgent(researcher, usage_limits=UsageLimits(request_limit=35), timeout_seconds=600, max_calls=1)], max_depth=3, forward_usage=True, inherit_tools=False, shared_capabilities=(), include_self=False, agent_folders='agents', contain_errors=False, tool_retries=2)` exposes a single `delegate_task(agent_name, task)` tool; children can also be loaded from Markdown files in an `agents/` folder. A child receives the parent's `deps`, shared usage accounting (unless per-delegate limits isolate it), the parent's model unless a `models` menu overrides it, and any `shared_capabilities`, but not the parent's conversation history, run-level capabilities or the delegate tool itself (unless `include_self=True`); depth is capped at `max_depth=3` counting the top-level run, and runs at the limit are not offered the tool. The parent gets back `str(result.output)`, or a steering message on soft outcomes (timeout, budget exhaustion, contained crash), and `DelegationEndEvent` records outcome (`ok`/`timeout`/`budget`/`failed`/`contained`), usage and duration; unknown agent names raise `ModelRetry`. The Coder harness uses `SubAgents(include_self=True)` so `delegate_task` spawns "a fresh run of the same agent" inheriting model, workspace, instructions and capabilities including any approval gate or guardrail bound next to Coder, up to three levels deep. `DynamicWorkflow(agents=[...])` instead gives the model one `run_workflow` tool in which sub-agents are `async` functions it can `asyncio.gather`, chain or vote over in a Monty script, with a host-enforced `max_agent_calls=50`, `sub_agent_usage_limits`, 256 MB `resource_limits`, `workflow.reveal(agent)` mid-run, and a rule that sub-agents must not themselves carry DynamicWorkflow. Advisor and TrajectoryJudge are complementary second-model patterns (consult a stronger model; a judge that reviews the last `window=20_000` tokens every `every=10` requests and enqueues `Steer` messages).
dimensions.providers: Model agnosticism is Pydantic AI's core pitch ("swap the string for any provider's"): direct providers include `openai:`, `anthropic:`, `google:`, `xai:`, `bedrock:`, `groq:`, `mistral:`, `cohere:`, `huggingface:`, `openrouter:`, `cerebras:`, `crusoe:`, `github-copilot:`, `snowflake:`, `zai:`, though v2 slimmed default extras to OpenAI/Anthropic/Google with the rest opt-in. Local models go through OpenAI-compatible endpoints: `ollama:qwen3` via `OllamaProvider` (default `http://localhost:11434/v1`; self-hosted Ollama ≥0.5.0 enforces `json_schema` through llama.cpp's grammar-constrained decoder, Ollama Cloud silently ignores it), `vllm:` via `VLLMProvider(base_url=...)`/`VLLM_BASE_URL` (server needs `--enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser`), LiteLLM, Rapid-MLX, and any server via `OpenAIProvider(base_url=..., api_key=...)`; llama.cpp is not a named provider and is only reachable this way. The docs warn that a custom `base_url` does not change the `ModelProfile` (a `TypedDict` with `supports_tools`, `supports_json_schema_output`, etc.), so thinking or tool settings may be misapplied, and unknown/local endpoints fall back to a 200K context window for compaction unless `context_window=` is set. Weak-model support is a stated concern of many capabilities: `RepairToolArguments` fixes trailing commas, single-quoted keys and incomplete JSON before validation; most provider-native features have model-agnostic fallbacks (WebSearch → DuckDuckGo, ToolSearch → local `search_tools`, Compaction → local strategies, MCP → local FastMCP client, Advisor → local agent); `Advisor('anthropic:claude-opus-4-8', max_uses=1)` lets a cheaper executor consult a stronger model, and `TrajectoryJudge(model='anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5')` steers drifting runs. Native paths (server-side tool search, MCP connectors, compaction) are Anthropic/OpenAI/xAI-first, so local models get the fallback tier throughout.
dimensions.mcp: MCP client support is first-class in core and used by the harness: `MCP(url)` or `MCP(local=...)` is "the primary entry point", backed by `MCPToolset` which wraps the FastMCP client for stdio scripts, Streamable HTTP, SSE (URLs ending `/sse`), transport objects or in-process `FastMCP` servers, with `.prefixed('weather')` for name collisions, sampling via `agent.set_mcp_sampling_model()`, an `elicitation_handler`, and `defer_loading=True` so an MCP server's tools stay collapsed until searched. `native=True` (or an explicit `MCPServerTool(id, url, authorization_token, allowed_tools, headers)`) opts into provider-side connectors, supported only by OpenAI Responses, Anthropic and xAI and requiring a publicly reachable server; the default is local ("local by default, provider-native connectors opt-in"). The harness itself ships a growing set of hosted-MCP-backed capabilities (Ordinal, Grain, Day AI, PostHog, Pylon in 0.36.0; LogfireMCP, GitHub, Linear, Notion, Google Workspace, Slack in 0.35.0). ACP (Agent Client Protocol) is experimental under `pydantic_ai_harness.experimental.acp`: `run_acp_stdio_sync(agent)` serves the agent over stdio JSON-RPC to Zed-style clients (Zed `agent_servers` config), with `session_config` workspace rooting, `requires_approval` rendering, model menus, `InMemorySessionStore` and `session.mcp_servers` passthrough; the docs warn it "may still be removed, not just changed". A2A is no longer in-tree: FastA2A moved to `datalayer/fasta2a` after community feedback, `Agent.to_a2a()` was removed in v2 and replaced by `agent_to_a2a()`, and harness issue #128 requesting A2A support remains open. `Skills` reads the portable Agent Skills spec (`SKILL.md` frontmatter), accepting but not implementing `allowed-tools`/`hooks` fields.
dimensions.evals: Not documented. The repository has no benchmarks or evals directory (top level is `pydantic_ai_harness/`, `tests/`, `integration_tests/`, `docs/`, `examples/`, `agent_docs/`, `pydantic-clai2/`), the harness docs and README publish no SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench or other scores, and the Trajectory Judge page explicitly contains no effectiveness data. The closest quantitative claims are borrowed or anecdotal: the Code Mode article (8 Apr 2026) cites Anthropic's 150,000 → 2,000 token reduction and an internal Logfire triage example dropping from ~39K to ~1.5K tokens of intermediate JSON and six calls to one; the Dynamic Workflows post (28 Jul 2026) recounts Bun's Zig-to-Rust rewrite ("64 Claudes at a time at peak", eleven days, ~50 workflows, 100% of tests passing) without cost or success-rate metrics. Pydantic markets a separate Pydantic Evals product and Logfire eval workflows, but neither is applied publicly to the harness. Winder.ai's August 2026 comparison lists it as not in their fleet, and the arXiv convergence paper (2608.23953) on deepagents/pi/dsh does not include it. No harness-vs-model ablation exists.
dimensions.distinctive: Three ideas stand out. First, "capabilities all the way down": one primitive bundling tools, hooks, instructions and model settings, with a written core/harness boundary rule, a `combine()` policy for duplicate ids, 100% branch coverage and a `defer_loading` catalog so the harness scales to 50+ capabilities without prompt bloat; Coder itself is just FileSystem+Shell+RepoContext+SubAgents+context controls you can decompose. Second, prompt-cache discipline as an architectural constraint: reminders, plans and limit warnings ride the request tail behind a `CachePoint` and never enter history, compaction documents its cache-write cost, and `WarnOnCacheBusts` treats a collapsed `cache_read_tokens` as a bug signal. Third, code-as-action in a purpose-built sandbox (Monty) for both tools (`CodeMode` with speculative and eager execution) and agents (`DynamicWorkflow` with a hard `max_agent_calls`), paired with source-level context control (`ToolOutputLimits` spill handles, tiered compaction). Loudest criticisms: Winder.ai calls it "a library, not an application, and still on 0.x versioning" (eight minor releases in September 2026, a 3-month breaking-change window in core); MCP.Directory flags the Monty sandbox's no-PyPI restriction, the linear rather than graph-shaped loop versus LangGraph, and training-data lag causing coding models to emit the pre-v2 `Agent()` API; the docs themselves concede shell allowlists are "not a security boundary" while the prebuilt Coder and clai2 default to unrestricted shell/filesystem; native-first paths favour Anthropic/OpenAI/xAI with local models on the fallback tier; and there are no published benchmarks to back the harness thesis.

unknowns: evals: no benchmarks (SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench or otherwise) and no harness-vs-model ablations are published anywhere in the repo, docs or Pydantic articles

identity: the pypistats download figure (~2.55M/30 days) could not be cross-checked and may be inflated by CI or by pydantic-ai extras; the earlier `pydantic-harness` name is inferred from a DeepWiki snapshot and fork names, not from a primary source

providers: llama.cpp is not documented as a named provider (only reachable via generic OpenAI-compatible base_url or as Ollama's backend); no documented guidance on tuning for small/weak local models beyond RepairToolArguments and fallbacks
permissions: no named permission modes (plan / auto-accept / ask) exist; gating is only per-capability allow/deny plus requires_approval deferral
mcp: exposing a Pydantic AI agent as an MCP server is not documented in the harness docs (only asserted by a secondary source about core)
context: RepoContext documents no size limits for CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md files
distinctive: independent third-party criticism is thin; HN, Lobsters and dev.to searches returned nothing, and two Medium comparisons were inaccessible (403)

missing.name: Hermes Agent (Nous Research)
missing.why: The most-cited open harness of 2026 that is not on our list. NousResearch/hermes-agent (MIT, Python, launched 25 Feb 2026) sits at ~249k GitHub stars, the fastest-growing repo of the year, and it is one of the eleven systems dissected in the arXiv source-code study 'Harness Engineering: Anatomy, Architecture, and Evolution of Coding Agents' (2609.00006), characterised as a 'self-improving skill loop with lineage compaction'. Tencent Cloud's five-way (dsh vs Pi vs OpenCode vs Hermes vs Claude Code) and deepseekagent.io's five-way (dsh vs Codex vs Claude Code vs Hermes vs OpenCode) both put it in the same row as dsh. Honest caveat: it is a general-purpose personal agent (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp gateway, cron, 40+ tools) rather than a coding-first tool, and the press compares it anyway because it moved the goalposts on agent-curated memory, autonomous skill creation (agentskills.io standard), and pluggable terminal backends (local, Docker, SSH, Singularity, Modal, Daytona, Vercel Sandbox). For cornac it is the other Python open harness at the top tier, so it is the natural row for 'what does memory/skills look like when done at scale'. OpenClaw (~347k stars, also in the arXiv eleven, 'multi-channel gateway delegating coding via plugins') is the same class; if the matrix takes only one personal-agent-class row, Hermes is the one the harness press actually compares.

missing.name: GitHub Copilot CLI (GitHub/Microsoft)
missing.why: The most frequently head-to-headed closed vendor CLI after Claude Code and Codex, and absent from our list. GA on 25 Feb 2026 (github.blog changelog; InfoQ Apr 2026). It ships Plan mode, a fully autonomous Autopilot mode, parallel specialised sub-agents (Explore, Task, Code Review, Plan), repository memory across sessions, hooks, plugins, a built-in GitHub MCP server and BYOK, and since July 2026 runs Claude models itself. It appears in Tembo's 15-agent guide, arcbjorn's mid-2026 'platform tier' (with Junie CLI), openchamber's 36-tool survey, Faros' developer-review roundup, and Bustamante's 'Model-Harness Fit' essay, which analyses exactly three harnesses: Codex CLI, Claude Code, Copilot CLI. It is closed source (github/copilot-cli issue #3241 asks to open it; only the SDK is open), so it is the clearest example of the 'black-box loop, hidden system prompt' trade-off the press keeps raising, and a useful foil for cornac's transparency story. Related correction for an existing row: Gemini CLI stopped serving consumer/Pro/Ultra tiers on 18 June 2026 and Google's live product is now the closed-source Go rewrite Antigravity CLI (the Apache-2.0 repo remains; enterprise Code Assist licences keep access), so our Gemini CLI profile describes a retired product and Copilot CLI is now arguably the third big vendor CLI.
missing.hint: Product: github.com/github/copilot-cli (issues/releases; issue #3241 for open-source status). GA announcement: github.blog/changelog/2026-02-25-github-copilot-cli-is-now-generally-available; infoq.com/news/2026/04/github-copilot-cli-ga. Head-to-heads: devleader.ca 2026/07/31 Copilot CLI vs Claude Code; thepromptshelf.dev github-copilot-cli-vs-claude-code-cli-2026; nicolasbustamante.com/blog/model-harness-fit. Gemini CLI retirement: developers.googleblog.com 'transitioning Gemini CLI to Antigravity CLI'; theregister.com 2026/05/20.

missing.name: Kilo (Kilo Code extension + Kilo CLI, Kilo-Org/kilocode)
missing.why: Kilo is the maintained successor of two rows we already have: the extension is a fork of Roo Code (itself a Cline fork) and reads .roomodes/.roo/rules on startup, which matters because RooCodeInc/Roo-Code was archived on 15 May 2026; and Kilo CLI 1.0 (3 Feb 2026) is a fork of OpenCode running on the OpenCode server. MIT, ~27k stars, 3M+ users, ~10T tokens/month routed, and Anaconda acquired it on 15 July 2026, so it is the first open harness to be absorbed into an enterprise data-platform vendor. It appears in Tembo's 15, Pinggy's open-source CLI list, arcbjorn's mid-2026 survey, openchamber's 36, Faros ('emerging') and kilo.ai's own (self-promoting) comparison. Honest assessment: the engineering novelty is low; its value to our matrix is as the reference for what 'platformising' an open harness looks like: Kilo Gateway (500+ models, zero markup, BYOK), Agent Manager with git-worktree isolation for parallel agents, sandboxed auto mode (workspace-only writes, read-only git protection, network deny), MCP marketplace, VS Code + JetBrains + CLI + cloud agents + Slack. It is also the answer to 'where did Roo's users go'.
missing.hint: Repo: github.com/Kilo-Org/kilocode. CLI origin statement: kilo.ai/cli ('built on OpenCode') and kilo.ai/docs/code-with-ai/platforms/cli. Third-party comparison with columns: morphllm.com/comparisons/opencode-vs-kilo-code (209k vs 27k stars, both MIT).

missing.name: Pydantic AI Harness (pydantic/pydantic-ai-harness)
missing.why: The closest thing in the industry to cornac's own category: a Python, provider-agnostic, library-first harness rather than a CLI product. Winder.ai counts it among its nine harnesses of 2026 ('best for adding harness behaviour to a Python service you are already writing'; main weakness 'a library, not an application, and still on 0.x versioning'; not in Winder's fleet). Shipped alongside Pydantic AI v2 (23 Jun 2026), MIT, releasing weekly (v0.31.0 on 11 Sep 2026). It packages 50+ composable capabilities: Coder and Researcher harness stacks, FileSystem/Shell/Modal Sandbox execution environments, Planning/SubAgents/Dynamic Workflow, Code Mode/Tool Output Limits/Compaction for context, Memory (file or Postgres), Skills, Guardrails, Prompt Injection Defender, Spend Limits, Tool Approval, Durable execution, Step Persistence, Instrumentation. That list is essentially cornac's feature surface (permissions, hooks, sandbox, sub-agents) done by a well-funded peer, so it is the row where cornac's 'mid-tier scope' claim gets tested honestly, and its README is a ready-made checklist of what a Python harness library is expected to have in 2026. Alternate if the parent wants a Python library competitor with published benchmark numbers instead: LangChain deepagents / 'Deep Agents Code' (MIT, Python, Terminal-Bench rank #26 at 66.5% on Terminal Trove), which arXiv 2608.23953 treats as a full harness alongside Pi and dsh.

wrong_claims.claim: "the Minimal preset exposes only `bash` and `str_replace_editor`" (tools dimension) and "presets like Minimal (two tools)" (distinctive dimension)
wrong_claims.correction: Both the Web `minimal` agent preset and the `sdk-minimal` profile mount exactly ONE tool: a persistent shell (`bash` via dsh-tool-bash-persistent on Linux/macOS, `pwsh` on Windows), plus a complete persona 'You are a helpful software engineer assistant.' with runtime context off. No editor tool of any kind is mounted. `str_replace_editor` is not even in dsh-base by default: 'Default file editing uses read, write, and edit. The str_replace_editor tool remains available as an explicit opt-in.' The sdk-minimal README states: 'the only advertised tool is owner-scoped persistent bash on Linux/macOS or pwsh on Windows; runtime context, filesystem tools, workspace instructions, skills, jobs controls, compaction, and Harness identity are absent.' This also matters for the evals dimension: V4 'minimal mode' scores were produced with a single shell tool.

wrong_claims.claim: "Because the loop is itself a plugin it can be replaced outright. Shipped alternatives: Code Mode / PTC ..., a `ralph` tool ..., a `workflow` tool ..., and `/plan` plan mode"
wrong_claims.correction: The repo ships exactly one loop implementation and none of the four items is an alternative loop. agent-loop README: 'The package is the one concrete implementation of the public Agent contract'; docs/subsystems/core.md repeats this. PTC/Code Mode is a tool PRESENTATION mode on the dsh-tools row (`mode: native | ptc | both`) or per-preset via dsh-agent-tool-presentation; `run_code` sub-calls 're-enter the complete guarded tool pipeline', and docs/subsystems/ptc-runtime.md says 'PTC execution is optional rather than part of the agent-loop spine'. `ralph` and `workflow` are ordinary tools registered on ctx.tools that drive ctx.workflowEngine/ctx.subagents; plan mode is `ctx.planMode` collaboration state. All of them execute inside the same ReactLoopAgent driver. The loop is swappable in principle (AgentFactory via ctx.agents.setFactory; 'Choose a custom Agent implementation only when the standard lifecycle is insufficient'), but no alternative ships.
wrong_claims.source: packages/core/agent-loop/README.md (Design concept); docs/subsystems/core.md line ~20; packages/core/tools/README.md (Configure the presentation mode, PTC mode); docs/subsystems/ptc-runtime.md; docs/tool-catalog.md rows for ralph/workflow; packages/workflow/README.md; packages/plan/README.md

wrong_claims.claim: The package README says there are no inherent step limits and "budgeting requires external policy enforcement"
wrong_claims.correction: The quoted phrase does not appear anywhere in the README. The actual text (Known Limitations) is: 'No built-in turn budget — tool calls or steering continue the current turn; a policy that bounds runaway turns must cancel from an existing lifecycle extension point such as agent/turn-stopping.' The substance is correct; the quotation is fabricated and should be replaced with the real wording.

wrong_claims.claim: "Exit-code semantics for shell hooks are not documented" (hooks dimension and unknowns list)
wrong_claims.correction: They are documented in the shared hook-protocol library README: 'a hook that exits with code 2 stops the prompt or tool call, and its error output is shown as the reason' and 'any exit code other than 2 is a non-blocking failure: the action proceeds and the failure is logged, and a hook that cannot be started at all is treated the same way.' JSON stdout is also decoded (`additionalContext` consumed; `updatedInput` parsed but not honored; `{"continue": false}` recorded but has no run-level effect). Remove this from the unknowns.
wrong_claims.source: packages/hooks/hook-protocol/README.md (What a hook can do; Known Limitations)

wrong_claims.claim: A turn ends "on model/tool dispatch failure, or when the serial `agent/turn-stopping` extension point ends it"
wrong_claims.correction: Two inaccuracies. (1) Tool failures do NOT end a turn: unknown tools, throwing tools, denials and timeouts become structured errors (`UNKNOWN_TOOL`, `TOOL_TIMEOUT`, `ABORTED_BEFORE_DISPATCH`) 'so a call fails without ending the turn'; what closes a turn is extension/plugin failure ('Middleware, result-processing, tool, and other extension failures remain thrown and close the turn directly — plugin failure ends the turn, not the loop'), and a model dispatch failure is terminal only if no `agent/request-error` listener returns `{ kind: 'retry' }`. (2) `agent/turn-stopping` does not end the turn; it fires when 'the model owes no response (no live tool calls, no fresh steering)' and is the point where a listener can PREVENT closure by calling `agent.steer(...)` ('fresh steering runs another step, none closes the turn'). Turn closure can also be forced from inside a step by a tool result carrying `concludesTurn`.
wrong_claims.source: packages/core/agent-loop/README.md (Failure and cancellation); packages/core/tools/README.md (Execution and cancellation); docs/subsystems/core.md (`agent/turn-stopping` — serial)

wrong_claims.claim: Hooks "can block prompts or tool calls with model-visible messages" (stated as applying to prompts too)
wrong_claims.correction: For prompts the block is silent to the model: 'a blocked prompt is discarded with no model-visible message, ending the turn as `blocked`'. Model-visible text applies only to tool denials (`Error: blocked by PreToolUse hook`), PostToolUse feedback (`blocked by PostToolUse hook`) and Stop steering (`continue: blocked by Stop hook`). The group README's summary sentence is looser than the bridge README's Model Experience section.
wrong_claims.source: packages/hooks/hooks-claude-code/README.md (Model Experience: Blocked prompt or tool outcome) vs packages/hooks/README.md

wrong_claims.claim: "docs/architecture.md lists the pluggable seams: ... `ctx.agentPresets` and personas, system-prompt sections, skills, and the Web UI itself"
wrong_claims.correction: architecture.md does not mention `ctx.agentPresets`, personas or skills. Its core-packages table lists ctx.sessions, ctx.systemPrompt, ctx.tools, ctx.agents, ctx.agentLoop, ctx.llm and ctx.webhookRuntime, and its 'Where new behavior goes' table adds ctx.shell, ctx.terminals, ctx.commands, ctx.jobs, ctx.fs, ctx.sandbox, ctx.sessionTitle, ctx.goals, ctx.agentTeams and the SessionPersistence interface; it references presets only as 'compose an agent preset'. `ctx.agentPresets` comes from packages/preset/README.md. Attribution should be corrected.
wrong_claims.source: docs/architecture.md (Core packages; Where new behavior goes); packages/preset/README.md

wrong_claims.claim: A third party "publishes an npm package named `dsh-<name>`"
wrong_claims.correction: No naming requirement is documented. `dsh-hello-plugin` is simply the tutorial's example package name; the only documented discoverability convention is adding the `dsh-plugin` GitHub topic. What IS required is the `"dsh": { "bundle": { "patch": "./cordis.patch.yml" } }` manifest (a package without it installs as a plain dependency and 'activates no layer').

wrong_claims.claim: "Four shipped agent presets (Standard, Code/PTC, Minimal, Creator ...) are themselves plugin bundles"
wrong_claims.correction: The shipped preset ids are `standard`, `ptc`, `minimal`, `cordis` ('One @deepseek-ai/dsh-agent-preset declaration per shipped preset (standard, ptc, minimal, cordis)'). 'Creator' is the UI name used for `cordis`; I found no 'Code' label in the repo. They are not separate npm bundles: each is a `@deepseek-ai/dsh-agent-preset` declaration row (a declarative list of child plugins) shipped as a patch file inside the single dsh-web-app bundle (`presets/<id>.patch.yml`), selected per session by the registry (default `standard`). The Creator/cordis claim is otherwise right: it adds the `tool-cordis` row (cordis_inspect_list/query) plus preset-authoring skills; the `ptc` preset differs from `standard` only by an `agent-tool-presentation` row with `mode: ptc`.

wrong_claims.correction: The GitHub contents listing of packages/ shows 54 top-level directories (acp, api, attachment, boot, browser-use, bundle, client, compaction, computer-use, context, core, credentials, deliverables, document, experimental, extensions, feedback, fs, goal, guard, hooks, host, identity, interaction, jobs, llm, lsp, mcp, plan, preset, ptc-runtime, runtime-diagnostics, sandbox, schedule, sdk, session-query, session, settings, shell, skill, spill, ssh, storage, subagent, subprocess, terminal, test-support, todo, typert, util, web, webhook, workflow, workspace). confirmed_key_facts: Plugin model: README calls it an 'everything-is-a-plugin' architecture on Cordis (arXiv 2608.25512); architecture.md: 'Every part of the product is a plugin, including the model adapter, the tool registry, the session log, and the agent loop itself, so each is replaceable from configuration' and 'There is no privileged core to patch ... registrations are effects that unwind when their plugin unloads'.

A plugin exports `name`, optional `inject` (e.g. ['tools']), `apply(ctx, config)` and a same-named Schemastery `Config` schema; 'The schema runs while the plugin loads. Invalid configuration fails the load with an actionable error.' Anything registered through ctx is cleaned up on unload; `ctx.effect()` supplies explicit disposers. Function, object and class (Service) forms exist. (docs/user/develop/basic/index.md, config.md)

Composition layering order verified in three places (architecture.md, apps/cli/README.md, publish.md): each bundle patch in `dsh.profile.bundles` order -> the profile's cordis.patch.yml -> `$DSH_HOME/cordis.patch.yml` -> each `--patch` overlay in argv order; a patch replaces a row's WHOLE config (no deep merge). Inspect with `--dump-config`, `--dump-default-config`, `--dump-config-schema`. Local dev: `pnpm dsh web --patch ./x/cordis.yml` with an `insert:` row pointing at an absolute .ts path.

Shipped profiles: web, headless, sdk, sdk-minimal, acp; bundles: dsh-base, dsh-web-app, dsh-headless, dsh-sdk-app, dsh-acp-app, dsh-sdk-minimal. sdk-minimal 'is the deliberate exception: one bundle owns its complete explicit SDK tree and does not apply dsh-base'. Install third-party bundles with `dsh plugin --profile <name> add <pkg | github:user/repo#sha | ./x.tgz>`; git installs need a `prepare` script and an `allowBuilds` entry.

Loop: the driver class is `ReactLoopAgent` ('call model, run tools, repeat'); 'A step is one model request plus the tools it calls. A turn is zero or more steps.' Verbatim flow: turn/start -> claim input -> assemble prompt+tools -> agent/pre-step -> step/start -> agent/request -> prepareCall -> llm/stream -> agent/assistant-stream -> assistant/message|attempt -> tool/call* -> tools/pre-execute -> tools/execute -> tools/post-execute -> tool/result* -> step/end -> (loop) -> agent/turn-stopping -> turn/end. `agent/pre-step`, `agent/request`, `llm/stream` and the three `tools/*` events are waterfalls that must call next(); `agent/turn-stopping` is serial with no next(). turn/*, step/*, system/message, user/message, assistant/message, assistant/attempt and tool/* are durable session events.

`maxParallelToolCalls` defaults to 10 (src/constants.ts: `DEFAULT_MAX_PARALLEL_TOOL_CALLS = 10`; '1 is serial'); exclusive calls 'run alone as ordering barriers'; 'Retries reuse the same rendered assembly without repeating assembly, agent/pre-step, or user admission'; cancellation is cooperative and 'a cancelled stream finalizes the text already delivered to the user'; 'No built-in turn budget'.

Loop swappability mechanism: `dsh-agent` owns the public `Agent` contract and `ctx.agents`; `dsh-agent-loop` registers itself as the `AgentFactory` via `ctx.agents.setFactory()`, and 'extension plugins depend on agent ... and never on agent-loop directly, so the loop stays swappable'. Only this one driver ships.

'Model-visible means logged. A runtime invariant checks model requests are reconstructable from the log.' `deriveMessages()` projects model history from the append-only session log; fork/resume/replay derive from it.

Tools: `ctx.tools.register(defineTool({ name, description, parameters, output: { schema, render }, execute }))`; DSL types string/number/integer/boolean/null/array/object/author-only json/exact-one oneOf; raw JSON Schema 'is the wire-level counterpart shared with subagents, workflows, and MCP'; 'Registering a tool is enough to make it visible'.

Tool pipeline verbatim: 'tools/pre-execute (extensible allow/deny/ask) -> registered monotonic guards -> tools/execute (around-dispatch wrappers) -> tools/post-execute (inspect/replace, attach context) -> definition-owned finalizeContent -> the observe-only tools/result event'. `ctx.tools.guard()` is monotonic: 'a returned reason denies the call, and no later listener can turn that denial back into permission'. `ctx.tools.restrict(filter)` applies allow/deny masks per agent; 'masks intersect'. An `ask` proceeds only on `allowed-once`; a missing approval channel turns ask into deny.

Tool failures do not end the turn: invalid input is 'a normal error result'; `UNKNOWN_TOOL`, `TOOL_TIMEOUT`, `ABORTED_BEFORE_DISPATCH`, `ABORTED` are structured errors. Known limits: 'tools/pre-execute deliberately cannot rewrite exec.arguments'; 'timeoutMs on a definition is declarative only ... enforcement requires the @deepseek-ai/dsh-tool-call-timeout-policy wrapper' (which dsh-base mounts).

PTC/Code Mode: dsh-tools `mode: native | ptc | both` (default native), `maxParallelSubCalls` 10; per-preset override via dsh-agent-tool-presentation. `run_code` runs in 'a fresh Node process under the configured sandbox policy'; 'Each run starts without state from earlier programs'; the child 'replaces the program-visible process.env with an empty dictionary'; Node default timeout 120,000 ms, cap 600,000 ms; `maxOutputBytes` default 67,108,864 (the 'worker hard cap'), V8 heap 512 MiB; 'only the outer run_code output has the worker's configurable hard cap' while intermediate values are 'unbounded by bytes'.

Tool catalog (docs/tool-catalog.md) confirmed: bash/pwsh (fresh + persistent packages), str_replace_editor, read/write/edit/read_image, glob/grep (grep uses the packaged @vscode/ripgrep), web_search/web_fetch, subagent/list_subagent_models, send_message/interrupt_agent/list_agents, skill, todo_write, exit_plan_mode, ask_user_question, run_code, cordis_inspect_list/query, six terminal_* tools, job_kill/list/output, create/get/update_goal, schedule_create/delete/list/update, lsp, ralph, workflow, present, plugin_manager, three MCP resource tools, five session_* tools, six stagehand_* tools. Omitted by the profile: `load_workspace_dependencies` and the experimental agent-team tools spawn_teammate, team_task_create/get/list/update, wait_agent (plus team-scoped send_message/interrupt_agent/list_agents).

Presets: the Web presets are `@deepseek-ai/dsh-agent-preset` rows ('Define an Agent's child plugins in ordinary Cordis YAML. Declare several presets and let sessions select one'); the registry (`ctx.agentPresets`) defaults to `standard`; 'The Host shares the Agent loop; each Agent sees the tools, prompts and skills of its selected revision.' Presets 'are not security sandboxes: YAML and plugins can execute Host code.'

Plan mode: '/plan enters and leaves it'; 'Plan mode guides rather than restricts: every tool stays available, and limits such as sandbox mode and approval prompts are configured separately'; `exit_plan_mode` 'presents the finished plan for your review'. dsh-base's plan-mode guidance says 'The tool catalog stays the same across modes for request-cache stability'.
Guards: `repeat-tool-reminder` ('Reminds the model when it repeats the same tool call') and `timeout-policy` ('Times out tool calls that declare a limit'); 'Both ship enabled in the dsh base bundle'.

Hooks group: `hook-protocol` (shared engine), `hooks-claude-code`, `hooks-codex`. Claude Code bridge supports exactly 7 events (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, SubagentStart, SubagentStop) and lists 23 unsupported 'of Claude Code's current 30' (PermissionRequest, SessionEnd, PreCompact, etc.). Capability table verbatim: PreToolUse 'block the tool, or ask for approval before it runs'; PostToolUse 'block the result with feedback, or attach extra context'; Stop 'force another step with a reason'; SubagentStart 'attach context to a still-running subagent (in-process only)'; SubagentStop 'observe only'. Codex bridge supports 5 of Codex's 10 events and cannot `ask`.

Hook bridge mapping and limits: UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse map to the `agent/pre-step`/`tools/pre-execute` waterfalls, PostToolUse to `tools/post-execute`, Stop to `agent/turn-stopping` via `steer()`. PreToolUse `allow` does not pre-approve and `updatedInput` is not honored; Stop has no consecutive-block cap ('An unconditionally blocking hook therefore force-continues every step unless it self-limits'); SessionStart runs detached and 'context can miss the first request'; hooks run serially in config order; only shell `command` handlers run; one `configPath` read once at startup; default timeout 600,000 ms; `transcript_path` is always ''.

Subagents: backends spawn, fork, acp, codex, claude-code, dsh-sdk confirmed (packages/subagent/README.md). dsh-base mounts spawn + fork and exposes them as `subagent` and `subagent_fork` tools; Codex/Claude Code providers are 'optional provider bundles you can install on top'. Tool fields: `task`, `run_in_background` (enableRunInBackground default true; backgroundMode default `one-shot`), optional provider/model/reasoning_effort only when `modelSelectionSettings: true` (default false), which also registers `list_subagent_models`. 'Shipped fork tools cannot select a child LLM route'; ACP, Codex and Claude Code 'reject agentOptions'.

Fork semantics: 'The seed ends at the parent's last completed turn ... that in-flight turn is never included'; the seed is 'a balanced completed-turn prefix of the parent's log — the parent's events up to and including its last turn/end', captured once; 'The seed carries conversation history only: the child still gets a fresh tool scope and none of the parent's authority.' Spawn children start 'with an empty conversation' but inherit cwd, lineage, provider, model, reasoning effort and output-token limit unless `agentOptions` overrides.

Depth: `maxDepth` defaults to the Host setting `subagent.maxDepth`, 'initially 1'; `0` forbids delegation; `'provider-managed'` sends no cap to out-of-process providers; depth is durable in `SessionHeader.delegationDepth` and cold resume cannot lower it. Per-child `toolFilter`, `persona` and `agentOptions` require the matching provider capability. Budgets: only a per-request `agentOptions.maxTokens` output cap and a `'max-tokens'` stop reason exist for plain subagents; `ralph` has `maxRounds` (default 256; 64 in the cordis preset) and the workflow engine a `maxTotalAgents` backstop; no total token or concurrency budget for subagents is documented.

Subagent return values verbatim: foreground 'Success contains only the child's final text; other outcomes become Error: <stop reason>, followed by a safe provider diagnostic when present and then any partial assistant text'; background returns exactly 'started background subagent job <id>' (one-shot; collected with job_output, stopped with job_kill) or 'started subagent <childId>' (continuable; follow-ups via send_message).

Agent Teams: `ctx.agentTeams` is a 'published opt-in coordination seam' shipped as the separate experimental bundle `@deepseek-ai/dsh-experimental-agent-team-profile`, which 'ships with dsh switched off' and is enabled from the Plugins page or `dsh plugin add`; enabling it disables the ordinary `subagent`/`subagent_fork` tools; requires durable session storage; limits maxMembers 16, maxTasks 256, maxPendingMessagesPerMember 64, maxMessageBytes 65,536; tasks are compare-and-set with `revision` and an acyclic `blockedBy` DAG; 'Messages are never lost and never delivered twice'.

`ralph` and `workflow`: `ralph` is mounted in dsh-base but its description says 'Use only when the direct human explicitly asks for Ralph or fresh-agent iteration'; each round 'opens a new child with no parent conversation or prior child session'. `workflow` runs 'a JavaScript workflow script that orchestrates subagents at scale' on the shared sandboxed PTC Node runtime.

Commentator claims the repo itself confirms: CONTRIBUTING.md says 'We are sorry that we cannot accept external pull requests at the moment'; GitHub API reports has_issues=false and has_discussions=true (feedback via Discussions, `dsh-plugin` topic for plugins, Discord). MIT license; README: 'THERE WILL BE COMPATIBILITY-BREAKING CHANGES'; `npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web` on http://127.0.0.1:3080. wrong_claims.claim: "built on DeepSeek's own Cordis plugin kernel (@deepseek-ai/cordis, arXiv 2608.25512)"
wrong_claims.correction: Cordis is a pre-existing third-party framework, not a DeepSeek creation. The upstream `cordis` npm package (author Shigma) dates from 2022-04-21 and the GitHub repo cordiverse/cordis was created 2022-05-17. DeepSeek source-vendors it under vendor/cordis and re-scopes it to `@deepseek-ai/cordis` (vendor/README.md: copied "so that the harness fully owns its framework layer"; manifest lists upstream cordis 4.0.0-rc.7 from cordiverse/cordis). The arXiv paper (submitted 2026-08-26) lists Yifan Shi (PKU/DeepSeek-AI), Wei Zhang (PKU), Tianyi Cui (DeepSeek-AI), so DeepSeek is involved in the paper and the upstream repo now points its homepage at the harness docs, but the kernel predates the harness by four years. Say "vendored Cordis kernel" rather than "DeepSeek's own".

wrong_claims.correction: packages/ holds 54 group directories (60 entries minus AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, README*.md, tsdown.worker.ts). The git tree today has 312 package.json files under packages/*/*, plus 4 under apps/ and 9 under vendor/.

cornac_has_that_most_lack: A fail-closed hook gate: a pre_tool_use callback that crashes counts as a veto (HOOK_FAILED). Cursor, Goose and Copilot default to fail-open on hook errors or timeouts; only OpenHands/Claude Code treat exit 2 as block, and none document crash-as-veto.

Headless safety by construction: ASK with no approver becomes DENY, and a tool runs only on an explicit Decision.ALLOW. Goose (auto default), OpenHands (NeverConfirm), OpenCode (allow-by-default), Cline CLI (--auto-approve true), Amp and Pi (no approval at all) default the other way.

Asymmetric allow/deny matching that bails on any shell metacharacter or extra argument, derived from real bypasses found in testing. Only Claude Code (subcommand splitting), OpenCode (tree-sitter), Codex (Starlark execpolicy) and Roo (prefix lists with substitution guard) do syntax-aware command gating; most use no patterns.

Sub-agents that cannot escalate: children share the parent's Policy, approver and veto objects by reference, one child budget spans the whole tree, and child tokens roll up into RunResult. Most harnesses give children their own permission mode or only forward deny rules (OpenCode, Kilo); dsh and Codex give children fresh tool scopes.

A compile()-before-write syntax gate for Python plus a 'REMOVED top-level: def X' change report on write_file. No profiled harness documents a pre-write syntax check; the closest are OpenCode/Kilo feeding LSP diagnostics back after the edit and SWE-agent's linter-gated windowed edits.

An honest end state: RunResult.text is None with stop_reason='max_steps' rather than a fabricated answer. OpenCode and Kilo inject a 'MAXIMUM STEPS REACHED, summarise' prompt; Codex, Pi, Crush, Copilot and dsh have no step cap at all.

A published harness-only ablation on a frozen weak local model: same tasks, seeds and prompts, only the harness changed, 12/27 to 26/27, with per-feature attribution and a record of what did not work. Only Qwen Code (harness-version ablation), Cline's harness-vs-harness repo, Hermes toolperf and Copilot's A/B posts publish anything similar, none on a 4B local model.

Unforgeable harness voice: any '[cornac]' inside tool output is rewritten to '[cornac?]' and the 'Sub-agent reply:' header cannot be spoofed by a child. No other profile documents marker neutralisation; dsh's <compacted-summary> framing and Hermes's [BLOCKED] rewriting are the nearest ideas.

Small enough to read end to end: ~4k lines and 440 tests, versus ~1M TypeScript lines for dsh and ~1M Python lines for Hermes. Only mini-swe-agent (~100-line loop) is in the same weight class, and it deliberately has no permissions, hooks or sub-agents.

cornac_lacks_that_most_have.gap: Prompt caching on the Anthropic provider
cornac_lacks_that_most_have.who_has_it: Claude Code, dsh, OpenCode, Aider, Goose, Hermes, Pydantic, OpenHands all set cache breakpoints; Codex uses server-side compaction
cornac_lacks_that_most_have.why: Week 5 spends real credit on the two Haiku rows; the system prompt and tool schemas are identical across the 15 tasks and the append-only design already keeps the prefix stable. Marking the system block and tool list as cacheable is a small change that makes the design rule pay for itself.

cornac_lacks_that_most_have.gap: MCP client (mount an MCP server's tools into the registry)
cornac_lacks_that_most_have.who_has_it: 13 of 15; only Aider and SWE-agent lack it; Claude Code, Codex and Hermes are also MCP servers
cornac_lacks_that_most_have.why: Already the first v2 item and the Tool ABC is deliberately MCP-shaped, so the adapter is mostly a stdio transport plus schema mapping. It is not needed to prove the thesis, and adding it before the benchmark risks the tool catalog growing past what a 4B model handles.

cornac_lacks_that_most_have.gap: OS-level sandbox (bubblewrap/Landlock/Seatbelt or a container) for run_bash and run_python
cornac_lacks_that_most_have.who_has_it: dsh (read-only default), Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Qwen, Cursor, Copilot, Kilo have OS sandboxes; Hermes, OpenHands, SWE-agent, Aider offer Docker backends
cornac_lacks_that_most_have.why: A correct bwrap/Landlock backend with fail-closed semantics is dsh's whole sandbox package group; it is not a learning-project deliverable. Say plainly that Workspace is a path fence, not a boundary (Claude Code's docs say the same about permission rules), and ship a Docker recipe in docs so the honest answer to 'where does containment belong' is 'outside cornac'.

cornac_lacks_that_most_have.gap: Hook input rewriting and context injection (updatedInput, additionalContext)
cornac_lacks_that_most_have.who_has_it: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Crush, Kilo, OpenCode, Hermes, Pydantic let hooks modify arguments or add context; Copilot modifiedArgs
cornac_lacks_that_most_have.why: Veto-only keeps the fail-closed story simple and testable; a hook that can rewrite a command reopens the allow/deny asymmetry you closed. Add it when a concrete use (redacting secrets from tool output) demands it.

cornac_lacks_that_most_have.gap: Parallel tool calls and background or parallel sub-agents
cornac_lacks_that_most_have.who_has_it: 12 of 15: dsh 10 parallel, Claude Code read-only concurrency, Codex 64 PTYs, OpenCode uncapped, OpenHands tool_concurrency_limit, Hermes ThreadPoolExecutor, Copilot /fleet
cornac_lacks_that_most_have.why: On one 6 GB GPU serving one 4B model, parallel calls queue at Ollama anyway, so the benchmark gains nothing and the sequential trace stays readable for the stepper pages. Revisit when a hosted model is the primary target.

cornac_lacks_that_most_have.who_has_it: 13 of 15; Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Qwen, Kimi, Copilot, Kilo, OpenHands, Goose, Hermes, Cline, Pydantic, dsh
cornac_lacks_that_most_have.why: An ecosystem surface needs users; cornac has none yet and the profiles show plugin ecosystems as a liability early on (dshbase found install failures in a third of dsh plugins). SKILL.md loading could ride on the AGENTS.md loader later if ever needed.

cornac_lacks_that_most_have.who_has_it: 10 of 15: Claude Code auto memory, Codex memories, Hermes MEMORY.md/USER.md, Goose Memory extension, Kilo Memory, Copilot Memory, Pydantic Memory, OpenHands, Gemini, Qwen
cornac_lacks_that_most_have.why: For a coding harness measured on isolated tasks memory is out of scope, and Winder credits Claude Code with being 'thin on durable memory by design'. State it as a non-goal in the architecture note rather than leaving readers to assume it was forgotten.

cornac_lacks_that_most_have.who_has_it: 14 of 15 stream tokens; only mini-swe-agent's batch runner does not care
cornac_lacks_that_most_have.why: There is no UI to stream into, RunResult is the product, and the Provider ABC's single complete() method is part of what makes the loop teachable. Add only if the CLI grows an interactive mode people actually use.

deepseek_vs_cornac: DeepSeek Harness's central idea is 'everything is a plugin' on a vendored Cordis kernel (a 2022 third-party framework DeepSeek re-scoped, not its own creation), where the model adapter, tools, sandbox, storage and even the agent loop are replaceable rows in YAML; cornac should consciously reject this for v1, because the price is 312 packages and roughly a million lines of TypeScript, and a teaching harness earns its value from a loop you can read in one sitting.

Worth learning: dsh's invariant 'model-visible means logged', where the append-only session log is the source of truth and the context sent to the model is derived from it, so fork, resume and keyless deterministic replay come for free; cornac already follows the append-only rule but never writes the log down, and a JSONL transcript per run is the cheapest way to borrow the idea.

Worth learning and naming: dsh treats fail-closed as vocabulary (SandboxUnavailableError, the 'unavailable' approval outcome, monotonic guards where 'no later listener can turn that denial back into permission'); cornac's HOOK_FAILED veto, ASK-to-DENY and ALLOW-only execution are the same instinct, so the architecture note should state the invariant in one sentence instead of leaving readers to infer it from tests.

A convergence worth pointing out: in dsh a tool failure never ends the turn (UNKNOWN_TOOL, TOOL_TIMEOUT and denials come back as structured errors), and cornac's registry.execute never raises either; the difference is that dsh has no turn budget at all ('No built-in turn budget'), while cornac's max_steps with an honest stop_reason is the better choice for a harness whose job is to show a weak model failing rather than looping forever.

Be careful how you cite dsh's benchmarks: DeepSeek's V4 code-agent scores were produced in 'minimal mode', which today mounts exactly one persistent shell tool and no editor, so the 'harness' behind those numbers is close to nothing; that is a useful reminder that cornac's ablation must always name its exact tool set, prompt and preset, and it is also an argument for a bash-only rung in the capability ladder.

Do not try to match dsh's sandbox: it confines file effects with bwrap, Landlock, Seatbelt or Windows ACLs, defaults to read-only, and refuses to run unconfined, but even dsh says network and process visibility are 'outside this vocabulary' and DataCamp watched it fail on Windows; cornac's Workspace path fence is a weaker analogue and should be described as such, with containment delegated to Docker.

dsh's presets (standard, ptc, minimal, cordis) are the same idea as cornac's planned stage_0 to stage_5 scripts expressed as plugin trees, and the fact that the minimal preset outscores the standard one on DeepSeek's own model card is exactly the kind of same-model-different-harness result cornac's ladder is designed to make visible, so build the ladder before adding features.

Finally, dsh's loudest criticisms (developer-preview churn, no security audit, PRs not accepted, a plugin ecosystem where a third of listed plugins failed to install, and roughly 95k input tokens per task) are all consequences of scale; cornac's honest position is the opposite end of that trade, and the README should say so rather than pretending to compete on surface area.
compare.positioning_sentence: cornac is a ~4,000-line MIT Python teaching harness that keeps only the parts of Claude Code, Codex and DeepSeek Harness that decide whether a tool runs (fail-closed permissions, vetoing hooks, privilege-preserving sub-agents) plus the scaffolding a small local model needs, and proves the point with a harness-only ablation that lifted a frozen 4B Ollama model from 12/27 to 26/27 on its own coding spike; it has no compaction, MCP, sandbox, CLI or public benchmark yet, and says so.
three_lines_for_the_user: Your safety core (fail-closed hooks, headless ASK becomes DENY, sub-agents sharing the parent's policy) is stricter than the defaults of Goose, OpenHands, OpenCode and Cline.
You lack three things almost every harness has: instruction-file loading, a saved transcript, and context compaction; the first two cost hours, do them before publishing.
The 12/27 to 26/27 ablation is the real differentiator; nobody publishes a frozen-4B-model harness ablation, so finish the ladder and benchmark before adding features.
